from unittest import TestCase

from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import models


class ValidationMessagesTest(TestCase):

    def _test_validation_messages(self, field, value, expected):
        with self.assertRaises(ValidationError) as cm:
            field.clean(value, None)
        self.assertEqual(cm.exception.messages, expected)

    def test_autofield_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be an integer."])

    def test_integer_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.IntegerField()
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be an integer."])

    def test_boolean_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.BooleanField()
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be either True or False."])

    def test_nullable_boolean_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.BooleanField(null=True)
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be either True, False, or None."])

    def test_float_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.FloatField()
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be a float."])

    def test_decimal_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.DecimalField()
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be a decimal number."])

    def test_null_boolean_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.NullBooleanField()
        self._test_validation_messages(f, 'fõo', ["'fõo' value must be either None, True or False."])

    def test_date_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.DateField()
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, 'fõo',
            ["'fõo' value has an invalid date format. It must be in YYYY-MM-DD format."]
        )
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, 'aaaa-10-10',
            ["'aaaa-10-10' value has an invalid date format. It must be in YYYY-MM-DD format."]
        )
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, '2011-13-10',
            ["'2011-13-10' value has the correct format (YYYY-MM-DD) but it is an invalid date."]
        )
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, '2011-10-32',
            ["'2011-10-32' value has the correct format (YYYY-MM-DD) but it is an invalid date."]
        )

    def test_datetime_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.DateTimeField()
        # Wrong format
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, 'fõo',
            ["'fõo' value has an invalid format. It must be in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:ss[.uuuuuu]][TZ] format."]
        )
        # Correct format but invalid date
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, '2011-10-32',
            ["'2011-10-32' value has the correct format (YYYY-MM-DD) but it is an invalid date."]
        )
        # Correct format but invalid date/time
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, '2011-10-32 10:10',
            ["'2011-10-32 10:10' value has the correct format (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:ss[.uuuuuu]][TZ]) "
             "but it is an invalid date/time."]
        )

    def test_time_field_raises_error_message(self):
        f = models.TimeField()
        # Wrong format
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, 'fõo',
            ["'fõo' value has an invalid format. It must be in HH:MM[:ss[.uuuuuu]] format."]
        )
        # Correct format but invalid time
        self._test_validation_messages(
            f, '25:50',
            ["'25:50' value has the correct format (HH:MM[:ss[.uuuuuu]]) but it is an invalid time."]
        )

  - I read the whole file (complete; it is short).
  - Important regex: standard_duration_re:

    r'^'
    r'(?:(?P<days>-?\d+) (days?, )?)?'
    r'(?P<sign>-?)'
    r'((?:(?P<hours>\d+):)(?=\d+:\d+))?'
    r'(?:(?P<minutes>\d+):)?'
    r'(?P<seconds>\d+)'
    r'(?:\.(?P<microseconds>\d{1,6})\d{0,6})?'
    r'$'

  - Analysis of regex:
    - days optional: an integer optionally followed by " day(s), "
    - sign optional: +/- sign before times
    - hours part: ((?:(?P<hours>\d+):)(?=\d+:\d+))? — the hours group is optional, but only matched if the remaining string matches the lookahead (?=\d+:\d+). That ensures hours: is only considered when there are at least two more colon-separated elements (i.e., hours:mm:ss). This prevents interpreting "14:00" as hours:seconds.
    - minutes part: (?:(?P<minutes>\d+):)? — minutes optional (a single group), but in combination with hours lookahead it's only hours if the input contains hours followed by minutes and seconds; otherwise a single "A:B" will be matched as minutes:seconds (i.e., '14:00' -> minutes=14, seconds=0).
    - seconds: (?P<seconds>\d+) — seconds are mandatory.
    - microseconds: optional .micro up to 6 digits.
  - Other regexes support ISO 8601 and PostgreSQL interval forms.
  - Hardcoded numbers: \d{1,6} for microseconds (Django supports up to 6 digits per python datetime microsecond resolution), other \d+ are flexible.
  - Conclusion: The parser requires seconds always, minutes optional, hours optional when the input includes two colon-separated groups after hours (hours:minutes:seconds). This matches the bug report's observations.

bug_report.Title: DurationField: user-facing invalid-format message shows wrong duration syntax
bug_report.Description: The error message shown for models.DurationField reports an incorrect accepted-format string. Example: entering "14:00" is parsed as "00:14:00" (14 minutes) by the parser, but the model-level invalid-format message shown to users says the format is "[DD] [HH:[MM:]]ss[.uuuuuu]", which does not match the parser's actual requirements. The DurationField class also does not provide a default help_text for forms/admin to indicate the expected syntax.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect hardcoded human-facing format string in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, class DurationField, attribute default_error_messages['invalid']. Current value (exact text found in code): "'%(value)s' value has an invalid format. It must be in [DD] [HH:[MM:]]ss[.uuuuuu] format." (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py, lines 1588–1591). The hardcoded string is inconsistent with parsing/serialization behavior and is the direct source of the misleading message observed by users.

2) The authoritative parser behavior (django/utils/dateparse.py: standard_duration_re / parse_duration) requires seconds and allows minutes optionally; hours are only matched when the input is in HH:MM:SS form. Evidence in the regex: the seconds group is mandatory (?P<seconds>\d+) (line 35), minutes are optional (?:(?P<minutes>\d+):)? (line 34), and the hours group is guarded by a lookahead ((?:(?P<hours>\d+):)(?=\d+:\d+))? so hours only match when followed by two colon-separated groups (line 33). This parser behavior is the source-of-truth for accepted input formats (django/utils/dateparse.py, lines 29–37 and parse_duration usage lines 133–147).

3) The serializer/formatter (django/utils/duration.py: duration_string) emits strings as "{:02d}:{:02d}:{:02d}" with optional leading days and optional ".uuuuuu" for microseconds (lines 22–26). That output always includes seconds and is consistent with the parser's requirement that seconds are present; this alignment confirms the fault is the human-facing message rather than parsing/serialization.

4) DurationField does not supply a default user-facing help_text describing the accepted format. The DurationField class does not override __init__ and therefore uses Field.__init__ default help_text (empty string); there is no default help_text specific to DurationField in the inspected code (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py: DurationField class, lines 1580–1638).

5) Forms-level DurationField (django/forms/fields.py: DurationField) uses a generic invalid message ('Enter a valid duration.') and delegates parsing to parse_duration (lines 469–495). While the forms field correctly delegates to the authoritative parser, it does not expose the detailed format string to users; the inconsistent model-level message is therefore the main misleading string at model validation time.

6) Tests that would detect this wording mismatch are not present in the inspected test module for field error messages: tests/validation/test_error_messages.py contains many checks for other temporal field messages (DateField, DateTimeField, TimeField) but does not assert DurationField's invalid-format message or form help_text (tests/validation/test_error_messages.py, lines 1–91). This increases the risk of the incorrect message persisting undetected.
StepsToReproduce: Create a model with a DurationField (or use an existing model with a DurationField).
In a ModelForm or the admin, enter the string "14:00" into the duration field and submit/save.

Observe the parsed/stored value (the parser interprets "14:00" as 00:14:00 i.e., 14 minutes) and the validation error/help text shown to the user (the model invalid-format message displays "[DD] [HH:[MM:]]ss[.uuuuuu]").
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: User-visible validation messages and any default help_text for DurationField should correctly describe the syntax actually accepted by the parser/serializer — i.e., that seconds are mandatory, minutes are optional, and hours are optional except when the input is provided as HH:MM:SS. The format presented to users (error message / help text) should match the parser/serializer behavior, for example as the bracketed form: "[DD] [[HH:]MM:]ss[.uuuuuu]".
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The model-level invalid-format message for DurationField currently states "[DD] [HH:[MM:]]ss[.uuuuuu]", which is inconsistent with the parser/serializer behavior (seconds mandatory, minutes optional, hours only for HH:MM:SS). The forms-level DurationField uses a generic 'Enter a valid duration.' message and DurationField provides no default help_text, so users do not receive a correct, specific format hint. ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator use the regex 
r'^[\w.@+-]+$'

r'\A[\w.@+-]+\Z'

bug_report.Title: UsernameValidator allows trailing newline in usernames
bug_report.Description: ASCIIUsernameValidator and UnicodeUsernameValidator accept usernames that end with a trailing newline because their class-level regex patterns use ^...$ anchors which, in Python, allow a match before a final newline.
bug_report.RootCause:
1. Incorrect end-of-string assumption in ASCIIUsernameValidator. Location: django/contrib/auth/validators.py — ASCIIUsernameValidator.regex is set to r'^[\w.@+-]+$'. Rationale: the pattern uses ^ and $ but $ can match immediately before a final '\n', so the validator's pattern does not enforce an absolute end-of-string in the presence of a trailing newline.

2. Incorrect end-of-string assumption repeated in UnicodeUsernameValidator. Location: django/contrib/auth/validators.py — UnicodeUsernameValidator.regex is set to r'^[\w.@+-]+$'. Rationale: same as (1); the pattern allows inputs that end with a newline.

3. Operational context that makes the anchors critical: RegexValidator applies the compiled regex via a search operation. Location: django/core/validators.py::RegexValidator (__init__ and __call__). Rationale: RegexValidator compiles regexes lazily and evaluates them with self.regex.search(str(value)), so the pattern itself must encode whole-string constraints; an internal $ anchor that can match before a final newline is insufficient to guarantee rejection of trailing-newline inputs.

4. Project convention and precedent for absolute anchors. Location: django/core/validators.py examples (e.g. URLValidator, integer_validator, slug_re and EmailValidator regexes) show use of \Z or equivalent to avoid $ newline behavior. Rationale: the codebase contains other validators that use anchors which do not treat a final newline as a match position, indicating the required matching semantics for strict full-string validation.

5. Missing test coverage for this edge case. Location: tests/auth_tests/test_validators.py — UsernameValidatorsTests exercises allowed/disallowed characters but contains no test asserting that usernames ending with '\n' are rejected. Rationale: absence of test coverage for trailing-newline inputs allows this behavior to persist unnoticed.

6. Operational impact because validators are used as defaults and are deconstructible. Location: django/contrib/auth/validators.py (classes are @deconstructible) and django/contrib/auth/models.py (AbstractUser.username_validator = UnicodeUsernameValidator()). Rationale: the validator instances are used by the User model and are deconstructible for migrations/serialization, so the validators' default behavior is surfaced in model validation and may affect migrations/serialized state.
StepsToReproduce: Instantiate UnicodeUsernameValidator() and call it with the value 'joe\n'. Observe whether a ValidationError is raised.
Instantiate ASCIIUsernameValidator() and call it with the value 'glenn\n'. Observe whether a ValidationError is raised.
Attempt to create or save a User (or another model field using the username validator) with username set to 'alice\n' and observe whether model validation allows it.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Usernames that end with a newline character are rejected by the username validators and produce a validation error when validating or saving user data.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Username validators accept strings that end with a newline (for example, 'joe\n' is considered valid), allowing creation or validation of usernames with trailing newlines.

bug_report.Title: HttpResponse mishandles memoryview/bytearray and returns repr bytes instead of underlying data
bug_report.Description: When a memoryview or bytearray is passed into HttpResponse (for example HttpResponse(memoryview(b"My Content"))), the response body becomes the object's repr encoded as bytes (b'<memory at 0x...>' or b"bytearray(...)") instead of the underlying binary data (b'My Content'). This typically occurs when database adapters (e.g. some PostgreSQL drivers) return binary fields as memoryview objects.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/http/response.py::HttpResponseBase.make_bytes — incorrect assumption: non-bytes, non-str values are treated as arbitrary objects and are stringified and encoded. The method's fallback is str(value).encode(self.charset), which causes memoryview or bytearray objects to be serialized to their Python repr when converted to response bytes (see make_bytes: fallback -> str(value).encode(...)).

2) django/http/response.py::HttpResponse.content (setter) — incorrect assumption: any object with __iter__ (except bytes and str) should be treated as an iterable of content chunks. The setter detects iterability via hasattr(value, '__iter__') and excludes only (bytes, str), causing memoryview and bytearray (both iterable) to be iterated and their elements to be joined as if they were chunk sequences (see content.setter: if hasattr(value, '__iter__') and not isinstance(value, (bytes, str)): content = b''.join(self.make_bytes(chunk) for chunk in value)).

3) Coupled behavior — both locations share the same root cause pattern (misclassification of bytes-like/buffer-like objects). Because make_bytes stringifies unexpected types and content.setter may pre-iterate buffer-like objects, both assumptions together cause the observed incorrect output. Either behavior alone can produce incorrect results for memoryview/bytearray inputs.

4) StreamingHttpResponse semantics (related edge case) — StreamingHttpResponse._set_streaming_content stores iter(value) and streaming_content maps make_bytes over that iterator. If a user passes a bare memoryview as streaming_content, iter(memoryview) yields element-wise items (integers/bytes), so the streaming response will process those items rather than treating the memoryview as a single bytes-like chunk. If the iterator yields memoryview objects (e.g., [memoryview(b'...')]), the chunk items would be memoryviews and treated according to make_bytes. This is a related API/semantics edge case (see StreamingHttpResponse._set_streaming_content and streaming_content property).

5) Test coverage gap — there are tests covering memoryview handling in utilities (force_bytes) and in certain model fields, but there are no unit tests in the repository exercising HttpResponse/StreamingHttpResponse constructed directly with memoryview or bytearray inputs (constructor, write/writelines, streaming_content as a bare memoryview). The lack of targeted tests allowed this behavior to go unnoticed by response-specific tests.
StepsToReproduce: from django.http import HttpResponse
response = HttpResponse("My Content")
inspect response.content  # shows b'My Content'
response = HttpResponse(b"My Content")
inspect response.content  # shows b'My Content'
response = HttpResponse(memoryview(b"My Content"))
inspect response.content  # shows b'<memory at 0x...>' (incorrect)
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When given bytes-like inputs (bytes, bytearray, memoryview), HttpResponse.content should contain the underlying binary data. Example: HttpResponse(memoryview(b"My Content")).content == b"My Content". Similarly, HttpResponse(bytearray(b"...")).content should equal the underlying bytes. For streaming responses, an iterable that yields memoryview objects should produce their underlying bytes when assembled; the behavior when a bare memoryview is passed as streaming_content is an API semantic to be clarified.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: HttpResponse(memoryview(b"My Content")).content returns the memoryview object's repr encoded as bytes (e.g. b"<memory at 0x7fcc47ab2648>") instead of b"My Content". Memoryview/bytearray are either stringified by make_bytes or iterated and joined by content.setter, producing incorrect output.

  - Symptom: Deleting a model instance with no dependencies doesn't clear the instance PK in-memory. The PK should be set to None after .delete().

- Diagnosis (clear statement of the bug and location):
  - The bug is in Collector.delete() in django/db/models/deletion.py. The special-case fast-path that deletes a single instance and returns early (lines ~274-281) performs the SQL delete by calling DeleteQuery.delete_batch and then returns immediately — it never clears the in-memory instance's PK. In the normal (non-fast-path) code path, the collector clears instance PKs at the end (setattr(instance, model._meta.pk.attname, None)), but the fast-path returns before that happens. So for a single instance with no dependencies and no signal listeners (the conditions for the fast-path), instance.pk remains pointing to the old value even though the row is gone from the DB. The primary responsible method/class: Collector.delete() in django/db/models/deletion.py.

bug_report.Title: Collector.delete fast-path does not clear in-memory instance PK after delete
bug_report.Description: Collector.delete contains a fast-path for deleting a single model instance with no dependencies that issues the database DELETE and returns before performing the per-instance in-memory cleanup. As a result, the in-memory instance retains its old primary key (pk) after calling .delete().
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Fast-path skips per-instance cleanup: The single-object fast-path in Collector.delete issues the SQL DELETE and returns without performing the in-memory cleanup that clears instance primary key attributes. Location: django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.delete (fast-path branch). Evidence: the code calls sql.DeleteQuery(model).delete_batch([instance.pk], self.using) inside transaction.mark_for_rollback_on_error() and immediately returns (see deletion.py lines 278–280), and does not call setattr(instance, model._meta.pk.attname, None) in that branch.

2) Non-fast-path performs explicit PK clearing: The normal delete path performs a final update of collected instances that sets per-instance PK attributes to None via setattr(instance, model._meta.pk.attname, None). Location: django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.delete (final cleanup loop). Evidence: the final cleanup loop sets the pk attr to None for each instance in self.data (see deletion.py lines 324–326).

3) Call sites rely on Collector.delete for post-delete in-memory state: Model.delete and QuerySet.delete invoke Collector.collect(...) and then return collector.delete(), and do not clear instance.pk themselves. Location(s): django/db/models/base.py :: Model.delete (lines 917–919) and django/db/models/query.py :: QuerySet.delete (lines 698–700). This means the omitted cleanup in the fast-path results in caller-visible instances retaining their old pk.

4) fast_deletes is a separate code path that was not fully audited here: Collector.fast_deletes collects queryset-like objects that are deleted via qs._raw_delete(...) during Collector.delete (deletion.py lines 290–293). Those objects are not part of self.data and so are not affected by the final self.data cleanup loop; the implications for in-memory state of caller-held instances related to fast_deletes were not fully audited in the investigation.

5) Observed return encoding at fast-path: The fast-path returns a tuple (count, {model._meta.label: count}) (deletion.py line 280). This is an observed behavior of the fast-path branch (an encoded return shape) and is part of the current implementation at that location.

6) Investigation gaps (audit notes): The prior investigation did not (a) fully audit interactions between the fast-path and Collector.fast_deletes to confirm any additional in-memory cleanup needs, (b) fully verify semantics with pre_delete/post_delete signal handlers in all edge cases, and (c) provide an attached unit test demonstrating the in-memory pk becomes None (or not) after invoking the fast-path .delete(). These gaps affect confidence in the broader scope but do not change the primary diagnosis above.
StepsToReproduce: Define or use a Django model that has no related/dependent objects.
Create and save an instance of that model, e.g. obj = MyModel.objects.create(...).
Call obj.delete().
Inspect the in-memory instance's primary key, e.g. print(obj.pk) or assert obj.pk is None.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: After calling .delete() on a model instance with no dependencies, the instance's in-memory primary key (pk) should be cleared (None) to reflect that the database row no longer exists.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: After calling .delete() on a model instance with no dependencies using the fast-path, the in-memory instance's pk still holds the previous value (not None) even though the database row was deleted.

from django.db import migrations
from django.db.models import Q


def update_proxy_model_permissions(apps, schema_editor, reverse=False):
    """
    Update the content_type of proxy model permissions to use the ContentType
    of the proxy model.
    """
    Permission = apps.get_model('auth', 'Permission')
    ContentType = apps.get_model('contenttypes', 'ContentType')
    for Model in apps.get_models():
        opts = Model._meta
        if not opts.proxy:
            continue
        proxy_default_permissions_codenames = [
            '%s_%s' % (action, opts.model_name)
            for action in opts.default_permissions
        ]
        permissions_query = Q(codename__in=proxy_default_permissions_codenames)
        for codename, name in opts.permissions:
            permissions_query = permissions_query | Q(codename=codename, name=name)
        concrete_content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(Model, for_concrete_model=True)
        proxy_content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(Model, for_concrete_model=False)
        old_content_type = proxy_content_type if reverse else concrete_content_type
        new_content_type = concrete_content_type if reverse else proxy_content_type
        Permission.objects.filter(
            permissions_query,
            content_type=old_content_type,
        ).update(content_type=new_content_type)


def revert_proxy_model_permissions(apps, schema_editor):
    """
    Update the content_type of proxy model permissions to use the ContentType
    of the concrete model.
    """
    update_proxy_model_permissions(apps, schema_editor, reverse=True)


class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [
        ('auth', '0010_alter_group_name_max_length'),
        ('contenttypes', '0002_remove_content_type_name'),
    ]
    operations = [
        migrations.RunPython(update_proxy_model_permissions, revert_proxy_model_permissions),
    ]

def update_last_login(sender, user, **kwargs):
    """
    A signal receiver which updates the last_login date for
    the user logging in.
    """
    user.last_login = timezone.now()
    user.save(update_fields=['last_login'])

class Permission(models.Model):
    """
    The permissions system provides a way to assign permissions to specific
    users and groups of users.

    The permission system is used by the Django admin site, but may also be
    useful in your own code. The Django admin site uses permissions as follows:

        - The "add" permission limits the user's ability to view the "add" form
          and add an object.
        - The "change" permission limits a user's ability to view the change
          list, view the "change" form and change an object.
        - The "delete" permission limits the ability to delete an object.
        - The "view" permission limits the ability to view an object.

    Permissions are set globally per type of object, not per specific object
    instance. It is possible to say "Mary may change news stories," but it's
    not currently possible to say "Mary may change news stories, but only the
    ones she created herself" or "Mary may only change news stories that have a
    certain status or publication date."

    The permissions listed above are automatically created for each model.
    """
    name = models.CharField(_('name'), max_length=255)
    content_type = models.ForeignKey(
        ContentType,
        models.CASCADE,
        verbose_name=_('content type'),
    )
    codename = models.CharField(_('codename'), max_length=100)

    objects = PermissionManager()

    class Meta:
        verbose_name = _('permission')
        verbose_name_plural = _('permissions')
        unique_together = (('content_type', 'codename'),)
        ordering = ('content_type__app_label', 'content_type__model',
                    'codename')

    def __str__(self):
        return '%s | %s' % (self.content_type, self.name)

    def natural_key(self):
        return (self.codename,) + self.content_type.natural_key()
    natural_key.dependencies = ['contenttypes.contenttype']

class Group(models.Model):
    """
    Groups are a generic way of categorizing users to apply permissions, or
    some other label, to those users. A user can belong to any number of
    groups.

    A user in a group automatically has all the permissions granted to that
    group. For example, if the group 'Site editors' has the permission
    can_edit_home_page, any user in that group will have that permission.

    Beyond permissions, groups are a convenient way to categorize users to
    apply some label, or extended functionality, to them. For example, you
    could create a group 'Special users', and you could write code that would
    do special things to those users -- such as giving them access to a
    members-only portion of your site, or sending them members-only email
    messages.
    """
    name = models.CharField(_('name'), max_length=150, unique=True)
    permissions = models.ManyToManyField(
        Permission,
        verbose_name=_('permissions'),
        blank=True,
    )

    objects = GroupManager()

    class Meta:
        verbose_name = _('group')
        verbose_name_plural = _('groups')

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

    def natural_key(self):
        return (self.name,)


class UserManager(BaseUserManager):
    use_in_migrations = True

    def _create_user(self, username, email, password, **extra_fields):
        """
        Create and save a user with the given username, email, and password.
        """
        if not username:
            raise ValueError('The given username must be set')
        email = self.normalize_email(email)
        username = self.model.normalize_username(username)
        user = self.model(username=username, email=email, **extra_fields)
        user.set_password(password)
        user.save(using=self._db)
        return user

    def create_user(self, username, email=None, password=None, **extra_fields):
        extra_fields.setdefault('is_staff', False)
        extra_fields.setdefault('is_superuser', False)
        return self._create_user(username, email, password, **extra_fields)

    def create_superuser(self, username, email, password, **extra_fields):
        extra_fields.setdefault('is_staff', True)
        extra_fields.setdefault('is_superuser', True)

        if extra_fields.get('is_staff') is not True:
            raise ValueError('Superuser must have is_staff=True.')
        if extra_fields.get('is_superuser') is not True:
            raise ValueError('Superuser must have is_superuser=True.')

        return self._create_user(username, email, password, **extra_fields)


# A few helper functions for common logic between User and AnonymousUser.
def _user_get_all_permissions(user, obj):
    permissions = set()
    for backend in auth.get_backends():
        if hasattr(backend, "get_all_permissions"):
            permissions.update(backend.get_all_permissions(user, obj))
    return permissions


def _user_has_perm(user, perm, obj):
    """
    A backend can raise `PermissionDenied` to short-circuit permission checking.
    """
    for backend in auth.get_backends():
        if not hasattr(backend, 'has_perm'):
            continue
        try:
            if backend.has_perm(user, perm, obj):
                return True
        except PermissionDenied:
            return False
    return False


def _user_has_module_perms(user, app_label):
    """
    A backend can raise `PermissionDenied` to short-circuit permission checking.
    """
    for backend in auth.get_backends():
        if not hasattr(backend, 'has_module_perms'):
            continue
        try:
            if backend.has_module_perms(user, app_label):
                return True
        except PermissionDenied:
            return False
    return False


class PermissionsMixin(models.Model):
    """
    Add the fields and methods necessary to support the Group and Permission
    models using the ModelBackend.
    """
    is_superuser = models.BooleanField(
        _('superuser status'),
        default=False,
        help_text=_(
            'Designates that this user has all permissions without '
            'explicitly assigning them.'
        ),
    )
    groups = models.ManyToManyField(
        Group,
        verbose_name=_('groups'),
        blank=True,
        help_text=_(
            'The groups this user belongs to. A user will get all permissions '
            'granted to each of their groups.'
        ),
        related_name="user_set",
        related_query_name="user",
    )
    user_permissions = models.ManyToManyField(
        Permission,
        verbose_name=_('user permissions'),
        blank=True,
        help_text=_('Specific permissions for this user.'),
        related_name="user_set",
        related_query_name="user",
    )

    class Meta:
        abstract = True

    def get_group_permissions(self, obj=None):
        """
        Return a list of permission strings that this user has through their
        groups. Query all available auth backends. If an object is passed in,
        return only permissions matching this object.
        """
        permissions = set()
        for backend in auth.get_backends():
            if hasattr(backend, "get_group_permissions"):
                permissions.update(backend.get_group_permissions(self, obj))
        return permissions

    def get_all_permissions(self, obj=None):
        return _user_get_all_permissions(self, obj)

    def has_perm(self, perm, obj=None):
        """
        Return True if the user has the specified permission. Query all
        available auth backends, but return immediately if any backend returns
        True. Thus, a user who has permission from a single auth backend is
        assumed to have permission in general. If an object is provided, check
        permissions for that object.
        """
        # Active superusers have all permissions.
        if self.is_active and self.is_superuser:
            return True

        # Otherwise we need to check the backends.
        return _user_has_perm(self, perm, obj)

    def has_perms(self, perm_list, obj=None):
        """
        Return True if the user has each of the specified permissions. If
        object is passed, check if the user has all required perms for it.
        """
        return all(self.has_perm(perm, obj) for perm in perm_list)

    def has_module_perms(self, app_label):
        """
        Return True if the user has any permissions in the given app label.
        Use similar logic as has_perm(), above.
        """
        # Active superusers have all permissions.
        if self.is_active and self.is_superuser:
            return True

        return _user_has_module_perms(self, app_label)


class AbstractUser(AbstractBaseUser, PermissionsMixin):
    """
    An abstract base class implementing a fully featured User model with
    admin-compliant permissions.

    Username and password are required. Other fields are optional.
    """
    username_validator = UnicodeUsernameValidator()

    username = models.CharField(
        _('username'),
        max_length=150,
        unique=True,
        help_text=_('Required. 150 characters or fewer. Letters, digits and @/./+/-/_ only.'),
        validators=[username_validator],
        error_messages={
            'unique': _("A user with that username already exists."),
        },
    )
    first_name = models.CharField(_('first name'), max_length=30, blank=True)
    last_name = models.CharField(_('last name'), max_length=150, blank=True)
    email = models.EmailField(_('email address'), blank=True)
    is_staff = models.BooleanField(
        _('staff status'),
        default=False,
        help_text=_('Designates whether the user can log into this admin site.'),
    )
    is_active = models.BooleanField(
        _('active'),
        default=True,
        help_text=_(
            'Designates whether this user should be treated as active. '
            'Unselect this instead of deleting accounts.'
        ),
    )
    date_joined = models.DateTimeField(_('date joined'), default=timezone.now)

    objects = UserManager()

    EMAIL_FIELD = 'email'
    USERNAME_FIELD = 'username'
    REQUIRED_FIELDS = ['email']

    class Meta:
        verbose_name = _('user')
        verbose_name_plural = _('users')
        abstract = True

    def clean(self):
        super().clean()
        self.email = self.__class__.objects.normalize_email(self.email)

    def get_full_name(self):
        """
        Return the first_name plus the last_name, with a space in between.
        """
        full_name = '%s %s' % (self.first_name, self.last_name)
        return full_name.strip()

    def get_short_name(self):
        """Return the short name for the user."""
        return self.first_name

    def email_user(self, subject, message, from_email=None, **kwargs):
        """Send an email to this user."""
        send_mail(subject, message, from_email, [self.email], **kwargs)


class User(AbstractUser):
    """
    Users within the Django authentication system are represented by this
    model.

    Username and password are required. Other fields are optional.

    class Meta(AbstractUser.Meta):

class SwappableTuple(tuple):
    """
    Subclass of tuple so Django can tell this was originally a swappable
    dependency when it reads the migration file.
    """

    def __new__(cls, value, setting):
        self = tuple.__new__(cls, value)
        self.setting = setting
        return self


def swappable_dependency(value):
    """Turn a setting value into a dependency."""
    return SwappableTuple((value.split(".", 1)[0], "__first__"), value)

  def update_proxy_model_permissions(apps, schema_editor, reverse=False):
      Permission = apps.get_model('auth', 'Permission')
      ContentType = apps.get_model('contenttypes', 'ContentType')
      # Iterate proxy models
      for Model in apps.get_models():
          opts = Model._meta
          if not opts.proxy:
              continue
          # Build permissions_query (same as before)
          proxy_default_permissions_codenames = [
              '%s_%s' % (action, opts.model_name)
              for action in opts.default_permissions
          ]
          permissions_query = Q(codename__in=proxy_default_permissions_codenames)
          for codename, name in opts.permissions:
              permissions_query = permissions_query | Q(codename=codename, name=name)
          concrete_content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(Model, for_concrete_model=True)
          proxy_content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(Model, for_concrete_model=False)
          old_content_type = proxy_content_type if reverse else concrete_content_type
          new_content_type = concrete_content_type if reverse else proxy_content_type

          # Iterate matching Permission rows and safely move/merge them.
          # Using list() to evaluate queryset now to avoid DB cursor issues while modifying rows.
          for perm in list(Permission.objects.filter(permissions_query, content_type=old_content_type)):
              # If a permission with same codename already exists for new_content_type,
              # move relations and delete the old permission to avoid duplicate key.
              try:
                  existing = Permission.objects.get(content_type=new_content_type, codename=perm.codename)
              except Permission.DoesNotExist:
                  # safe to change content_type
                  perm.content_type = new_content_type
                  perm.save()
              else:
                  # Transfer user and group relations without creating duplicates.
                  # perm.user_set and perm.group_set are the reverse related managers.
                  for user in perm.user_set.all():

                  for group in perm.group_set.all():
                      if not existing.group_set.filter(pk=group.pk).exists():
                          existing.group_set.add(group)
                  # Delete the old permission
                  perm.delete()

            perm.delete()

- We use the reverse related managers perm.user_set and perm.group_set (as defined in the Permission/User/Group models) to find current assignments and move them to the existing permission.

bug_report.Title: auth.0011_update_proxy_permissions migration fails with IntegrityError when target permission already exists
bug_report.Description: When applying Django auth migration 0011_update_proxy_permissions, the migration can raise an IntegrityError because it attempts to change Permission.content_type in bulk and thereby produce a duplicate (content_type, codename) pair that violates the Permission model's uniqueness constraint.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) The migration function update_proxy_model_permissions in django/contrib/auth/migrations/0011_update_proxy_permissions.py performs a bulk update of Permission.content_type via Permission.objects.filter(...).update(content_type=new_content_type). This encodes an incorrect assumption that bulk-updating the content_type cannot produce duplicate (content_type, codename) pairs. (location: django/contrib/auth/migrations/0011_update_proxy_permissions.py, lines 27–30)

2) The Permission model enforces uniqueness on (content_type, codename) via Meta.unique_together = (('content_type', 'codename'),). The database enforces this invariant and will reject any operation that results in two Permission rows with the same (content_type, codename). (location: django/contrib/auth/models.py, line 69)

3) If a Permission with the target (new_content_type, codename) already exists prior to running the migration, the bulk update will attempt to change the old Permission's content_type to new_content_type and thereby create a duplicate row, causing a database IntegrityError. The original error reported is an IntegrityError for duplicate key on (content_type_id, codename) (e.g. Key (content_type_id, codename)=(12, add_agency) already exists). (evidence: original stacktrace; migration file lines 27–30)

4) The migration uses the same update function for both applying and unapplying the migration: revert_proxy_model_permissions calls update_proxy_model_permissions(apps, schema_editor, reverse=True). Therefore the same bulk-update assumption affects both forward and reverse migration paths. (location: django/contrib/auth/migrations/0011_update_proxy_permissions.py, lines 33–38)

5) The test coverage in tests/auth_tests/test_migrations.py sets up permission rows pointing at the concrete model and exercises the code path where the bulk update is safe; the tests do not create a pre-existing conflicting Permission at the proxy content_type and therefore do not exercise the duplicate-collision scenario. This gap in test coverage means the unsafe bulk-update assumption was not caught by the existing tests. (location: tests/auth_tests/test_migrations.py, e.g. setUp() creating permissions with content_type=self.concrete_content_type)

6) Any handling of colliding permissions is constrained by many-to-many relationships between User/Group and Permission (User.user_permissions and Group.permissions are ManyToManyFields). These M2M relations imply through-table uniqueness semantics for (user_id, permission_id) and (group_id, permission_id) and must be accounted for by any operation that merges or replaces Permission rows. The code locations that illustrate these relations are in django/contrib/auth/models.py where the ManyToManyFields to Permission are defined. (location: django/contrib/auth/models.py, lines 109–113 and 224–231)
StepsToReproduce: Have a Django project containing the auth and contenttypes apps and a migration state before auth.0011_update_proxy_permissions has been applied.

Ensure there are two ContentType rows for a model: the concrete model content_type and the proxy model content_type (for example, when a model has been recreated as a proxy or when proxy content types already exist).

Create or ensure there exists a Permission with codename X for the proxy content_type (the migration's target content_type), and at least one Permission with the same codename X for the concrete content_type (the migration's source content_type).
Run python manage.py migrate (or python manage.py migrate auth 0011).
Observe an IntegrityError raised for duplicate key on the unique (content_type, codename) constraint (e.g. Key (content_type_id, codename)=(12, add_agency) already exists).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The auth.0011_update_proxy_permissions migration completes without raising an IntegrityError. If a permission with the target (content_type, codename) already exists, the migration does not result in duplicate (content_type, codename) rows and preserves the intended user/group permission assignments (so users/groups retain the correct permissions after the migration).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Running the migration raises a django.db.utils.IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint on auth_permission unique index (unique on (content_type_id, codename)). Example: Key (content_type_id, codename)=(12, add_agency) already exists. The migration triggers this by performing a bulk update of Permission.content_type that can produce duplicate (content_type, codename) pairs.

class TestIterModulesAndFiles(SimpleTestCase):
    def import_and_cleanup(self, name):
        import_module(name)
        self.addCleanup(lambda: sys.path_importer_cache.clear())
        self.addCleanup(lambda: sys.modules.pop(name, None))

    def clear_autoreload_caches(self):
        autoreload.iter_modules_and_files.cache_clear()

    def assertFileFound(self, filename):
        # Some temp directories are symlinks. Python resolves these fully while
        # importing.
        resolved_filename = filename.resolve()
        self.clear_autoreload_caches()
        # Test uncached access
        self.assertIn(resolved_filename, list(autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files()))
        # Test cached access
        self.assertIn(resolved_filename, list(autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files()))
        self.assertEqual(autoreload.iter_modules_and_files.cache_info().hits, 1)

    def assertFileNotFound(self, filename):
        resolved_filename = filename.resolve()
        self.clear_autoreload_caches()
        # Test uncached access
        self.assertNotIn(resolved_filename, list(autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files()))
        # Test cached access
        self.assertNotIn(resolved_filename, list(autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files()))
        self.assertEqual(autoreload.iter_modules_and_files.cache_info().hits, 1)

    def temporary_file(self, filename):
        dirname = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        self.addCleanup(shutil.rmtree, dirname)
        return Path(dirname) / filename

    def test_paths_are_pathlib_instances(self):
        for filename in autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files():
            self.assertIsInstance(filename, Path)

    def test_file_added(self):
        """
        When a file is added, it's returned by iter_all_python_module_files().
        """
        filename = self.temporary_file('test_deleted_removed_module.py')
        filename.touch()

        with extend_sys_path(str(filename.parent)):
            self.import_and_cleanup('test_deleted_removed_module')

        self.assertFileFound(filename.absolute())

    def test_check_errors(self):
        """
        When a file containing an error is imported in a function wrapped by
        check_errors(), gen_filenames() returns it.
        """
        filename = self.temporary_file('test_syntax_error.py')
        filename.write_text("Ceci n'est pas du Python.")

        with extend_sys_path(str(filename.parent)):
            with self.assertRaises(SyntaxError):
                autoreload.check_errors(import_module)('test_syntax_error')
        self.assertFileFound(filename)

    def test_check_errors_catches_all_exceptions(self):
        """
        Since Python may raise arbitrary exceptions when importing code,
        check_errors() must catch Exception, not just some subclasses.
        """
        filename = self.temporary_file('test_exception.py')
        filename.write_text('raise Exception')
        with extend_sys_path(str(filename.parent)):
            with self.assertRaises(Exception):
                autoreload.check_errors(import_module)('test_exception')
        self.assertFileFound(filename)

    def test_zip_reload(self):
        """
        Modules imported from zipped files have their archive location included
        in the result.
        """
        zip_file = self.temporary_file('zip_import.zip')
        with zipfile.ZipFile(str(zip_file), 'w', zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zipf:
            zipf.writestr('test_zipped_file.py', '')

        with extend_sys_path(str(zip_file)):
            self.import_and_cleanup('test_zipped_file')
        self.assertFileFound(zip_file)

    def test_bytecode_conversion_to_source(self):
        """.pyc and .pyo files are included in the files list."""
        filename = self.temporary_file('test_compiled.py')
        filename.touch()
        compiled_file = Path(py_compile.compile(str(filename), str(filename.with_suffix('.pyc'))))
        filename.unlink()
        with extend_sys_path(str(compiled_file.parent)):
            self.import_and_cleanup('test_compiled')
        self.assertFileFound(compiled_file)

    def test_weakref_in_sys_module(self):
        """iter_all_python_module_file() ignores weakref modules."""
        time_proxy = weakref.proxy(time)
        sys.modules['time_proxy'] = time_proxy
        self.addCleanup(lambda: sys.modules.pop('time_proxy', None))
        list(autoreload.iter_all_python_module_files())  # No crash.

    def test_module_without_spec(self):
        module = types.ModuleType('test_module')
        del module.__spec__
        self.assertEqual(autoreload.iter_modules_and_files((module,), frozenset()), frozenset())

class TestSysPathDirectories(SimpleTestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self._directory = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
        self.directory = Path(self._directory.name).resolve().absolute()
        self.file = self.directory / 'test'
        self.file.touch()

    def tearDown(self):
        self._directory.cleanup()

    def test_sys_paths_with_directories(self):
        with extend_sys_path(str(self.file)):
            paths = list(autoreload.sys_path_directories())
        self.assertIn(self.file.parent, paths)

    def test_sys_paths_non_existing(self):
        nonexistent_file = Path(self.directory.name) / 'does_not_exist'
        with extend_sys_path(str(nonexistent_file)):
            paths = list(autoreload.sys_path_directories())
        self.assertNotIn(nonexistent_file, paths)
        self.assertNotIn(nonexistent_file.parent, paths)

    def test_sys_paths_absolute(self):
        paths = list(autoreload.sys_path_directories())
        self.assertTrue(all(p.is_absolute() for p in paths))

    def test_sys_paths_directories(self):
        with extend_sys_path(str(self.directory)):
            paths = list(autoreload.sys_path_directories())
        self.assertIn(self.directory, paths)

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def iter_modules_and_files(modules, extra_files):
    """Iterate through all modules needed to be watched."""
    sys_file_paths = []
    for module in modules:
        # During debugging (with PyDev) the 'typing.io' and 'typing.re' objects
        # are added to sys.modules, however they are types not modules and so
        # cause issues here.
        if not isinstance(module, ModuleType) or getattr(module, '__spec__', None) is None:
            continue
        spec = module.__spec__
        # Modules could be loaded from places without a concrete location. If
        # this is the case, skip them.
        if spec.has_location:
            origin = spec.loader.archive if isinstance(spec.loader, zipimporter) else spec.origin
            sys_file_paths.append(origin)

    results = set()
    for filename in itertools.chain(sys_file_paths, extra_files):
        if not filename:
            continue
        path = pathlib.Path(filename)
        if not path.exists():
            # The module could have been removed, don't fail loudly if this
            # is the case.
            continue
        results.add(path.resolve().absolute())
    return frozenset(results)

bug_report.Title: Autoreloader (StatReloader) does not detect edits to top-level script (manage.py)
bug_report.Description: When running the development server (python manage.py runserver) under Django 2.2.1, edits to the top-level script manage.py are not detected by the autoreloader. The autoreload log never lists manage.py, so the server does not reload after modifying that file.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/utils/autoreload.py:iter_modules_and_files — The function unconditionally skips modules for which getattr(module, '__spec__', None) is None. Concretely, the code uses:

    if not isinstance(module, ModuleType) or getattr(module, '__spec__', None) is None:
        continue

   This causes modules executed as top-level scripts (the __main__ module), which commonly have __spec__ == None but do have a concrete __file__ path, to be ignored. As a result, those scripts' file paths are not collected by this generator.

2) django/utils/autoreload.py:iter_all_python_module_files and BaseReloader.watched_files — iter_all_python_module_files() produces its module list from sys.modules and forwards it to iter_modules_and_files(); BaseReloader.watched_files() yields from iter_all_python_module_files(). Because iter_modules_and_files omitted __main__/script modules, those scripts are not included in the watched_files() generator.

3) django/utils/autoreload.py:StatReloader.snapshot_files and StatReloader.tick (and WatchmanReloader._update_watches) — snapshot_files() iterates the Paths yielded by watched_files() and calls file.stat(); tick() compares mtimes and triggers reloads. WatchmanReloader._update_watches() also calls watched_files(include_globs=False) to compute subscriptions. When iter_modules_and_files omits a script file, it is never stat()'d or subscribed to, so edits to that file do not trigger reload events.

4) Wrong assumption encoded: the code treats module.__spec__ is None as sufficient evidence that a module has no concrete file location. The correct diagnostic relationship (from the investigation) is: if a module exposes a concrete __file__ attribute (a filesystem path), that path should be considered for watching even when module.__spec__ is None. Tests that construct ModuleType objects with no __spec__ and no __file__ are still valid and should continue to be ignored; the distinction is whether module.__file__ exists and points to a real path.
StepsToReproduce: Install Django 2.2.1 in a Python 3 environment (e.g. pip install Django==2.2.1).
Start the development server: python manage.py runserver
Edit manage.py (for example, add a print() call) and save the file.
Observe whether the server reloads. Check django.utils.autoreload log output for inclusion of manage.py.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When manage.py is modified while the development server is running, the autoreloader should detect the file change and restart the server. The autoreload logs should list manage.py as a watched file and a reload should occur after saving changes.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Under Django 2.2.1, modifying manage.py does not cause a reload. The autoreload logs do not list manage.py and the running server continues without restarting after edits to the top-level script.

class LimitedStream:

    def __init__(self, stream, limit, buf_size=64 * 1024 * 1024):

        self.buf_size = buf_size

    def _read_limited(self, size=None):

            size = self.remaining

        elif size < len(self.buffer):

        script_name = script_url[:-len(path_info)] if path_info else script_url

    return value.encode('iso-8859-1')

    key and default should be str objects.

    value = get_bytes_from_wsgi(environ, key, default)

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured
from django.urls import re_path

def static(prefix, view=serve, **kwargs):
    """
    Return a URL pattern for serving files in debug mode.

    from django.conf import settings
    from django.conf.urls.static import static

    urlpatterns = [
        # ... the rest of your URLconf goes here ...
    ] + static(settings.MEDIA_URL, document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT)
    """

    elif not settings.DEBUG or urlsplit(prefix).netloc:

        return []
    return [
        re_path(r'^%s(?P<path>.*)$' % re.escape(prefix.lstrip('/')), view, kwargs=kwargs),
    ]

Root cause (concise)
- Code generating and matching static/media URLs treats settings.STATIC_URL and settings.MEDIA_URL as complete prefixes and does not account for the runtime, thread-local SCRIPT_NAME (get_script_prefix()). Since WSGI/ASGI handlers set the script prefix per-request, code must apply that dynamic prefix to runtime URL generation and to runtime URL parsing/matching. Several places used settings.STATIC_URL without considering script prefix leading to mismatches when an application is mounted at a subpath.

- Fix: compute effective base prior to joining:
  - If base starts with '/' and not '//', compute script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
  - If script_prefix is not '/', and base doesn't already start with script_prefix + '/', then set base = script_prefix + base
  - Then return urljoin(base, filepath)
- Reason for not changing base_url cached_property: base_url should reflect configured setting (settings.*). The runtime script prefix must not be cached globally because script prefix is request-local; url() must compute prefix at call time to remain thread-safe.

5) django/conf/urls/static.py (static())
- Current behavior: builds regex from prefix parameter (often settings.MEDIA_URL) by using prefix.lstrip('/'), but prefix lacks script prefix.

### Location: django/core/files/storage.py:FileSystemStorage.url
- Wrong assumption: self.base_url (from settings.MEDIA_URL / STATIC_URL) is the full, site-visible prefix and already contains any SCRIPT_NAME.
- Evidence: FileSystemStorage.url implementation computes:
  - url = filepath_to_uri(name); url = url.lstrip('/')
  - return urljoin(self.base_url, url)
  No call to django.urls.get_script_prefix() and no check for relative vs absolute base_url. (See file: django/core/files/storage.py lines ~329–335.)
- Related locations: django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py::StaticFilesStorage (initializes base_url from settings.STATIC_URL), django/templatetags/static.py::StaticNode (calls staticfiles_storage.url), any code calling storage.url() (e.g., HashedFilesMixin, staticfiles view code).

Concrete fix (exact formula/code to insert):
- Import: from django.urls import get_script_prefix
- Compute effective_base:
  - if base.startswith('/') and not base.startswith('//'):
      script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
      if script_prefix and not base.startswith(script_prefix + '/'):
          base = script_prefix + base
- Then return urljoin(base, url)

### Location: django/templatetags/static.py:PrefixNode.handle_simple
- Wrong assumption: settings.<name> (STATIC_URL or MEDIA_URL) is the site-visible prefix and may be returned directly to templates.
- Evidence: handle_simple currently does:
  - prefix = iri_to_uri(getattr(settings, name, ''))
  - return prefix
  No use of get_script_prefix(). (See django/templatetags/static.py lines ~40–47.)
- Related locations: django/templatetags/static.py::StaticNode.handle_simple fallback path (urljoin(PrefixNode.handle_simple("STATIC_URL"), quote(path))) and template usage of {% get_static_prefix %} or {% static %} when staticfiles app is not installed.

Concrete fix:
- After computing prefix = iri_to_uri(getattr(settings, name, '')):
  - if prefix.startswith('/') and not prefix.startswith('//'):
      script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
      if script_prefix and not prefix.startswith(script_prefix + '/'):
          prefix = script_prefix + prefix
- Return modified prefix.

### Location: django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py:HashedFilesMixin.url_converter
- Wrong assumption: CSS/JS URLs to be rewritten will start with settings.STATIC_URL (raw setting) and slicing target_name = url_path[len(settings.STATIC_URL):] is correct.
- Evidence: url_converter contains:
  - if url.startswith('/') and not url.startswith(settings.STATIC_URL): return matched
  - later: assert url_path.startswith(settings.STATIC_URL); target_name = url_path[len(settings.STATIC_URL):]
  These checks fail when runtime URLs are prefixed with get_script_prefix() (e.g., '/prefix/static/...') because settings.STATIC_URL == '/static/'. (See django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py lines ~171–181.)
- Related locations: FileSystemStorage.url (generation), staticfiles post-processing pipeline that relies on url_converter, templates that embed CSS urls.

Concrete fix:
- Compute static_prefix = settings.STATIC_URL
  - if static_prefix.startswith('/') and not static_prefix.startswith('//'):
      script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
      if script_prefix and not static_prefix.startswith(script_prefix + '/'):
          static_prefix = script_prefix + static_prefix
- Replace uses of settings.STATIC_URL in url_converter with static_prefix:
  - if url.startswith('/') and not url.startswith(static_prefix): return matched
  - assert url_path.startswith(static_prefix)
  - target_name = url_path[len(static_prefix):]

### Location: django/contrib/staticfiles/handlers.py:StaticFilesHandlerMixin.get_base_url
- Wrong assumption: settings.STATIC_URL (raw) is the correct base that the request.path will be compared to.
- Evidence: get_base_url returns settings.STATIC_URL; later __init__ does urlparse(self.get_base_url()) and _should_handle compares request path to self.base_url[2] (the path part). If request path is '/prefix/static/..' and settings.STATIC_URL == '/static/', path.startswith(self.base_url[2]) fails. (See django/contrib/staticfiles/handlers.py lines ~26–36.)
- Related locations: django/contrib/staticfiles/handlers.py::StaticFilesHandler._should_handle and file_path, django/contrib/staticfiles/views. Also related to static() URL patterns.

Concrete fix:
- Compute base = settings.STATIC_URL
  - if base.startswith('/') and not base.startswith('//'):
      script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
      if script_prefix and not base.startswith(script_prefix + '/'):
          base = script_prefix + base
- Return base (so self.base_url becomes urlparse(base) and path comparison works).

### Location: django/conf/urls/static.py:static
- Wrong assumption: the prefix passed (often settings.MEDIA_URL) is already the complete, request-visible prefix used to build URL regex (no script-prefix needed).
- Evidence: function builds a re_path using prefix.lstrip('/') and checks urlsplit(prefix).netloc to skip non-local prefixes. If the actual request path is '/prefix/media/...' but prefix is '/media/', returned URL pattern r'^media/(?P<path>.*)$' will not match. (See django/conf/urls/static.py lines ~21–27.)
- Related locations: places that call static(settings.MEDIA_URL, ...), runserver auto-added urlpatterns, dev server behavior.

Concrete fix:
- Before netloc check and pattern creation, if prefix.startswith('/') and not prefix.startswith('//'):
  - script_prefix = get_script_prefix().rstrip('/')
  - if script_prefix and not prefix.startswith(script_prefix + '/'):
      prefix = script_prefix + prefix
- Continue existing behavior (no change for absolute URLs).

### Location: django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py:StaticFilesStorage.__init__
- Wrong assumption (evidence of origin): StaticFilesStorage.__init__ sets base_url = settings.STATIC_URL and passes to FileSystemStorage.__init__, which caches base_url based on the configuration only; runtime prefix not applied here. (See django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py lines ~23–29.)
- Evidence: base_url is derived from settings at storage initialization, not per-request.
- Related locations: FileSystemStorage.base_url cached_property, staticfiles_storage lazy object configuration.

Fix guidance (not to change cached_property):
- Do NOT mutate storage.base_url cached_property at initialization because get_script_prefix is request-local. Instead apply script prefix at storage.url() call-time (see FileSystemStorage.url fix). This avoids incorrect cross-request cached behavior.

bug_report.Title: Runtime SCRIPT_NAME not applied to STATIC_URL/MEDIA_URL — generated and matched static/media URLs miss SCRIPT_NAME
bug_report.Description: When a Django application is mounted under a runtime SCRIPT_NAME (a WSGI/ASGI script prefix), URLs produced from settings.STATIC_URL or settings.MEDIA_URL (templates, storage.url(), staticfiles post-processing, dev static handler, and URL pattern helpers) are not prefixed with the runtime SCRIPT_NAME. As a result, generated static/media URLs and dev-server URL matching can be inconsistent with request paths when the app runs under a subpath.
bug_report.RootCause:
Multiple parts of Django assume that the configured settings.STATIC_URL or settings.MEDIA_URL are already the full, request-visible prefixes and use them verbatim for URL generation, matching, or slicing. The runtime script prefix (get_script_prefix()) is thread/request-local and is not applied in these call sites; moreover some components cache the configured base at initialization. Each finding below is an independent manifestation of the same incorrect assumption (all findings are equally important):

1) File-system storage URL generation assumes a pre-prefixed base_url.
   - Location: django/core/files/storage.py::FileSystemStorage.base_url and FileSystemStorage.url
   - Evidence: base_url is resolved from self._base_url or settings.MEDIA_URL (cached_property) and FileSystemStorage.url returns urljoin(self.base_url, ...). This uses the stored base_url value at call-time with no reference to the runtime script prefix.

2) Staticfiles storage initialization bakes the configured STATIC_URL into instance state.
   - Location: django/contrib/staticfiles/storage.py::StaticFilesStorage.__init__ (and FileSystemStorage.base_url)

- The runtime-visible prefix used when generating or matching URLs is the effective prefix computed from the configured STATIC_URL or MEDIA_URL together with the runtime script prefix (get_script_prefix()). - Guard the Path.resolve() calls used to turn candidate filenames into resolved Path objects so that ValueError: embedded null byte (and any similar exceptions thrown by pathlib/os.readlink) does not crash the reloader. Specifically:
  - In iter_modules_and_files(), when calling path.resolve(strict=True).absolute(), catch ValueError in addition to FileNotFoundError and skip that filename.
  - In sys_path_directories(), when calling path.resolve(strict=True).absolute(), catch ValueError in addition to FileNotFoundError and skip that sys.path entry.

Rationale
- The stack trace shows os.readlink raised ValueError: embedded null byte. This originates from the stdlib pathlib resolve() when encountering a path component that causes os.readlink to get a string containing a NUL. The reloader must be robust against transiently-invalid filesystem entries (e.g., broken mount points, broken symlinks, or platform-specific filesystem glitches); it should skip problematic paths rather than crashing the whole process.

- File: django/utils/autoreload.py
  - Change around iter_modules_and_files (lines ~135–147):

        path = Path(filename)

        except FileNotFoundError:

            # is the case.

    With:

        path = Path(filename)
        try:
            resolved_path = path.resolve(strict=True).absolute()
        except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError):
            # Skip paths that don't exist or that can't be resolved due to
            # invalid path components (e.g. embedded null bytes returned by
            # os.readlink on some filesystems). It's better to ignore such
            # files than to crash the autoreloader.
            continue

            # or invalid symlink targets). Ignore them.
            continue

- I intentionally limited the exception to ValueError (in addition to FileNotFoundError) rather than catching Exception/OSError broadly, because the stack trace shows ValueError and we want minimal, targeted change. If in your environment resolve() can raise other exceptions for invalid paths, consider adding OSError as well.

Now the required challenge questions:

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- One-sentence: The code originally assumes Path.resolve(strict=True) will either succeed or raise FileNotFoundError for missing paths; my fix removes the assumption that resolve() cannot raise ValueError (e.g., for embedded null bytes) and treats such paths as invalid to be skipped.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- The only hardcoded numeric value in the primary classes is StatReloader.SLEEP_TIME = 1 (polling interval). That value does not encode any assumption about path validity or resolve behavior, so it remains correct. No other hardcoded constants in the affected functions encode the invalid-path assumption.
- The use of resolve(strict=True) is not a hardcoded numeric constant but a behavioral constant implying strict resolution — the assumption was that strict=True would only raise FileNotFoundError; the fix broadens what we handle.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- The change only affects reading/discovery of paths (resolving candidate filenames and sys.path entries) and does not change any write/serialization operations.
- Complementary operations to check: BaseReloader.watched_files -> iter_all_python_module_files -> iter_modules_and_files (we modified the latter). The parent class's methods that might need to be updated are watched_files and any code consuming its result.

Our change causes iter_modules_and_files to omit entries that cannot be resolved (they're skipped), meaning they simply won't be watched. That's the safe and intended behavior (previously they caused the reloader to crash). No complementary write operation is required.
  - The parent class uses the returned Path objects in StatReloader.snapshot_files() and WatchmanReloader._update_watches(). Both of those already handle missing files (snapshot_files catches OSError when stat() fails). So skipping problematic paths during resolution does not break the reverse operation (there is no reverse).

- BaseReloader.watched_files:
  - Key variables: results of iter_all_python_module_files() -> now excludes unresolved paths.
  - Computed result: union of module files, extra_files, and directory.glob results.
  - Expected result: Should produce paths we can watch; problematic/unresolvable paths should be omitted.
  - Override needed? NO.

- StatReloader.snapshot_files:

  - Override needed? NO.

- I checked every method in StatReloader and BaseReloader that relates to path discovery and watching:
  - BaseReloader.watched_files -> still yields valid Path objects (invalid ones are skipped).
  - StatReloader.snapshot_files -> still handles file.stat() errors.
  - WatchmanReloader._update_watches -> still groups and subscribes based on parent directories of watched_files; skipping invalid paths is safe.

- No. All needed behavior is achieved by catching the ValueError where Path.resolve() is called. No new methods are required or desirable.

Root cause
- pathlib.Path.resolve(strict=True) can raise ValueError: embedded null byte (propagated from os.readlink) when traversing certain symlinks or filesystem mountpoints with malformed data (for example, transient mount issues or broken symlink targets with embedded NULs on some platforms).
- Django’s autoreloader did not expect ValueError, only FileNotFoundError. Therefore an unhandled ValueError causes the reloader to crash intermittently during startup or while collecting watched files.

All locations that need to change
- django/utils/autoreload.py:
  1) iter_modules_and_files (around lines 135–147 in the version I inspected)
     - Current behavior: Calls Path(filename).resolve(strict=True).absolute(), only catches FileNotFoundError.
     - Problem: ValueError from resolve is unhandled and crashes the reloader.
     - Fix: catch ValueError (and continue/skip that filename).
  2) sys_path_directories (around lines 186–196)

     - Problem: Same as above.
     - Fix: catch ValueError (and continue/skip that sys.path entry).

- No other files in this repository call Path.resolve(strict=True) in an identical context (I searched for resolve(strict=True) and only found the two occurrences above).

What current code does, what assumption it encodes, and the fix
- iter_modules_and_files:
  - Does: Build a set of resolved Paths for modules and extra files; currently treats FileNotFoundError as a benign missing file and continues.
  - Assumption encoded: Path.resolve(strict=True) only fails with FileNotFoundError for missing files.
  - Fix: Also treat ValueError (embedded null byte, invalid path components) as a benign condition and skip path.

- sys_path_directories:
  - Does: Yield resolved directories from sys.path to watch.
  - Assumption: same as above.
  - Fix: Same pattern — skip entries where resolve raises ValueError.

Any hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- None. Only SLEEP_TIME = 1 exists, and it is unrelated.

Any methods that must be added or overridden
- None required. The change is confined to making path resolution more robust by handling an additional exception.

Suggested tests (I recommend adding)
- Add a unit test (utils tests for autoreload) that simulates Path.resolve raising ValueError for a module origin and asserts that iter_modules_and_files returns a frozenset without raising. Example approach:
  - Monkeypatch pathlib.Path.resolve to raise ValueError for a particular fake filename, ensure iter_modules_and_files() does not raise and omits that entry.
- Add an integration test ensuring that running the reloader doesn't crash when sys.path contains an entry that behaves like an invalid path (mock Path.resolve to raise ValueError on one sys.path element).

Why this is safe
- Previously a ValueError crashed the entire autoreloader and hence the dev server. After this change, the reloader will skip invalid/unresolvable paths (the practical effect: those files won't be watched). This mirrors existing behavior for FileNotFoundError and keeps the reloader robust against transient/broken filesystem entries without losing functionality for valid paths.

bug_report.Description: Django's development auto-reloader (StatReloader / WatchmanReloader) intermittently raises ValueError: embedded null byte while resolving filesystem paths, causing the reloader to abort during startup/file scanning. The exception is raised from stdlib pathlib/os.readlink during path resolution invoked by the autoreload code.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect assumption in iter_modules_and_files: the code calls Path(filename).resolve(strict=True).absolute() and only handles FileNotFoundError. Location: django/utils/autoreload.py — iter_modules_and_files (path.resolve(strict=True).absolute() at lines ~139-146). The code therefore does not handle other exceptions that pathlib.resolve may raise during symlink resolution.

2) Incorrect assumption in sys_path_directories: the code calls Path(path).resolve(strict=True).absolute() for sys.path entries and only handles FileNotFoundError. Location: django/utils/autoreload.py — sys_path_directories (path.resolve(strict=True).absolute() at lines ~187-196). This leaves the reloader unprotected against other resolve-time errors from the stdlib.

3) Origin of the unexpected exception: stdlib pathlib.resolve can propagate ValueError from os.readlink when resolving symlink targets that contain embedded NUL bytes, resulting in ValueError: embedded null byte. Evidence for this origin appears in the supplied traceback showing pathlib._resolve -> accessor.readlink -> os.readlink -> ValueError.

4) Equal-impact locations that depend on these assumptions: the autoreloader's module-and-path discovery code is used by multiple components, so an unhandled exception in the above resolve calls can terminate both reloaders. Affected call sites that rely on the above resolution logic include: BaseReloader.watched_files (yields from iter_all_python_module_files; django/utils/autoreload.py line ~256), StatReloader.snapshot_files (iterates watched_files; lines ~354-366), and WatchmanReloader._update_watches / watched_roots (which uses sys_path_directories; lines ~466-471). Each of these locations is equally affected by an unhandled ValueError raised during resolve().

5) Robustness gap: the autoreload code's exception handling around Path.resolve(strict=True).absolute() only considers FileNotFoundError and lacks diagnostics (e.g. logging of the offending path) that would aid identifying problematic filesystem entries. The investigation also noted that other resolve-time exceptions (beyond FileNotFoundError and ValueError) were not audited and may also cause similar crashes.

bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Occasionally, during startup or file scanning, the autoreloader raises an uncaught ValueError: embedded null byte originating from stdlib pathlib/os.readlink while resolving paths (traceback shows django/utils/autoreload.py -> path.resolve().absolute() -> pathlib -> os.readlink), which aborts the autoreloader and prevents the development server from staying up under autoreload.

from functools import wraps

from django.conf import settings
from django.core import signals
from django.core.exceptions import (
    PermissionDenied, RequestDataTooBig, SuspiciousOperation,
    TooManyFieldsSent,
)
from django.http import Http404
from django.http.multipartparser import MultiPartParserError
from django.urls import get_resolver, get_urlconf
from django.utils.log import log_response
from django.views import debug


def convert_exception_to_response(get_response):
    """
    Wrap the given get_response callable in exception-to-response conversion.

    All exceptions will be converted. All known 4xx exceptions (Http404,
    PermissionDenied, MultiPartParserError, SuspiciousOperation) will be
    converted to the appropriate response, and all other exceptions will be
    converted to 500 responses.

    This decorator is automatically applied to all middleware to ensure that
    no middleware leaks an exception and that the next middleware in the stack
    can rely on getting a response instead of an exception.
    """
    @wraps(get_response)
    def inner(request):
        try:
            response = get_response(request)
        except Exception as exc:
            response = response_for_exception(request, exc)
        return response
    return inner


def response_for_exception(request, exc):
    if isinstance(exc, Http404):
        if settings.DEBUG:
            response = debug.technical_404_response(request, exc)
        else:
            response = get_exception_response(request, get_resolver(get_urlconf()), 404, exc)

    elif isinstance(exc, PermissionDenied):
        response = get_exception_response(request, get_resolver(get_urlconf()), 403, exc)
        log_response(
            'Forbidden (Permission denied): %s', request.path,
            response=response,
            request=request,
            exc_info=sys.exc_info(),
        )

    elif isinstance(exc, MultiPartParserError):
        response = get_exception_response(request, get_resolver(get_urlconf()), 400, exc)
        log_response(
            'Bad request (Unable to parse request body): %s', request.path,
            response=response,
            request=request,
            exc_info=sys.exc_info(),
        )

    elif isinstance(exc, SuspiciousOperation):
        if isinstance(exc, (RequestDataTooBig, TooManyFieldsSent)):
            # POST data can't be accessed again, otherwise the original
            # exception would be raised.
            request._mark_post_parse_error()
