bug_report.Title: Migrations serialize Enum members by value (translated) instead of by name, causing migration import-time ValueError
bug_report.Description: When an Enum member whose .value is a gettext_lazy Promise (or otherwise unstable) is used as a default for a CharField, the migration serializer emits code that reconstructs the member from its .value (for example, Status('Good')) instead of a stable module-qualified attribute reference. Because serializer_factory materializes gettext_lazy Promise instances to str() at serialization time, translated literals are embedded in the migration file; if translations change, importing or running those migrations can raise ValueError when the literal no longer matches any Enum value.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Enum serialization uses member.value (unstable key) for reconstruction. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class EnumSerializer, method serialize. Evidence: EnumSerializer calls serializer_factory(self.value.value).serialize() and returns an expression formatted as "%s.%s(%s)" (module.EnumClass(<value>)), which embeds the serialized form of the enum member's .value into migration source. This assumes enum member.value is a stable canonical key for reconstruction; that assumption is false when .value is a gettext_lazy Promise or another runtime-dependent object.

2) Choices serialization shares the same pattern. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class ChoicesSerializer, method serialize. Evidence: ChoicesSerializer returns serializer_factory(self.value.value).serialize(), which passes the underlying choice value into serializer_factory and therefore is subject to the same Promise materialization and embedding behavior.

3) serializer_factory materializes gettext_lazy Promise instances early. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, function serializer_factory. Evidence: serializer_factory begins with "if isinstance(value, Promise): value = str(value)", causing gettext_lazy Promise objects to be converted to their current-language string at serialization time. When EnumSerializer or ChoicesSerializer passes an enum/choice .value that is a Promise, that translated literal is embedded into the migration file.

4) Migration writer embeds serializer output verbatim, so the unstable representation is persisted. Location: django/db/migrations/writer.py, classes OperationWriter and MigrationWriter. Evidence: OperationWriter and MigrationWriter consume serializer output (string and imports) and insert them directly into generated migration files without altering the expression; any instability in serializer output therefore ends up in the migration source.

5) Tests encode the current, unstable serialized form and must be updated to assert the stable representation. Location: tests/migrations/test_writer.py. Evidence: tests currently expect strings like "migrations.test_writer.TextEnum('a-value')" for enum members; equivalent expectations exist for BinaryEnum and IntEnum. The stable, import-time-safe representation is a module-qualified attribute reference using the enum member name (e.g. "module.EnumClass.NAME" such as "migrations.test_writer.TextEnum.A").
StepsToReproduce:
Define an Enum whose member values are gettext_lazy Promises, for example:
  from enum import Enum
  from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _
  class Status(Enum):
    GOOD = _('Good')
    BAD = _('Bad')
    def __str__(self):
      return self.name
Use the Enum member as a model field default, e.g. status = models.CharField(default=Status.GOOD, max_length=128)
Run python manage.py makemigrations to generate a migration
Observe the generated migration contains a constructor-style reference, e.g. ('status', models.CharField(default=Status('Good'), max_length=128))

Change the active language (so gettext_lazy resolves to a different translated string) and try to import or run the migration; observe ValueError: "'<translated-string>' is not a valid Status" because the literal in the migration no longer matches any Enum.value
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Migration files should contain a stable, import-time-safe reference to the Enum member that does not depend on runtime translation of the Enum.value. Example stable representation: a module-qualified attribute access by member name, formatted as "module.EnumClass.NAME" (e.g. migrations.test_writer.TextEnum.A). This representation is unaffected by translation of the Enum.value.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The serializer produces migration source that reconstructs Enum members from their .value (e.g. Status('Good')). gettext_lazy Promises used as Enum values are materialized to their current-language string at serialization time, causing translated string literals to be embedded in migrations. If translations change later, importing the migration can fail with ValueError("'<translated-string>' is not a valid <EnumClass>").

"""
This module contains helper functions for controlling caching. It does so by
managing the "Vary" header of responses. It includes functions to patch the
header of response objects directly and decorators that change functions to do
that header-patching themselves.

For information on the Vary header, see:

    https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-7.1.4

Essentially, the "Vary" HTTP header defines which headers a cache should take
into account when building its cache key. Requests with the same path but
different header content for headers named in "Vary" need to get different
cache keys to prevent delivery of wrong content.

An example: i18n middleware would need to distinguish caches by the
"Accept-language" header.
"""
import hashlib
import re
import time

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.cache import caches
from django.http import HttpResponse, HttpResponseNotModified
from django.utils.encoding import iri_to_uri
from django.utils.http import (
    http_date, parse_etags, parse_http_date_safe, quote_etag,
)
from django.utils.log import log_response
from django.utils.timezone import get_current_timezone_name
from django.utils.translation import get_language

cc_delim_re = re.compile(r'\s*,\s*')


def patch_cache_control(response, **kwargs):
    """
    Patch the Cache-Control header by adding all keyword arguments to it.
    The transformation is as follows:

    * All keyword parameter names are turned to lowercase, and underscores
      are converted to hyphens.
    * If the value of a parameter is True (exactly True, not just a
      true value), only the parameter name is added to the header.
    * All other parameters are added with their value, after applying
      str() to it.
    """
    def dictitem(s):
        t = s.split('=', 1)
        if len(t) > 1:
            return (t[0].lower(), t[1])
        else:
            return (t[0].lower(), True)

    def dictvalue(t):
        if t[1] is True:
            return t[0]
        else:
            return '%s=%s' % (t[0], t[1])

    if response.get('Cache-Control'):
        cc = cc_delim_re.split(response['Cache-Control'])
        cc = dict(dictitem(el) for el in cc)
    else:
        cc = {}

    # If there's already a max-age header but we're being asked to set a new
    # max-age, use the minimum of the two ages. In practice this happens when
    # a decorator and a piece of middleware both operate on a given view.
    if 'max-age' in cc and 'max_age' in kwargs:
        kwargs['max_age'] = min(int(cc['max-age']), kwargs['max_age'])

    # Allow overriding private caching and vice versa
    if 'private' in cc and 'public' in kwargs:
        del cc['private']
    elif 'public' in cc and 'private' in kwargs:
        del cc['public']

    for (k, v) in kwargs.items():
        cc[k.replace('_', '-')] = v
    cc = ', '.join(dictvalue(el) for el in cc.items())
    response['Cache-Control'] = cc


def get_max_age(response):
    """
    Return the max-age from the response Cache-Control header as an integer,
    or None if it wasn't found or wasn't an integer.
    """
    if not response.has_header('Cache-Control'):
        return
    cc = dict(_to_tuple(el) for el in cc_delim_re.split(response['Cache-Control']))
    try:
        return int(cc['max-age'])
    except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError):
        pass


def set_response_etag(response):
    if not response.streaming:
        response['ETag'] = quote_etag(hashlib.md5(response.content).hexdigest())
    return response


def _precondition_failed(request):
    response = HttpResponse(status=412)
    log_response(
        'Precondition Failed: %s', request.path,
        response=response,
        request=request,
    )
    return response


def _not_modified(request, response=None):
    new_response = HttpResponseNotModified()
    if response:
        # Preserve the headers required by Section 4.1 of RFC 7232, as well as
        # Last-Modified.
        for header in ('Cache-Control', 'Content-Location', 'Date', 'ETag', 'Expires', 'Last-Modified', 'Vary'):
            if header in response:
                new_response[header] = response[header]

        # Preserve cookies as per the cookie specification: "If a proxy server
        # receives a response which contains a Set-cookie header, it should
        # propagate the Set-cookie header to the client, regardless of whether
        # the response was 304 (Not Modified) or 200 (OK).
        # https://curl.haxx.se/rfc/cookie_spec.html
        new_response.cookies = response.cookies
    return new_response


def get_conditional_response(request, etag=None, last_modified=None, response=None):
    # Only return conditional responses on successful requests.
    if response and not (200 <= response.status_code < 300):
        return response

    # Get HTTP request headers.
    if_match_etags = parse_etags(request.META.get('HTTP_IF_MATCH', ''))
    if_unmodified_since = request.META.get('HTTP_IF_UNMODIFIED_SINCE')
    if_unmodified_since = if_unmodified_since and parse_http_date_safe(if_unmodified_since)
    if_none_match_etags = parse_etags(request.META.get('HTTP_IF_NONE_MATCH', ''))
    if_modified_since = request.META.get('HTTP_IF_MODIFIED_SINCE')
    if_modified_since = if_modified_since and parse_http_date_safe(if_modified_since)

    # Step 1 of section 6 of RFC 7232: Test the If-Match precondition.
    if if_match_etags and not _if_match_passes(etag, if_match_etags):
        return _precondition_failed(request)

    # Step 2: Test the If-Unmodified-Since precondition.
    if (not if_match_etags and if_unmodified_since and
            not _if_unmodified_since_passes(last_modified, if_unmodified_since)):
        return _precondition_failed(request)

    # Step 3: Test the If-None-Match precondition.
    if if_none_match_etags and not _if_none_match_passes(etag, if_none_match_etags):
        if request.method in ('GET', 'HEAD'):
            return _not_modified(request, response)
        else:
            return _precondition_failed(request)

    # Step 4: Test the If-Modified-Since precondition.
    if (not if_none_match_etags and if_modified_since and
            not _if_modified_since_passes(last_modified, if_modified_since)):
        if request.method in ('GET', 'HEAD'):
            return _not_modified(request, response)

    # Step 5: Test the If-Range precondition (not supported).
    # Step 6: Return original response since there isn't a conditional response.
    return response


def _if_match_passes(target_etag, etags):
    """
    Test the If-Match comparison as defined in section 3.1 of RFC 7232.
    """
    if not target_etag:
        # If there isn't an ETag, then there can't be a match.
        return False
    elif etags == ['*']:
        # The existence of an ETag means that there is "a current
        # representation for the target resource", even if the ETag is weak,
        # so there is a match to '*'.
        return True
    elif target_etag.startswith('W/'):
        # A weak ETag can never strongly match another ETag.
        return False
    else:
        # Since the ETag is strong, this will only return True if there's a
        # strong match.
        return target_etag in etags


def _if_unmodified_since_passes(last_modified, if_unmodified_since):
    """
    Test the If-Unmodified-Since comparison as defined in section 3.4 of
    RFC 7232.
    """
    return last_modified and last_modified <= if_unmodified_since


def _if_none_match_passes(target_etag, etags):
    """
    Test the If-None-Match comparison as defined in section 3.2 of RFC 7232.
    """
    if not target_etag:
        # If there isn't an ETag, then there isn't a match.
        return True
    elif etags == ['*']:
        # The existence of an ETag means that there is "a current
        # representation for the target resource", so there is a match to '*'.
        return False
    else:
        # The comparison should be weak, so look for a match after stripping
        # off any weak indicators.
        target_etag = target_etag.strip('W/')
        etags = (etag.strip('W/') for etag in etags)
        return target_etag not in etags


def _if_modified_since_passes(last_modified, if_modified_since):
    """
    Test the If-Modified-Since comparison as defined in section 3.3 of RFC 7232.
    """
    return not last_modified or last_modified > if_modified_since


def patch_response_headers(response, cache_timeout=None):
    """
    Add HTTP caching headers to the given HttpResponse: Expires and
    Cache-Control.

    Each header is only added if it isn't already set.

    cache_timeout is in seconds. The CACHE_MIDDLEWARE_SECONDS setting is used
    by default.
    """
    if cache_timeout is None:
        cache_timeout = settings.CACHE_MIDDLEWARE_SECONDS

bug_report.Title: parse_http_date uses a fixed two-digit-year pivot instead of RFC 7231 50-year rule
bug_report.Description: django.utils.http.parse_http_date interprets two-digit years using a hard-coded pivot (0–69 → 2000–2069, 70–99 → 1970–1999) instead of the RFC 7231 requirement to interpret a two-digit year relative to the current UTC year and to treat a candidate that would be more than 50 years in the future as representing the same last-two-digits in the previous century.
bug_report.RootCause:
1. Hard-coded two-digit-year pivot in django/utils/http.py::parse_http_date — the function contains a static mapping for two-digit years:
   - Exact code (django/utils/http.py):
       year = int(m.group('year'))
       if year < 100:
           if year < 70:
               year += 2000
           else:
               year += 1900
   This encoding (0–69 → add 2000; 70–99 → add 1900) is a fixed pivot and does not apply the RFC 7231 50-year relative rule.

2. Unit test enforces the static pivot in tests/utils_tests/test_http.py::test_parsing_year_less_than_70 — the test asserts a concrete four-digit year for the input with two-digit year '0037':
   - Exact code (tests/utils_tests/test_http.py):
       parsed = parse_http_date('Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 0037')
       self.assertEqual(datetime.utcfromtimestamp(parsed), datetime(2037, 11, 6, 8, 49, 37))
   Because the test hard-codes the expected year, it encodes and protects the current static mapping in test expectations.

3. Literal constants encode the static pivot — the constants 70, 1900, and 2000 appear in the parse_http_date logic and represent a century pivot that is static rather than computed from the current year. These numeric literals are only correct under the implicit assumption that the pivot is pinned to the 1970–2069 split; the correct interpretation depends on the current UTC year and a 50-year future window as described below.

4. Call sites that will observe different parsed timestamps if parsing behavior changes: parse_http_date is consumed directly or via its safe wrapper in multiple modules. Observed call sites include:
   - django/middleware/http.py: last_modified = last_modified and parse_http_date_safe(last_modified)
   - django/utils/cache.py: if_unmodified_since / if_modified_since use parse_http_date_safe
   - django/views/static.py: header_mtime = parse_http_date(matches.group(1)) in was_modified_since
   These consumers will receive different integer timestamps for two-digit-year inputs if the parsing rule changes; write-side formatting (http_date) emits four-digit years and is not the source of the bug.

5. Correct interpretation per RFC 7231 (diagnostic statement of the relationship): two-digit years must be interpreted relative to the current UTC year so that a candidate four-digit year formed from the current century is used unless that candidate would be more than 50 years in the future, in which case the corresponding year from the previous century is taken. Expressed as a rule (diagnostic, not an implementation prescription):
   - Let now be the current UTC year.
   - Let century = now - (now % 100).
   - Let candidate = century + two_digit_year.
   - If candidate - now > 50, then interpreted_year = candidate - 100; otherwise interpreted_year = candidate.
   This is the RFC 7231-compliant interpretation that the current code does not implement.

6. Investigation/test coverage omissions and risks that affect rollout confidence:
   - Tests that assert the current static mapping do not mock or freeze the current UTC time, making time-relative behavior non-deterministic unless tests are updated to control now.
   - The investigation did not exhaustively search the codebase for other occurrences of the same century/pivot literals beyond the parse_http_date site, nor did it verify whether external systems or persisted data rely on the static mapping. These gaps create risk that other code or external integrations may implicitly rely on the existing static behavior.
StepsToReproduce: In a Django environment, open a Python shell and run: from django.utils.http import parse_http_date
Call parse_http_date('Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 0037') and convert the returned epoch to a UTC datetime (e.g., datetime.utcfromtimestamp(parsed)). Observe the four-digit year returned.
Run the unit test tests/utils_tests/test_http.py::test_parsing_year_less_than_70 and observe that it asserts a concrete year (2037) for the '0037' input.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When given an rfc850-date with a two-digit year, the parser should interpret the two-digit year relative to the current UTC year per RFC 7231: form a candidate year from the current century and the two-digit value, and if that candidate would be more than 50 years in the future, interpret it as the same last-two-digits in the previous century. User-visible parsed timestamps (as UTC datetimes) should reflect this time-relative interpretation.

A unit test currently asserts the static mapping (for example, 'Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 0037' → 2037), thereby encoding and preserving the static behavior in tests.

    def split_exclude(self, filter_expr, can_reuse, names_with_path):
        """
        When doing an exclude against any kind of N-to-many relation, we need
        to use a subquery. This method constructs the nested query, given the
        original exclude filter (filter_expr) and the portion up to the first
        N-to-many relation field.

        For example, if the origin filter is ~Q(child__name='foo'), filter_expr
        is ('child__name', 'foo') and can_reuse is a set of joins usable for
        filters in the original query.

        We will turn this into equivalent of:
            WHERE NOT (pk IN (SELECT parent_id FROM thetable
                              WHERE name = 'foo' AND parent_id IS NOT NULL))

        It might be worth it to consider using WHERE NOT EXISTS as that has
        saner null handling, and is easier for the backend's optimizer to
        handle.
        """
        filter_lhs, filter_rhs = filter_expr
        if isinstance(filter_rhs, OuterRef):
            filter_expr = (filter_lhs, OuterRef(filter_rhs))
        elif isinstance(filter_rhs, F):
            filter_expr = (filter_lhs, OuterRef(filter_rhs.name))
        # Generate the inner query.
        query = Query(self.model)
        query._filtered_relations = self._filtered_relations
        query.add_filter(filter_expr)
        query.clear_ordering(True)
        # Try to have as simple as possible subquery -> trim leading joins from
        # the subquery.
        trimmed_prefix, contains_louter = query.trim_start(names_with_path)

        # Add extra check to make sure the selected field will not be null
        # since we are adding an IN <subquery> clause. This prevents the
        # database from tripping over IN (...,NULL,...) selects and returning
        # nothing
        col = query.select[0]
        select_field = col.target
        alias = col.alias
        if self.is_nullable(select_field):
            lookup_class = select_field.get_lookup('isnull')
            lookup = lookup_class(select_field.get_col(alias), False)
            query.where.add(lookup, AND)
        if alias in can_reuse:
            pk = select_field.model._meta.pk
            # Need to add a restriction so that outer query's filters are in effect for
            # the subquery, too.
            query.bump_prefix(self)
            lookup_class = select_field.get_lookup('exact')
            # Note that the query.select[0].alias is different from alias
            # due to bump_prefix above.
            lookup = lookup_class(pk.get_col(query.select[0].alias),
                                  pk.get_col(alias))
            query.where.add(lookup, AND)
            query.external_aliases.add(alias)

    lookup_name = 'isnull'
    prepare_rhs = False

    def get_prep_lookup(self):
        # Allow expressions (they'll be resolved by the compiler/run-time)
        if hasattr(self.rhs, 'resolve_expression'):
            return self.rhs
        # None should already be handled by Query.build_lookup which converts
        # None to an explicit isnull True. Only booleans are allowed as direct
        # values for this lookup.
        if not isinstance(self.rhs, bool):
            raise ValueError("The 'isnull' lookup expects a boolean value (True/False).")
        return self.rhs

    def as_sql(self, compiler, connection):
        sql, params = compiler.compile(self.lhs)
        if self.rhs is True:
            return "%s IS NULL" % sql, params
        else:
            return "%s IS NOT NULL" % sql, params

- The get_prep_lookup check rejects non-boolean direct RHS values passed programmatically, giving a clear error rather than silently treating them as truthy or falsey.

bug_report.Title: IsNull lookup accepts non-boolean RHS (uses truthiness) causing inconsistent SQL and join behavior
bug_report.Description: The __isnull lookup accepts non-boolean RHS values (e.g. non-empty strings, integers) and uses Python truthiness to emit "IS NULL" vs "IS NOT NULL" SQL. This leads to inconsistent query behavior because other parts of the ORM expect a strict boolean RHS for isnull during join-promotion and related checks.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/lookups.py: IsNull.as_sql — The method uses a Python truthiness test (if self.rhs:) to decide between "%s IS NULL" and "%s IS NOT NULL". Because any truthy non-boolean value (for example, a non-empty string or integer 1) will be treated as True by this test, non-boolean direct RHS literals can cause IS NULL to be emitted even though they are not boolean True.

2) django/db/models/lookups.py: IsNull.prepare_rhs/get_prep_lookup — IsNull sets prepare_rhs = False and does not override get_prep_lookup, so direct RHS literals are passed through unchanged (strings, ints, etc.). This encodes the implicit assumption that non-boolean direct RHS values are acceptable indicators of an isnull test; in reality, the join-promotion and other query logic expect an actual boolean value to indicate the special isnull True case.

3) django/db/models/sql/query.py: build_lookup / build_filter — Query.build_lookup already maps certain RHS values to an explicit isnull lookup with a boolean True (for example, an explicit None RHS for exact lookups and empty-string handling for backends that treat '' as NULL). Separately, build_filter decides join promotion using a strict identity test: require_outer is set when lookup_type == 'isnull' and condition.rhs is True. The query-side code therefore relies on condition.rhs being the boolean True to detect the isnull 'True' case; IsNull.as_sql's use of Python truthiness is inconsistent with that expectation.

4) django/contrib/admin/utils.py: prepare_lookup_value — The admin querystring parsing already coerces common string forms into booleans for __isnull (value = value.lower() not in ('', 'false', '0')). This demonstrates that at least one external path already normalizes to booleans before construction of lookups, and highlights that programmatic construction of lookups (e.g. .filter(field__isnull='abc')) can bypass that normalization and exhibit the inconsistency described above.
StepsToReproduce: In a Django project with models that produce a JOIN (for example, Parent has a nullable FK to Child), open the Django shell (python manage.py shell).
Execute a QuerySet using a non-boolean RHS for isnull, for example: Parent.objects.filter(child__name__isnull='abc').
Inspect the generated SQL: print(Parent.objects.filter(child__name__isnull='abc').query) — observe that the SQL contains "child.name IS NULL" (or IS NOT NULL based on truthiness of the RHS).

Compare result cardinality or join semantics with the same query using an actual boolean RHS: Parent.objects.filter(child__name__isnull=True) — observe that join promotion / returned rows can differ because the query construction code checks for condition.rhs is True when deciding join promotion.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Direct RHS values supplied to the __isnull lookup should be treated as booleans for the purpose of lookup semantics and join-promotion decisions. Programmatic uses of __isnull with a direct literal RHS should not silently accept arbitrary non-boolean values as boolean True/False. Admin querystring parsing (which already coerces common string forms into booleans) may continue to normalize values at the admin layer; the lower-level lookup/query machinery should present a consistent boolean-based contract to avoid inconsistent SQL and join behavior.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Non-boolean direct RHS values are silently accepted by IsNull and interpreted via Python truthiness when emitting SQL (IsNull.as_sql uses if self.rhs:). Because other parts of the ORM (e.g., query.build_filter) detect the isnull True case via a strict identity test (condition.rhs is True), queries constructed with non-boolean truthy RHS values can generate SQL that reads "IS NULL" while the join-promotion logic does not treat the condition as the special isnull True case, causing surprising or missing results.

    """

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):

    def repr_changes(self, changes, include_dependencies=False):
        output = ""
        for app_label, migrations in sorted(changes.items()):
            output += "  %s:\n" % app_label
            for migration in migrations:
                output += "    %s\n" % migration.name
                for operation in migration.operations:
                    output += "      %s\n" % operation
                if include_dependencies:
                    output += "      Dependencies:\n"
                    if migration.dependencies:
                        for dep in migration.dependencies:
                            output += "        %s\n" % (dep,)
                    else:
                        output += "        None\n"
        return output

    def assertNumberMigrations(self, changes, app_label, number):
        if len(changes.get(app_label, [])) != number:
            self.fail("Incorrect number of migrations (%s) for %s (expected %s)\n%s" % (
                len(changes.get(app_label, [])),
                app_label,
                number,
                self.repr_changes(changes),
            ))

    def assertMigrationDependencies(self, changes, app_label, position, dependencies):
        if not changes.get(app_label):
            self.fail("No migrations found for %s\n%s" % (app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No migration at index %s for %s\n%s" % (position, app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        migration = changes[app_label][position]
        if set(migration.dependencies) != set(dependencies):
            self.fail("Migration dependencies mismatch for %s.%s (expected %s):\n%s" % (
                app_label,
                migration.name,
                dependencies,
                self.repr_changes(changes, include_dependencies=True),
            ))

    def assertOperationTypes(self, changes, app_label, position, types):
        if not changes.get(app_label):
            self.fail("No migrations found for %s\n%s" % (app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No migration at index %s for %s\n%s" % (position, app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        migration = changes[app_label][position]
        real_types = [operation.__class__.__name__ for operation in migration.operations]
        if types != real_types:
            self.fail("Operation type mismatch for %s.%s (expected %s):\n%s" % (
                app_label,
                migration.name,
                types,
                self.repr_changes(changes),
            ))

    def assertOperationAttributes(self, changes, app_label, position, operation_position, **attrs):
        if not changes.get(app_label):
            self.fail("No migrations found for %s\n%s" % (app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No migration at index %s for %s\n%s" % (position, app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        migration = changes[app_label][position]
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No operation at index %s for %s.%s\n%s" % (
                operation_position,
                app_label,
                migration.name,
                self.repr_changes(changes),
            ))
        operation = migration.operations[operation_position]
        for attr, value in attrs.items():
            if getattr(operation, attr, None) != value:
                self.fail("Attribute mismatch for %s.%s op #%s, %s (expected %r, got %r):\n%s" % (
                    app_label,
                    migration.name,
                    operation_position,
                    attr,
                    value,
                    getattr(operation, attr, None),
                    self.repr_changes(changes),
                ))

    def assertOperationFieldAttributes(self, changes, app_label, position, operation_position, **attrs):
        if not changes.get(app_label):
            self.fail("No migrations found for %s\n%s" % (app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No migration at index %s for %s\n%s" % (position, app_label, self.repr_changes(changes)))
        migration = changes[app_label][position]
        if len(changes[app_label]) < position + 1:
            self.fail("No operation at index %s for %s.%s\n%s" % (
                operation_position,
                app_label,
                migration.name,
                self.repr_changes(changes),
            ))
        operation = migration.operations[operation_position]
        if not hasattr(operation, 'field'):
            self.fail("No field attribute for %s.%s op #%s." % (
                app_label,
                migration.name,
                operation_position,
            ))
        field = operation.field
        for attr, value in attrs.items():
            if getattr(field, attr, None) != value:
                self.fail("Field attribute mismatch for %s.%s op #%s, field.%s (expected %r, got %r):\n%s" % (
                    app_label,
                    migration.name,
                    operation_position,
                    attr,
                    value,
                    getattr(field, attr, None),
                    self.repr_changes(changes),
                ))

    def test_supports_functools_partial(self):
        def _content_file_name(instance, filename, key, **kwargs):
            return '{}/{}'.format(instance, filename)

        def content_file_name(key, **kwargs):
            return functools.partial(_content_file_name, key, **kwargs)

        # An unchanged partial reference.
        before = [ModelState("testapp", "Author", [
            ("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True)),
            ("file", models.FileField(max_length=200, upload_to=content_file_name('file'))),
        ])]
        after = [ModelState("testapp", "Author", [
            ("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True)),
            ("file", models.FileField(max_length=200, upload_to=content_file_name('file'))),
        ])]
        changes = self.get_changes(before, after)
        self.assertNumberMigrations(changes, 'testapp', 0)

        # A changed partial reference.
        args_changed = [ModelState("testapp", "Author", [
            ("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True)),
            ("file", models.FileField(max_length=200, upload_to=content_file_name('other-file'))),
        ])]
        changes = self.get_changes(before, args_changed)
        self.assertNumberMigrations(changes, 'testapp', 1)
        self.assertOperationTypes(changes, 'testapp', 0, ['AlterField'])
        # Can't use assertOperationFieldAttributes because we need the
        # deconstructed version, i.e., the exploded func/args/keywords rather
        # than the partial: we don't care if it's not the same instance of the
        # partial, only if it's the same source function, args, and keywords.
        value = changes['testapp'][0].operations[0].field.upload_to
        self.assertEqual(
            (_content_file_name, ('other-file',), {}),
            (value.func, value.args, value.keywords)
        )

        kwargs_changed = [ModelState("testapp", "Author", [
            ("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True)),
            ("file", models.FileField(max_length=200, upload_to=content_file_name('file', spam='eggs'))),
        ])]
        changes = self.get_changes(before, kwargs_changed)
        self.assertNumberMigrations(changes, 'testapp', 1)
        self.assertOperationTypes(changes, 'testapp', 0, ['AlterField'])
        value = changes['testapp'][0].operations[0].field.upload_to
        self.assertEqual(
            (_content_file_name, ('file',), {'spam': 'eggs'}),
            (value.func, value.args, value.keywords)
        )

That leads to migrations.AlterField(... to_field='field_wrong') appearing AFTER the RenameField, which is wrong — the FK should still implicitly point to the related model's PK, and no explicit to_field should be added.

===HIGH_LEVEL===

- Bug: When a model's PrimaryKey field is renamed (e.g. ModelA.field_wrong -> ModelA.field_fixed), makemigrations produces a RenameField for ModelA but also an incorrect AlterField on a ForeignKey that sets to_field='field_wrong' (the old name). The wrong assumption is that forcing new_field.remote_field.field_name to the old name is always safe.
- Root cause & location: In django/db/migrations/autodetector.py, MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields unconditionally does new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name when a related-field rename is detected; for PK renames this forces the old name into the FK and ForeignKey.deconstruct() then emits to_field='old_name'. (See generate_altered_fields and self.renamed_fields mapping.)
- Fix strategy: Only overwrite new_field.remote_field.field_name when the FK explicitly targets a non-PK field. Concretely, in generate_altered_fields check whether remote_field_name == related_model._meta.pk.name; if it is (FK implicitly targets PK), skip the overwrite. This prevents adding an explicit to_field with the old PK name.
- Scope: Single-line logical change in MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields; no migration-application code change required. Add a unit test in tests/migrations/test_autodetector.py to cover PK-rename + implicit-FK case.
- Hardcoded/assumed behavior to preserve: ForeignKey.deconstruct() omits to_field when remote_field.field_name == to_meta.pk.name — the fix relies on that existing behavior (do not mutate into a non-PK name).
- Investigation gaps: agent did not run test suite or search for other mutations of remote_field.field_name elsewhere; did not add the unit test or run it. Also did not examine multi-column ForeignObject cases in depth (they use to_fields/from_fields and have different deconstruct behavior).

### Finding 1: Root cause — unconditional overwrite of FK target name
What: MigrationAutodetector.generate_altered_fields overwrites new_field.remote_field.field_name with old_field.remote_field.field_name when a related-field rename is found. For a PK rename this forces the old PK name into the ForeignKey.  
Why it matters: That mutation makes ForeignKey.deconstruct() include kwargs['to_field'] = 'field_wrong', producing an erroneous migrations.AlterField(... to_field='field_wrong') after the RenameField.  
Location: django/db/migrations/autodetector.py, class MigrationAutodetector, method generate_altered_fields.  
Evidence: code path uses to_field_rename_key in self.renamed_fields then executes new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name.  
Checkpoint: 3 (mapping architecture) and 1 (initial detection).

### Finding 2: How deconstruct() makes the overwrite harmful
What: ForeignKey.deconstruct only emits to_field when remote_field.field_name != to_meta.pk.name; thus changing remote_field.field_name away from the new pk name causes to_field to be included.  
Why it matters: The overwrite in the autodetector turns an implicit-PK FK into an explicit to_field pointing at the OLD pk name.  
Location: django/db/models/fields/related.py, class ForeignKey (ForeignObject.deconstruct / ForeignKey.deconstruct). Exact condition:  
if self.remote_field.field_name and (not to_meta or (to_meta.pk and self.remote_field.field_name != to_meta.pk.name)): kwargs['to_field'] = self.remote_field.field_name

### Finding 3: Concrete fix — guard the overwrite
What: Change generate_altered_fields to skip assigning new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name when the FK in the new state points to the related model's PK (i.e. remote_field_name == related_model._meta.pk.name). Only perform the overwrite for explicit-to-field renames (non-PK targets).  
Why it matters: Prevents deconstruct() from including to_field='old_name' for implicit-PK FKs while preserving behavior for explicit to_field renames.  
Location: django/db/migrations/autodetector.py, class MigrationAutodetector, method generate_altered_fields.

bug_report.Title: makemigrations emits AlterField with old to_field when renaming a model PrimaryKey
bug_report.Description: When renaming a model field that is the PrimaryKey (e.g. ModelA.field_wrong -> ModelA.field_fixed), makemigrations produces a RenameField for the model but also emits an AlterField for an existing ForeignKey that sets to_field to the old PK name ('field_wrong'). This occurs even though the ForeignKey implicitly targets the PK (no explicit to_field in the model definition).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) MigrationAutodetector applies a renamed-field mapping to a related field's target name without checking whether the FK implicitly targets the related model's PK (django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:generate_altered_fields). Specifically, when detecting altered fields it computes a to_field_rename_key and, if present in self.renamed_fields, executes:
   new_field.remote_field.field_name = old_field.remote_field.field_name
   (see django/db/migrations/autodetector.py lines ~926-931). This assignment is governed only by the renamed_fields mapping and does not test whether the new remote_field.field_name equals the related model's pk.name; therefore it will replace an implicit-PK target name with the old name recorded in the rename mapping.

2) The rename mapping that the autodetector uses is populated by generate_renamed_fields as a mapping of shape (app_label, model_name, new_field_name) -> old_field_name (django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:generate_renamed_fields). Example entry: ('app1','modela','field_fixed') -> 'field_wrong' (see django/db/migrations/autodetector.py line ~844). generate_altered_fields looks up this mapping to decide whether to rewrite the related-field target name.

3) ForeignKey/ForeignObject deconstruction makes the mutation visible in generated migration code (django/db/models/fields/related.py). ForeignKey.deconstruct will include kwargs['to_field'] when remote_field.field_name is set and differs from the related model's primary key name (condition at django/db/models/fields/related.py lines ~869-873). Therefore, if the autodetector mutates remote_field.field_name from the new PK name back to the old name, deconstruct will emit to_field='<old_name>' and makemigrations will produce an AlterField with that to_field.

4) Related code that demonstrates how remote_field.field_name is treated elsewhere (relevant to understanding the mutation surface):
   - The autodetector handles multi-column ForeignObjects by mapping each to_fields/from_fields entry via self.renamed_fields (django/db/migrations/autodetector.py lines ~932-942). The single-field ForeignKey path uses the single mapping described above and lacks a PK-aware guard.
   - RenameField.state_forwards (django/db/migrations/operations/fields.py lines ~337-349) updates remote_field.field_name during the application of a RenameField operation to a ProjectState (it replaces occurrences of the old_name with new_name). This state-application mutation is expected when applying RenameField operations, but it is separate from the autodetector's rename-mapping rewrite that causes an implicit-PK FK to become an explicit to_field referencing the old PK name.

Summary: the concrete defect is that the autodetector uses the renamed_fields mapping to rewrite a related-field's remote_field.field_name without checking PK semantics, which transforms an implicit-PK ForeignKey into an explicit to_field pointing at the old PK name; ForeignKey.deconstruct then emits that old name into the generated migration's AlterField.
StepsToReproduce: Create app 'app1' with two models: ModelA with a CharField primary_key=True named 'field_wrong'; ModelB with a ForeignKey to ModelA (no to_field specified).
Run makemigrations and migrate to create/apply initial migrations.
Rename ModelA.field_wrong to ModelA.field_fixed in models.py (keep primary_key=True).
Run makemigrations.
Inspect the generated migration: observe a RenameField for ModelA and an AlterField for ModelB's FK that includes to_field='field_wrong'.

bug_report.ObservedBehavior: makemigrations generates a RenameField for ModelA and also generates an AlterField for the ForeignKey that includes to_field='field_wrong' (the old PK name), turning an implicit-PK FK into an explicit FK referencing the old name.

Why it matters: normalizing enums on assignment changes runtime values and could break code that relied on object identity rather than equality; these must be covered by tests.

Checkpoint: 4e (explicitly flagged as missing checks)

===LOW_LEVEL===

### Location: django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute (missing __set__)
- Wrong assumption: attribute assignment should always write raw values into instance.__dict__ and not be normalized by field logic.
- Evidence:
  - DeferredAttribute implements __get__ but there is no __set__ defined in query_utils.py. The agent read the whole file and explicitly noted absence of __set__. (Checkpoint 3a)
  - Model.__init__ uses setattr(..., field.attname, value); since DeferredAttribute has no __set__, Python stores the value directly in instance.__dict__, leaving enum.Enum objects intact.
- Related locations:
  - django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.descriptor_class (points to DeferredAttribute)
  - django/db/models/base.py:Model.__init__ and Model.from_db (call setattr on attname)

Suggested change (exact code to add)
- At top of django/db/models/query_utils.py add:
  import enum
- Add to DeferredAttribute:

  def __set__(self, instance, value):
      """
      If an enum.Enum member is assigned (TextChoices/IntegerChoices),
      store its underlying .value on the instance so created objects match
      DB-loaded objects.
      """
      if isinstance(value, enum.Enum):
          instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = value.value
      else:
          instance.__dict__[self.field.attname] = value

(Keep indentation and naming exactly as shown; this change was proposed in Checkpoint 4.)

### Location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.descriptor_class and Field.contribute_to_class
- Wrong assumption: attaching DeferredAttribute without a __set__ is sufficient for expected field behavior.
- Evidence:
  - Field has descriptor_class = DeferredAttribute (explicit class attribute).
  - Field.contribute_to_class assigns the descriptor instance to the model class (so most fields use the DeferredAttribute behavior). Agent read Field implementation and trace where contribute_to_class attaches descriptor_class(self) to the model (Checkpoint 2c).
- Related locations:
  - django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute (missing __set__)
  - Field subclasses (CharField, IntegerField) that depend on descriptor behavior

### Location: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:CharField.to_python and IntegerField.to_python
- Wrong assumption: DB->Python conversion mechanism and assignment path are equivalent (they are not).
- Evidence:
  - CharField.to_python: returns value if isinstance(value, str), else str(value) — DB values become primitive strings on load.
  - IntegerField.to_python converts to int.
  - The agent observed that DB-retrieved objects use these conversions, producing primitives, while assignment path left Enum members untouched (Checkpoint 3d).
- Related locations:
  - django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute (assignment path)
  - django/db/models/base.py:Model.from_db (DB->Python path)

### Location: django/db/models/base.py:Model.__init__ / Model.from_db
- Wrong assumption: setattr calls will be symmetrical with DB->Python conversion (they are only symmetrical if descriptors normalize on set).  
- Evidence:
  - Model.__init__ uses setattr(instance, field.attname, value) for constructor kwargs; because DeferredAttribute lacks __set__, this writes raw value to instance.__dict__. (Checkpoint 3d)
- Related locations:
  - django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute.__set__ (proposed)
  - django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.contribute_to_class

bug_report.Title: Assigning TextChoices/IntegerChoices enum member to field stores Enum on instance, causing type mismatch with DB-loaded primitives
bug_report.Description: When a TextChoices or IntegerChoices enum member is assigned to a model CharField/IntegerField at creation time, the in-memory model instance keeps the enum.Enum object (whose str() is like 'MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE'), while the same column loaded from the database yields the primitive underlying value ('first' or integer). This leads to inconsistent runtime types between freshly-created and DB-retrieved model instances and unexpected string/int values when serializing or sending to external systems.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Missing descriptor write hook: django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute implements __get__ (intercepts reads) but does not implement __set__. Because DeferredAttribute provides no write hook, assignments to field attributes fall back to writing directly into instance.__dict__, allowing any assigned object (including enum.Enum members) to be stored unchanged on the instance.

2) Descriptor used by core fields: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.descriptor_class is set to DeferredAttribute and Field.contribute_to_class attaches descriptor_class(self) to the model attribute (self.attname). As a result, most core Field subclasses (e.g., CharField, IntegerField and others inheriting Field) rely on DeferredAttribute for attribute access, so the missing write hook affects these fields uniformly.

3) Asymmetry between assignment and DB load conversion: Field subclasses perform DB→Python normalization (for example, CharField.to_python converts values to str; IntegerField.to_python converts values to int), so values read from the database become primitives. In contrast, assignment at creation time uses setattr on field.attname (via Model.__init__ and other assignment sites), and without a descriptor __set__ that normalizes assigned values, enum.Enum members stay as objects in instance.__dict__. The relevant locations encoding these behaviors are:
  - django/db/models/query_utils.py:DeferredAttribute (has __get__, no __set__).
  - django/db/models/fields/__init__.py: Field.descriptor_class = DeferredAttribute and Field.contribute_to_class attaching descriptor to cls (attname).
  - django/db/models/fields/__init__.py: CharField.to_python and IntegerField.to_python (DB→Python normalization to primitives).
  - django/db/models/base.py: Model.__init__ uses setattr(self, field.attname, value) when constructing instances; Model.from_db constructs via cls(*values) which triggers the same __init__ assignment path; refresh_from_db also calls setattr(self, field.attname, ...) when writing values from a DB-loaded instance.

4) Diagnostic expectation (behavioral specification): For consistency, a field declared with TextChoices/IntegerChoices exhibiting enum.Enum members as choice values leads to a mismatch between freshly-assigned and DB-loaded representations. Diagnostically, the runtime representation exposed on model instances should be consistent between assignment and DB load: either both should expose enum.Enum members or both should expose the enum member's underlying primitive value (the investigation shows DB-loading currently produces the primitive). The codebase currently encodes the assumption that DB-loaded values are normalized to primitives while assignments are stored verbatim.

5) Risks and gaps noted: The investigation did not enumerate or test code that may intentionally rely on identity or is-instance semantics for enum.Enum objects on freshly-created instances (e.g., 'is' comparisons, object identity expectations, pickling), which could be affected by normalizing assigned values. The investigation also did not run the full test-suite to detect regressions caused by a change to assignment-time behavior.
StepsToReproduce: Create an instance assigning the enum member: obj = MyObject.objects.create(my_str_value=MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE).

Inspect the in-memory instance immediately after creation: assert isinstance(obj.my_str_value, str) and assert str(obj.my_str_value) == 'first' (this assertion fails because the value is an enum.Enum instance and str(...) yields 'MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE').

Retrieve the same row from the DB: obj2 = MyObject.objects.last(); assert isinstance(obj2.my_str_value, str) and str(obj2.my_str_value) == 'first' (this passes because DB load normalized the value to the primitive).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For both freshly-created instances and DB-retrieved instances, a field declared with TextChoices/IntegerChoices should expose the same runtime representation and primitive value (user-visible): i.e., the value observed and serialized from the model attribute should be consistent so that str(field_value) yields the enum member's defined underlying value (e.g., 'first') regardless of whether the instance was just created or loaded from the database.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When assigning an enum.Enum member at creation, the model instance stores the enum.Enum object for the field (its str() is like 'MyChoice.FIRST_CHOICE'); when retrieving the same row from the database, the field value is the primitive underlying value (e.g., 'first'). This causes runtime-type and string-value inconsistencies between freshly-created and DB-retrieved instances.

Short summary / root cause (top-level):
- Root cause: Field.contribute_to_class unconditionally installs a generated get_<field>_display method on the model class (via setattr(..., partialmethod(...))). Model class construction in Django 2.2 adds ordinary (user-defined) methods to the new class earlier, and then calls contribute_to_class for fields. Because the Field code unconditionally calls setattr, it overwrites any user-defined get_<field>_display method. That is why user overrides of get_foo_bar_display() stopped working in Django 2.2+.
- Fix: Change the code that installs generated accessor methods to avoid overwriting an existing attribute on the class. Concretely, in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:
  - In Field.contribute_to_class, only set get_<name>_display if the model class does not already have that attribute.
  - Similarly, in DateField.contribute_to_class, only set get_next_by_<name> and get_previous_by_<name> if those methods do not already exist on the class.
- Files to change: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py (two small changes).
- Rationale: This preserves the ability for model authors to override those generated accessors in their model classes, while still providing the generated methods when they are not defined by the user.

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"

There's no numeric or positional hardcoded constant dependent on the assumption. The fix turns the installation into conditional behavior instead of unconditional. No other hardcoded constants in DeferredAttribute or RegisterLookupMixin depend on this assumption.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"

  - For inherited/abstract fields: When an abstract base class has a field, ModelBase copies fields into the child class and calls add_to_class on the new_field during new class creation (see lines ~271–279/277). Root cause

1) Verify Field.contribute_to_class claim
- Why I looked: The draft states Field.contribute_to_class unconditionally installs get_<field>_display and overwrites user methods. I needed to find the exact code lines to confirm.
- What I inspected: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py around Field.contribute_to_class.
- What I found: In fields/__init__.py, Field.contribute_to_class contains:
  - lines 756-766 show the body of contribute_to_class and the install of the descriptor and the generated accessor.
  - Specifically (lines quoted from the file):
    - line 756-759: self.set_attributes_from_name(name); self.model = cls; cls._meta.add_field(...)
    - lines 763-765: descriptor install with a guarded hasattr check for attname
    - lines 765-767: the unconditional install:
      - setattr(cls, 'get_%s_display' % self.name,
                partialmethod(cls._get_FIELD_display, field=self))
- Analysis: This confirms the claim: the code uses setattr to always assign 'get_<field>_display' on cls when self.choices is not None. There is no check for an existing attribute with that name.

2) Verify DateField.contribute_to_class claim
- Why I looked: The draft says DateField.contribute_to_class unconditionally installs get_next_by_<field> and get_previous_by_<field>.
- What I inspected: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py around DateField.contribute_to_class.
- What I found: In the DateField subclass (lines 1189-1199), the method contains:
  - call to super().contribute_to_class(...)
  - then unconditional setattr calls:
    - setattr(cls, 'get_next_by_%s' % self.name,
             partialmethod(cls._get_next_or_previous_by_FIELD, field=self, is_next=True))
    - setattr(cls, 'get_previous_by_%s' % self.name,
             partialmethod(cls._get_next_or_previous_by_FIELD, field=self, is_next=False))
- Analysis: This confirms the draft: DateField installs those accessors unconditionally (guarded only by not self.null), without checking whether such methods already exist on the class.

3) Verify Model class construction ordering claim
- Why I looked: The draft attributes the overwrite to the ordering in ModelBase.__new__/add_to_class — user methods are attached before field.contribute_to_class runs. I needed the relevant metaclass code to verify ordering.
- What I inspected: django/db/models/base.py in ModelBase.__new__ and add_to_class.
- What I found:
  - In ModelBase.__new__ (lines ~89-99 and 157-161), attrs are split into:
    - new_attrs: attributes with no contribute_to_class are passed to type.__new__ so they become part of the class object at creation time.
    - contributable_attrs: attributes with contribute_to_class are collected and added later.
  - After type.__new__ creates new_class, ModelBase loops over contributable_attrs and calls new_class.add_to_class(obj_name, obj) (lines 157-161).
  - add_to_class (lines 323-327) does:
    - if _has_contribute_to_class(value): value.contribute_to_class(cls, name)
    - else: setattr(cls, name, value)
- Analysis: This confirms that normal methods and attributes defined in the model body (including user-defined get_<field>_display methods, which are normal functions and do not have contribute_to_class) end up on the class before fields' contribute_to_class is invoked. Therefore, a later unconditional setattr in contribute_to_class will overwrite them.

bug_report.Title: Field.contribute_to_class unconditionally overwrites user-defined get_<field>_display (Django 2.2+)
bug_report.Description: Model-defined overrides of get_<field>_display() (for example get_foo_bar_display) are ignored in the examined Django 2.2+ code. During model class creation generated accessor methods are installed onto the model class after user-defined methods are attached, and those generated methods replace any existing attributes with the same name.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py :: Field.contribute_to_class — the method unconditionally assigns a generated accessor using setattr(cls, 'get_%s_display' % self.name, partialmethod(cls._get_FIELD_display, field=self)) when a field has choices. This encodes the assumption that it is always safe to overwrite any existing attribute named get_<field>_display on the model class, which is not true given the model-class construction ordering. (See fields/__init__.py: lines that call setattr for 'get_%s_display'.)

2) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py :: DateField.contribute_to_class — the method unconditionally assigns generated accessors using setattr(cls, 'get_next_by_%s' % self.name, ...) and setattr(cls, 'get_previous_by_%s' % self.name, ...) when appropriate. This encodes the assumption that it is always safe to overwrite any existing get_next_by_<field> and get_previous_by_<field> methods on the model class. (See fields/__init__.py: lines that call setattr for 'get_next_by_%s' and 'get_previous_by_%s'.)

3) django/db/models/base.py :: ModelBase.__new__ / add_to_class — the metaclass separates attributes that implement contribute_to_class from normal attributes and passes non-contributable attributes (including user-defined methods declared in the model body) into type.__new__ so they become part of the class object first; contributable attributes (field instances) are added afterward via add_to_class which calls value.contribute_to_class(cls, name). Because contribute_to_class for Field and DateField performs unconditional setattr after user methods already exist on the class, user-defined methods named get_<field>_display, get_next_by_<field>, or get_previous_by_<field> can be replaced.

4) Relationship between generated accessors and existing attributes — the generated accessor names correspond exactly to the field name (e.g., get_{field.name}_display, get_next_by_{field.name}, get_previous_by_{field.name}), and the code as written installs those names unconditionally. Given the metaclass ordering, this means the generated accessors will replace any user-defined attributes with the same names; the correct diagnostic relationship is that generated accessors for a field name will collide with any pre-existing attribute of the same name on the model class.
StepsToReproduce: Create and save an instance: FooBar.objects.create(foo_bar=1) or instantiate in the shell: FooBar(foo_bar=1).
Call print(str(instance)) or evaluate instance.__str__() / instance.get_foo_bar_display() and observe the returned value.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a model defines a method named get_<field>_display (e.g. get_foo_bar_display), calls to that method (including calls made from __str__ or other model code) should invoke the user-defined method and return its result (e.g. "something").
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: In the examined Django 2.2+ code, a user-defined get_<field>_display method is overwritten at class-creation time by a generated accessor installed by Field.contribute_to_class; the generated accessor is called instead and returns the field's choice label (e.g. 'foo' or 'bar') rather than the user method's result.

        Return an alternative connection to be used when there is no need to
        access the main database, specifically for test db creation/deletion.
        This also prevents the production database from being exposed to
        potential child threads while (or after) the test database is destroyed.
        Refs #10868, #17786, #16969.
        """

    def schema_editor(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """
        Return a new instance of this backend's SchemaEditor.
        """
        if self.SchemaEditorClass is None:
            raise NotImplementedError(
                'The SchemaEditorClass attribute of this database wrapper is still None')
        return self.SchemaEditorClass(self, *args, **kwargs)

    def on_commit(self, func):
        if self.in_atomic_block:
            # Transaction in progress; save for execution on commit.
            self.run_on_commit.append((set(self.savepoint_ids), func))
        elif not self.get_autocommit():
            raise TransactionManagementError('on_commit() cannot be used in manual transaction management')
        else:
            # No transaction in progress and in autocommit mode; execute
            # immediately.
            func()

    def run_and_clear_commit_hooks(self):
        self.validate_no_atomic_block()
        current_run_on_commit = self.run_on_commit
        self.run_on_commit = []
        while current_run_on_commit:
            sids, func = current_run_on_commit.pop(0)
            func()

    @contextmanager
    def execute_wrapper(self, wrapper):
        """
        Return a context manager under which the wrapper is applied to suitable
        database query executions.
        """
        self.execute_wrappers.append(wrapper)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            self.execute_wrappers.pop()

    def copy(self, alias=None):
        """
        Return a copy of this connection.

        For tests that require two connections to the same database.
        """
        settings_dict = copy.deepcopy(self.settings_dict)
        if alias is None:
            alias = self.alias
        return type(self)(settings_dict, alias)

I verified the draft report against the repository sources to confirm which claims are supported, which need correction/softening, and whether any secondary findings were omitted. Below are step-by-step verifications and findings.

A. Files/methods checked and why
- django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py — to confirm the SQLite backend's DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature implementation and how _get_test_db_name() is used. I expected to see whether the signature includes the computed test DB name (from TEST['NAME']) or whether it only used the production NAME.
- django/db/backends/base/creation.py — to confirm the BaseDatabaseCreation.test_db_signature canonical behavior and whether it includes self._get_test_db_name().
- django/test/utils.py — to confirm how the test runner groups databases (get_unique_databases_and_mirrors / setup_databases) and whether it keys/grouping by connection.creation.test_db_signature().
- tests/admin_views/test_multidb.py — to confirm the test scenario (setUpTestData creating users/saving across aliases) referenced in the bug report.

I fetched each file and inspected the relevant method bodies and call sites.

B. What the code shows (quoting lines and locations)

1) sqlite3 DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature
- File: django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py
- Relevant lines:
  - _get_test_db_name uses TEST['NAME'] or ':memory:' and maps ':memory:' to a shared memory URI per alias:
    - lines 17-21:
      test_database_name = self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['NAME'] or ':memory:'
      if test_database_name == ':memory:':
          return 'file:memorydb_%s?mode=memory&cache=shared' % self.connection.alias
  - test_db_signature obtains test_database_name but builds signature from production NAME only, and only appends alias for in-memory special-case:
    - lines 97-101:
      test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name()
      sig = [self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']]
      if self.is_in_memory_db(test_database_name):
          sig.append(self.connection.alias)
      return tuple(sig)

Analysis: sqlite3.test_db_signature calls _get_test_db_name() (so it is aware of the computed test name), but the returned signature tuple includes only connection.settings_dict['NAME'] (the configured/production NAME). The computed test database name (which picks up TEST['NAME'] when present, or a memory URI) is not included in the signature except for a special-case addition of the alias when the test database is in-memory.

2) BaseDatabaseCreation.test_db_signature
- File: django/db/backends/base/creation.py
- Relevant lines:
  - lines 285-297:
    def test_db_signature(self):
        settings_dict = self.connection.settings_dict
        return (
            settings_dict['HOST'],
            settings_dict['PORT'],
            settings_dict['ENGINE'],
            self._get_test_db_name(),
        )

Analysis: the base-class test_db_signature includes self._get_test_db_name() as a core component of the signature. That means the standard/backing contract is that the computed test database name (which reflects TEST['NAME'] when provided) is part of the identity used to deduplicate test DB creation.

3) Test runner grouping by signature
- File: django/test/utils.py
- Relevant lines:
  - get_unique_databases_and_mirrors uses connection.creation.test_db_signature() as the key to group aliases:
    - lines 270-275:
      item = test_databases.setdefault(
          connection.creation.test_db_signature(),
          (connection.settings_dict['NAME'], set())
      )
      item[1].add(alias)
  - setup_databases calls get_unique_databases_and_mirrors() and then creates the DB only once per signature and marks other aliases as mirrors:
    - lines 154-175 and 182-185 show the first alias creates the test DB and other aliases are configured as mirrors via set_as_test_mirror.

Analysis: the test runner will only create one test DB per signature returned by connection.creation.test_db_signature(). Other aliases that map to the same signature are treated as mirrors (i.e., they will be configured to point to the primary DB's NAME). Therefore, if a backend's test_db_signature omits the computed test DB name, aliases that were intended to use different TEST['NAME'] persistent files can be grouped together incorrectly.

4) Test reproduction path and manifestation
- File: tests/admin_views/test_multidb.py
- Relevant lines:
  - setUpTestData iterates connections and creates a superuser and saves Book objects using each alias:
    - lines 33-44:
      for db in connections:
          Router.target_db = db
          cls.superusers[db] = User.objects.create_superuser(
              username='admin', password='something', email='test@test.org',
          )
          b = Book(name='Test Book')
          b.save(using=db)
          cls.test_book_ids[db] = b.id

Analysis: This test performs writes to each database alias during class-level setup. If two aliases are incorrectly configured to use the same underlying SQLite file (because they were grouped by a signature that omitted TEST['NAME']), concurrent/open transactions and writes can collide, producing sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked — exactly what the bug report observed.

C. Verification of draft report claims against the code

- Claim: sqlite3 DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature assumes production NAME alone uniquely identifies the test DB and ignores computed test DB name.
  - Verified. The code builds sig = [self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']] and does not include test_database_name (the output of _get_test_db_name()) except for an in-memory alias special-case. (See sqlite3/creation.py lines 97-101 and _get_test_db_name implementation at 17-21.)

- Claim: Test runner groups database aliases by connection.creation.test_db_signature(), causing aliases with distinct TEST['NAME'] to be treated as mirrors if sqlite3 signature omitted the computed name.
  - Verified. get_unique_databases_and_mirrors uses connection.creation.test_db_signature() as the grouping key (django/test/utils.py lines 270-275). setup_databases then creates one DB per signature and sets other aliases as mirrors (lines 160-185).

- Claim: BaseDatabaseCreation.test_db_signature uses self._get_test_db_name() and sqlite3 deviated from the base-class pattern.
  - Verified. Base class includes self._get_test_db_name() (base/creation.py lines 285-297). sqlite3's override omits it from the returned signature (sqlite3/creation.py lines 97-101).

- Claim: The concrete consequence is that two aliases can end up pointing to the same SQLite file causing "database is locked" during concurrent writes in setUpTestData.
  - Supported by the test behavior seen in tests/admin_views/test_multidb.py and the reported stack trace in the original bug report (writes during create_superuser -> User.save). The code in the test performs writes across aliases at class setup time, which matches the observed failure mode.

bug_report.Title: admin_views.test_multidb fails with persistent per-alias SQLite test DBs: sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked
bug_report.Description: When using persistent per-alias SQLite test files (TEST['NAME']) together with --keepdb, tests that touch multiple database aliases can fail with sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked because two distinct aliases can be grouped as the same underlying test database and both attempt concurrent writes to the same file.
bug_report.RootCause:
1. django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py :: DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature builds the test-database signature from connection.settings_dict['NAME'] (the configured/production NAME) and omits the computed test database name returned by self._get_test_db_name(), except for a special-case addition of the alias for in-memory URIs. Evidence: sqlite3/creation.py lines showing _get_test_db_name() uses TEST['NAME'] and test_db_signature constructs sig = [self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']] (sqlite3/creation.py lines 17-21 and 97-101).

2. django/test/utils.py :: get_unique_databases_and_mirrors and setup_databases group database aliases by connection.creation.test_db_signature() and create one test database per signature, configuring other aliases with the same signature as mirrors. Because the sqlite3 signature omits the computed test DB name, aliases configured with distinct TEST['NAME'] values can receive identical signatures and be incorrectly treated as mirrors. Evidence: test utils code that keys test_databases by connection.creation.test_db_signature() and then creates the DB once per signature (django/test/utils.py lines 270-275 and 154-185).

3. django/db/backends/base/creation.py :: BaseDatabaseCreation.test_db_signature includes self._get_test_db_name() in the signature. The sqlite3 implementation therefore deviates from the base-class pattern/expectation that the computed test DB name (which reflects TEST['NAME'] when present) is part of the test-database identity used to deduplicate test DB creation. Evidence: base class test_db_signature returns a tuple including self._get_test_db_name() (base/creation.py lines 285-297).

4. The practical consequence: when two database aliases are intended to use different persistent SQLite test files (different TEST['NAME'] values) but are grouped by an incorrect signature, both aliases can be configured to use the same physical SQLite file. Tests that perform writes across aliases during setup (e.g., setUpTestData) can then perform concurrent or overlapping writes against the same SQLite file and raise sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked. Concrete repro path observed in tests/admin_views/test_multidb.MultiDatabaseTests.setUpTestData where create_superuser / model.save() are invoked for each alias. Evidence: tests/admin_views/test_multidb.py lines 33-44 and the original failure stack trace in the bug report showing the error during User.save() in setUpTestData.

5. Correct relationship that is missing from the sqlite3 signature (diagnostic statement): the test database identity used to deduplicate/test-creation decisions must reflect the computed test database name that will actually be created/used by the test runner (i.e., the value returned by _get_test_db_name(), which honors TEST['NAME'] and special memory URIs). The in-memory special-case (distinct in-memory DB URIs per alias) must continue to be handled so in-memory test DBs remain distinct as appropriate.
StepsToReproduce: Configure two sqlite DATABASES aliases (e.g. 'default' and 'other') and set distinct persistent test file names: TEST['NAME'] = 'test_default.sqlite3' and TEST['NAME'] = 'test_other.sqlite3'.

    class TypeSerializer(BaseSerializer):
        def serialize(self):
            special_cases = [
                (models.Model, "models.Model", []),
                (type(None), 'type(None)', []),
            ]
            for case, string, imports in special_cases:
                if case is self.value:
                    return string, set(imports)

    @staticmethod
    def _serialize_path(path):
        # path is like <module>.<qualname...> (qualname may contain dots for nested classes)
        # We want to import the real module (the importable prefix) and keep the full path for naming.
        # Split into left (all but last segment) and name (last segment)
        module_part, _ = path.rsplit(".", 1)

        # Find the longest importable module prefix from module_part (back off if needed)
        module_candidate = module_part
        while True:
            try:
                __import__(module_candidate)
                break
            except Exception:
                # Stop backing off if no more '.' to remove
                if '.' not in module_candidate:
                    # give up and use the original module_part
                    module_candidate = module_part
                    break
                module_candidate = module_candidate.rsplit('.', 1)[0]

            imports = {"from django.db import models"}
            name = "models.%s" % path.rsplit(".", 1)[1]
        else:
            imports = {"import %s" % module_candidate}
            name = path
