bug_report.Title: django.contrib.syndication.views.Feed.get_feed does not forward item_comments to feed.add_item
bug_report.Description: django.contrib.syndication.views.Feed.get_feed does not pass an item-level comments value to feed.add_item(), preventing Feed subclasses from defining item_comments(self, item) to set per-item comments. As a result callers must supply a 'comments' key via item_extra_kwargs to include comments in generated RSS items, despite the feed generator already supporting a comments field.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Missing forwarding of item-level comments in views.Feed.get_feed — location: django/contrib/syndication/views.py, class Feed, method get_feed (feed.add_item(...) invocation at lines 202–218). The method constructs explicit standard item arguments but never obtains or forwards the per-item item_comments value via _get_dynamic_attr('item_comments', item); only **self.item_extra_kwargs(item) is expanded.

2) views.Feed.get_feed treats item-level comments as not a first-class forwarded field — location: same as (1). The implementation makes an implicit assumption that callers will provide non-standard keys (including 'comments') through item_extra_kwargs rather than forwarding item_comments directly.

3) The feed generator already defines and emits a comments field — location: django/utils/feedgenerator.py, class SyndicationFeed.add_item (signature includes comments=None and stores item['comments'], lines 85–88 and 106) and class Rss201rev2Feed.add_item_elements (emits <comments> when item['comments'] is not None, lines 262–265). Therefore the missing behavior is an omission in the views adapter layer, not in the generation layer.

4) Duplicate-key and precedence risk when merging item_extra_kwargs with explicit fields — location: django/contrib/syndication/views.py, get_feed (add_item call expands **self.item_extra_kwargs(item) at line 217). If a future change adds an explicit comments=... argument while still expanding item_extra_kwargs, a 'comments' key present in item_extra_kwargs(item) could cause a duplicate-key TypeError or ambiguous overriding semantics. The diagnostic requirement is that a deterministic precedence be defined: the per-item item_comments hook should be considered a standard source of the comments value, with a clear rule for how it relates to any 'comments' key present in item_extra_kwargs (for example: prefer a non-None item_comments value, otherwise fall back to item_extra_kwargs['comments']).

5) Other arbitrary extra keys (e.g., geometry) are currently passed via item_extra_kwargs and must be preserved — location: django/contrib/gis/feeds.py, class Feed (subclassing views.Feed), methods feed_extra_kwargs and item_extra_kwargs return {'geometry': ...} (lines 136–140). Any change to how extra kwargs are merged must maintain forwarding of such non-standard keys to feed.add_item so existing consumers (Geo feeds) continue to receive them.

6) Missing tests and documentation coverage for item_comments — evidence: no occurrences of 'item_comments' found in the codebase search. There are no existing tests exercising the item_comments hook; this omission likely allowed the regression to go undetected.
StepsToReproduce: Create a Feed subclass and implement item_comments(self, item) to return a comments URL or text for each item.
Wire the Feed to a URL in a Django project and request the RSS feed from that URL.
Inspect the generated feed output for the item <comments> element — observe that it is absent.
As a control, implement item_extra_kwargs(self, item) to return {'comments': '<url-or-text>'}, request the feed again, and observe that the <comments> element is present.

Optionally, implement both item_comments and item_extra_kwargs returning different values and observe which value is used (current behavior: item_comments is not forwarded by get_feed and thus has no effect unless comments is supplied via item_extra_kwargs).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a Feed subclass defines item_comments(self, item), the returned value should be used for the per-item comments field passed to the feed generator so that RSS output includes an <comments> element for that item. If both item_comments and item_extra_kwargs provide a comments value, a deterministic precedence should apply (diagnostically: item_comments should be considered a first-class per-item source and take precedence when it returns a non-None value; otherwise fall back to any 'comments' in item_extra_kwargs). Other arbitrary keys returned by item_extra_kwargs (for example, 'geometry' used by Geo feeds) should continue to be forwarded unchanged to feed.add_item.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Defining item_comments(self, item) in a Feed subclass has no effect: views.Feed.get_feed does not forward item_comments to feed.add_item, so per-item comments are not emitted via the item_comments hook. Only providing 'comments' via item_extra_kwargs results in comments being present in RSS output. The codebase contains no tests referencing item_comments and no documentation examples exercising the hook.

    as actually performing it against a live database.

    optionally specified by the user (e.g. custom Python code snippets)

    considered immutable.

    reduces_to_sql = True

    # DDL transaction support (i.e., does it have no DDL, like RunPython)

        under django.db.migrations), positional arguments, and keyword
        arguments.

        return (
            self.__class__.__name__,
            self._constructor_args[0],
            self._constructor_args[1],
        )

        so that it matches what this migration would perform.

        raise NotImplementedError('subclasses of Operation must provide a state_forwards() method')

        Perform the mutation on the database schema in the normal
        (forwards) direction.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError('subclasses of Operation must provide a database_forwards() method')

    def database_backwards(self, app_label, schema_editor, from_state, to_state):

        Perform the mutation on the database schema in the reverse
        direction - e.g. if this were CreateModel, it would in fact
        drop the model's table.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError('subclasses of Operation must provide a database_backwards() method')

        """
        return "%s: %s" % (self.__class__.__name__, self._constructor_args)

class MigrationOptimizer:
    """
    Power the optimization process, where you provide a list of Operations
    and you are returned a list of equal or shorter length - operations
    are merged into one if possible.

    For example, a CreateModel and an AddField can be optimized into a
    new CreateModel, and CreateModel and DeleteModel can be optimized into
    nothing.
    """

    def optimize(self, operations, app_label):
        """
        Main optimization entry point. Pass in a list of Operation instances,
        get out a new list of Operation instances.

        Unfortunately, due to the scope of the optimization (two combinable
        operations might be separated by several hundred others), this can't be
        done as a peephole optimization with checks/output implemented on
        the Operations themselves; instead, the optimizer looks at each
        individual operation and scans forwards in the list to see if there
        are any matches, stopping at boundaries - operations which can't
        be optimized over (RunSQL, operations on the same field/model, etc.)

        The inner loop is run until the starting list is the same as the result
        list, and then the result is returned. This means that operation
        optimization must be stable and always return an equal or shorter list.
        """
        # Internal tracking variable for test assertions about # of loops
        if app_label is None:
            raise TypeError('app_label must be a str.')
        self._iterations = 0
        while True:
            result = self.optimize_inner(operations, app_label)
            self._iterations += 1
            if result == operations:
                return result
            operations = result

    def optimize_inner(self, operations, app_label):
        """Inner optimization loop."""
        new_operations = []
        for i, operation in enumerate(operations):
            right = True  # Should we reduce on the right or on the left.
            # Compare it to each operation after it
            for j, other in enumerate(operations[i + 1:]):
                result = operation.reduce(other, app_label)
                if isinstance(result, list):
                    in_between = operations[i + 1:i + j + 1]
                    if right:
                        new_operations.extend(in_between)
                        new_operations.extend(result)
                    elif all(op.reduce(other, app_label) is True for op in in_between):
                        # Perform a left reduction if all of the in-between
                        # operations can optimize through other.
                        new_operations.extend(result)
                        new_operations.extend(in_between)
                    else:
                        # Otherwise keep trying.
                        new_operations.append(operation)
                        break
                    new_operations.extend(operations[i + j + 2:])
                    return new_operations
                elif not result:
                    # Can't perform a right reduction.
                    right = False
            else:
                new_operations.append(operation)
        return new_operations

Root cause
- MigrationAutodetector._detect_changes emits AddIndex operations (generate_added_indexes) before emitting AlterOrderWithRespectTo operations (generate_altered_order_with_respect_to). - AlterOrderWithRespectTo's database_forwards is the operation that creates the _order field. Emitting it earlier guarantees that any AddIndex generated afterward will be applied after the _order field exists.
- The rest of the code (CreateModel.reduce, AddIndex.database_forwards, optimizer) is consistent with this ordering and requires no changes.

4) MigrationOptimizer.optimize behavior (preserving in-between operations on right reduction)
- Why I checked: the draft claims the optimizer preserves operations that stood between a CreateModel and a later AlterOrderWithRespectTo when doing a right reduction, so an AddIndex that was emitted earlier can remain before the folded CreateModel.
- What I fetched: MigrationOptimizer.optimize and optimize_inner in django/db/migrations/optimizer.py.
- What I found: optimize_inner scans each operation and searches forward for a matching operation to reduce. If operation.reduce(other) returns a list, it computes in_between = operations[i+1:i+j+1]. - Analysis: This behavior confirms the draft's claim: a right reduction will leave the in-between operations before the reduction result, which allows an AddIndex emitted earlier to remain earlier in the final list even after CreateModel+AlterOrderWithRespectTo folding.

bug_report.Title: AddIndex(fields=['look','_order']) generated/applied before AlterOrderWithRespectTo — migrations fail because implicit _order column does not exist
bug_report.Description: When a model declares order_with_respect_to and an Index references the implicit '_order' field (for example, Index(fields=['look', '_order'])), makemigrations can emit an AddIndex operation that references '_order' before it emits an AlterOrderWithRespectTo operation that creates the implicit column. Applying the resulting migration fails because the AddIndex operation runs while the '_order' column does not yet exist in the database.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:MigrationAutodetector._detect_changes (generate_added_indexes / generate_altered_order_with_respect_to)
   - _detect_changes calls generate_added_indexes() before generate_altered_order_with_respect_to(), so AddIndex operations can be appended into self.generated_operations earlier than the AlterOrderWithRespectTo operation that creates the implicit '_order' column. (See the generate_added_indexes()/generate_altered_order_with_respect_to call sequence in _detect_changes.)

2) django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:add_operation and _build_migration_list / _sort_migrations / _optimize_migrations
   - add_operation sets operation._auto_deps and appends (or inserts) operations into generated_operations in emission order. The generated_operations list is later chopped and sorted into migrations by _build_migration_list and _sort_migrations and then optimized in _optimize_migrations. These pieces preserve the relative ordering that can leave an earlier-emitted AddIndex before a later-emitted AlterOrderWithRespectTo in the final migration operations list.

3) django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:CreateModel.reduce
   - CreateModel.reduce contains a reduction that folds an AlterOrderWithRespectTo into a CreateModel by adding 'order_with_respect_to' to the CreateModel.options. That folding is performed when the optimizer attempts to reduce a CreateModel with a later AlterOrderWithRespectTo, producing a CreateModel that implies the implicit '_order' column exists as part of the CreateModel's effect.

4) django/db/migrations/optimizer.py:MigrationOptimizer.optimize
   - The optimizer performs right-side reductions and, when a reduction is applied on the right, it preserves the slice of operations that were in-between the pair (the in_between slice is copied before the reduction result). As a result, an AddIndex that was emitted between a CreateModel and its corresponding AlterOrderWithRespectTo can remain earlier than the folded CreateModel in the optimized operations list.

5) django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:AlterOrderWithRespectTo.database_forwards
   - AlterOrderWithRespectTo.database_forwards is the operation that actually creates (or removes) the implicit '_order' database column: it obtains to_model._meta.get_field('_order') and calls schema_editor.add_field(...) when adding order_with_respect_to. Therefore the database column '_order' comes into existence only once this operation (or an equivalent CreateModel that includes the option) has been applied.

6) django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:AddIndex.database_forwards (and state_forwards)
   - AddIndex.state_forwards appends the index to the model state's 'indexes' option, and AddIndex.database_forwards calls schema_editor.add_index(model, self.index). There is no implicit creation of the '_order' column by AddIndex; if the index references a non-existent column (like '_order' before AlterOrderWithRespectTo has run), schema_editor.add_index will fail. Any operation that produces DDL referencing the implicit '_order' column (AddIndex, AddConstraint, etc.) is subject to this ordering requirement.

Combined effect: the observed failure arises from the combination of (a) autodetector emitting AddIndex before emitting AlterOrderWithRespectTo, (b) add_operation/appending and migration chopping/sorting/optimizing preserving that relative emission order, and (c) CreateModel.reduce + MigrationOptimizer.optimize folding behavior that can produce a CreateModel that implies creation of '_order' while leaving AddIndex positioned earlier in the final operations list. The code paths above are the locations where this ordering behavior is encoded and where the mismatch between "when an index is emitted" and "when the implicit column is created" manifests.
StepsToReproduce: Define a new model with Meta.order_with_respect_to = 'look' and an Index that includes the implicit field, e.g. Index(fields=['look', '_order']).
Run python manage.py makemigrations to generate migrations for the new model.

Inspect the generated migration file: confirm the sequence contains CreateModel(...), AddIndex(model='lookimage', fields=['look','_order']), ..., AlterOrderWithRespectTo(name='lookimage', order_with_respect_to='look').
Run python manage.py migrate to apply the migration.
Observe the migration failing when applying AddIndex due to a missing column '_order'.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The generated migration sequence ensures the implicit '_order' column (created by AlterOrderWithRespectTo or by a CreateModel that includes order_with_respect_to) is created before any migration operation that performs database DDL referencing that column (such as AddIndex or AddConstraint). Migrations should apply successfully and an index on ['look', '_order'] should be created only after the '_order' column exists.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Makemigrations (autodetector) generates a migration where AddIndex(fields=['look','_order']) appears before the AlterOrderWithRespectTo that creates the implicit '_order' column; running migrate fails when the AddIndex operation attempts to create an index on the non-existent '_order' column.

Rationale and risk assessment
- These three locations are the central points where a filtered QuerySet is turned into choices for UI presentation. Distinctly deduplicating the queryset is the correct fix because:
  - The intent of choices is to show each related target instance once (selecting by primary key).
  - Other code in the admin already uses distinct() in similar places (AllValuesFieldListFilter).
  - Using distinct() is minimal and targeted — it only affects presentation and form validation/queryset used by ModelChoiceField, and it prevents duplicate choices visible to the user.
- Potential risks:
  - distinct() interacts with ORDER BY in SQL — in rare cases backends or combinations of annotations/orderings may raise errors or change results. However, Django already uses distinct().order_by(...) in other places, and when order_by is provided we call distinct() before order_by to match that pattern.
  - If a codepath relied on duplicated rows for some reason (unlikely for choice lists), that behavior changes; but duplicates in a select box are almost always a bug, not a feature.

Suggested regression test

- In apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield: call .distinct() after complex_filter

- Root cause and location: the root cause is omission of deduplication when building choice lists. Primary locations: Field.get_choices (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py::Field.get_choices) and ForeignObjectRel.get_choices (django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py::ForeignObjectRel.get_choices). These iterate qs = <manager>.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) without calling .distinct().
- Proposed fix strategy: after applying complex_filter(limit_choices_to) call .distinct() on the queryset (before applying order_by). Also apply .distinct() when forms apply limit_choices_to to ModelChoiceField querysets (django/forms/models.py::apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield) so forms and validation use the same de-duplicated queryset.
- Hardcoded values/constants: no numeric constants must be changed. The only relevant hardcoded strings/values are BLANK_CHOICE_DASH (["", "---------"]) and the fallback 'pk' attname; those remain correct. The fix is behavioral (call .distinct()), not changing constants.
- Add/override methods: none required. Change existing methods (three locations) only.
- Known investigation gaps: I did not run a concrete trace with actual model rows/SQL to show the duplicate rows before/after .distinct(), and I did not run/update the regression test in the repo — the proposed fix needs a regression test (Q() involving a join) to be added.

===MID_LEVEL===

### Finding 1: Field.get_choices builds choices from non-distinct queryset (Checkpoint 1 & 3)
What was discovered and why it matters: Field.get_choices (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py::Field.get_choices) does:
- qs = rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
- then iterates qs to return [(choice_func(x), str(x)) for x in qs]
Because complex_filter(limit_choices_to) can produce JOIN-induced duplicate rows for the same model instance, get_choices can produce duplicate options. This is the primary root cause.

### Finding 2: Reverse-rel analog also uses non-distinct queryset (Checkpoint 3)
What was discovered and why it matters: ForeignObjectRel.get_choices (django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py::ForeignObjectRel.get_choices) performs the same pattern:
- qs = self.related_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
- returns [(x.pk, str(x)) for x in qs]
It therefore shares the same duplication problem for reverse-rel choice lists.

### Finding 3: Model form helper applies limit_choices_to without distinct (Checkpoint 3)
What was discovered and why it matters: apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield (django/forms/models.py) does:
- formfield.queryset = formfield.queryset.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
It assigns the filtered queryset to the ModelChoiceField without calling .distinct(), so ModelChoiceIterator (which simply iterates formfield.queryset) will render duplicate options too. Fixing get_choices alone would not cover ModelChoiceField behavior in forms — apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield must be updated.

### Finding 4: ModelChoiceIterator iterates queryset as-is (Checkpoint 3)
What was discovered and why it matters: ModelChoiceIterator (django/forms/models.py::ModelChoiceIterator.__iter__) yields items by iterating self.queryset (optionally .iterator()) and has no deduplication. This explains why a duplicated queryset produces duplicate choice options in forms unless the queryset was distincted earlier.

### Finding 5: Admin callers rely on get_choices (Checkpoint 3)
What was discovered and why it matters: admin filters/options call Field.get_choices and/or remote_field.get_choices (django/contrib/admin/filters.py and django/contrib/admin/options.py). Because they rely on Field.get_choices to deduplicate, changing get_choices fixes admin UI duplicate options. Admin code already uses distinct() elsewhere (AllValuesFieldListFilter), so using distinct() here is consistent.

### Finding 6: Gaps — no concrete SQL/value trace & limited test coverage (Checkpoint 4)
What was discovered and why it matters: I did not execute a concrete trace with sample models/rows to show exact duplicate SQL rows produced by a particular Q() and I did not run or update the regression test referenced in the original bug report. The proposed change must be validated by a regression test that constructs a Q() requiring joins and asserts no duplicate choices are returned.

Thought: Phase 1 — Verification and completeness analysis

Summary of what I checked and why
- I inspected each source location named in the draft report to confirm whether the draft's claims match the actual code. Specifically I retrieved:
  - django/db/models/fields/__init__.py to verify Field.get_choices implementation and whether it deduplicates the queryset returned by complex_filter(...)
  - django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py to verify ForeignObjectRel.get_choices
  - django/forms/models.py to verify apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield and ModelChoiceIterator
  - django/contrib/admin/filters.py and django/contrib/admin/options.py to confirm admin callers that rely on Field.get_choices
  - django/db/models/query.py to confirm the behavior/definition of complex_filter
  - django/db/models/fields/related.py to locate other complex_filter usage found during search
- For each file I expected to discover whether the code:
  1) calls rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) (or equivalent),
  2) applies any deduplication (e.g., distinct()) before iterating or returning choices, and
  3) whether callers (forms/admin) rely on the methods that would be affected.

What the code shows (evidence + analysis)

1) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py::Field.get_choices
- Why I fetched it: the draft claims get_choices builds choices from rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) and iterates without deduplication.
- What I expected: to find complex_filter(...) returned queryset being iterated directly to build choices.
- What I found:
  - Field.get_choices defines:
    - choice_func = operator.attrgetter(... 'pk' or related attname)
    - qs = rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
    - if ordering: qs = qs.order_by(*ordering)
    - return (blank_choice if include_blank else []) + [(choice_func(x), str(x)) for x in qs]
  - Exact lines (from file):
    - "qs = rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)" (line 883)
    - "if ordering: qs = qs.order_by(*ordering)" (line 884-885)
    - "return ... + [(choice_func(x), str(x)) for x in qs]" (line 886-888)
- Analysis: The code indeed calls complex_filter(...) and then iterates the queryset directly to produce choice tuples. There is no call to distinct() or any other deduplication before iteration. This matches the draft claim.

2) django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py::ForeignObjectRel.get_choices
- Why I fetched it: the draft claims the reverse-rel analog also iterates complex_filter(...) without distinct().
- What I expected: to find self.related_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) used and iterated without deduplication.
- What I found:
  - get_choices does:
    - limit_choices_to = limit_choices_to or self.limit_choices_to
    - qs = self.related_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
    - if ordering: qs = qs.order_by(*ordering)
    - return (blank_choice if include_blank else []) + [(x.pk, str(x)) for x in qs]
  - Exact lines:
    - "qs = self.related_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)" (line 153)
    - "if ordering: qs = qs.order_by(*ordering)" (line 154-155)
    - "return ... + [(x.pk, str(x)) for x in qs]" (line 156-158)
- Analysis: This directly supports the draft claim: the reverse-rel choice builder also iterates the queryset returned by complex_filter without deduplication.

3) django/forms/models.py::apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield
- Why I fetched it: the draft claims apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield assigns formfield.queryset = formfield.queryset.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) without calling distinct().
- What I expected: to find that assignment and no distinct() call.
- What I found:
  - The function contains:
    - if hasattr(formfield, 'queryset') and hasattr(formfield, 'get_limit_choices_to'):
        limit_choices_to = formfield.get_limit_choices_to()
        if limit_choices_to is not None:
            formfield.queryset = formfield.queryset.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)
  - Exact lines:
    - The assignment "formfield.queryset = formfield.queryset.complex_filter(limit_choices_to)" (line 103)
- Analysis: The code does assign the filtered queryset back to the field's queryset and does not call distinct(). This supports the draft's claim that ModelChoiceField's queryset can contain duplicates unless deduplicated elsewhere.

4) django/forms/models.py::ModelChoiceIterator.__iter__
- Why I fetched it: the draft claims ModelChoiceIterator iterates the queryset as-is and does no de-duplication itself.
- What I expected: to find iteration over self.queryset (or queryset.iterator()) with no distinct/de-dupe.
- What I found:
  - __iter__ does:
    - if self.field.empty_label is not None: yield ("", empty_label)
    - queryset = self.queryset
    - if not queryset._prefetch_related_lookups: queryset = queryset.iterator()
    - for obj in queryset: yield self.choice(obj)
  - Exact lines:
    - "queryset = self.queryset" (line 1157)
    - the iterator() optimization and "for obj in queryset: yield self.choice(obj)" (lines 1158-1162)
- Analysis: ModelChoiceIterator does not perform any de-duplication; it relies on the provided queryset being appropriate (unique instances). This confirms the draft's Finding 4.

5) Admin callers that rely on Field.get_choices / remote_field.get_choices
- Why I fetched admin code: the draft claims admin filters/options call get_choices and therefore can surface duplicates.
- What I expected: to find Field.get_choices being called from admin/filter code.
- What I found:
  - django/contrib/admin/filters.py:
    - RelatedFieldListFilter.field_choices returns "return field.get_choices(include_blank=False, ordering=ordering)" (line 205-208)
    - RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter.field_choices calls "return field.get_choices(include_blank=False, limit_choices_to={'pk__in': pk_qs}, ordering=ordering)" (line 428-432)
    - AllValuesFieldListFilter uses distinct() explicitly in its lookup_choices: "self.lookup_choices = queryset.distinct().order_by(field.name).values_list(...)" (line 393)
  - django/contrib/admin/options.py:
    - formfield_for_choice_field sets kwargs['choices'] = db_field.get_choices(...) when building choice form fields (lines ~189-205). Specifically "if 'choices' not in kwargs: kwargs['choices'] = db_field.get_choices(...)" (lines 200-205)
- Analysis: Admin code calls db_field.get_choices (Field.get_choices) in multiple places (RelatedFieldListFilter and formfield_for_choice_field). Those call sites will receive whatever choices get_choices returns. AllValuesFieldListFilter does use distinct() already (evidence line 393), so the behavior is inconsistent between different admin components. This supports the draft's Finding 5.

6) Definition/behavior of complex_filter
- Why I fetched query.py: to confirm what complex_filter does and that it can accept Q objects which may add arbitrary joins.
- What I expected: complex_filter takes a Q or dict and returns a clone of the QuerySet with the Q applied.
- What I found:
  - complex_filter in QuerySet:
    - If filter_obj is a Q, it clones the queryset and does clone.query.add_q(filter_obj) and returns clone (lines 978-981)
    - This confirms that complex_filter accepts Q objects and adds them to the query, which can introduce JOINs when lookups cross relationships.
- Analysis: The function behaves as the draft assumes: complex_filter accepts Q objects that may produce additional joins.

7) Other locations using complex_filter
- Why I searched: to ensure there are no other choice-building sites that use complex_filter(...) without deduplication, and to capture all secondary findings that share the same root cause.
- What I found:
  - django/db/models/fields/related.py uses qs = qs.complex_filter(self.get_limit_choices_to()) in validate() (line 924). This is used to test for existence (.exists()) and is not a choice-builder; duplicates here are less relevant to visible duplicate choices but useful to note where complex_filter is used.
- Analysis: The primary pattern of concern (building choice lists from a complex_filter result without deduplication) is present in Field.get_choices, ForeignObjectRel.get_choices, and in forms via apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield combined with ModelChoiceIterator. There are other uses of complex_filter elsewhere (e.g., validation) but they do not generate user-visible choices.

Completeness check against the investigation analysis
- The investigation analysis enumerated five core findings (get_choices, reverse get_choices, apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield, ModelChoiceIterator iteration, admin callers) and a gap about missing SQL/regression test. All these findings are supported by the code.
- I confirmed each of the primary locations in the draft and also located the exact admin call sites (RelatedFieldListFilter.field_choices and RelatedOnlyFieldListFilter.field_choices in django/contrib/admin/filters.py, and formfield_for_choice_field in django/contrib/admin/options.py).
- I also confirmed AllValuesFieldListFilter uses distinct() (django/contrib/admin/filters.py line 393) which matches the draft's note that admin code is inconsistent: some callers use distinct() already.
- The search revealed complex_filter being used in other places (e.g., fields/related.py validate) but these do not produce choices; therefore they are not part of the exact root cause pattern (duplicate choices) but are related as additional complex_filter usage.

bug_report.Title: limit_choices_to using a Q() that forces JOINs can produce duplicate options in ForeignKey/form choices
bug_report.Description: When a ForeignKey (or reverse relation) has limit_choices_to supplied as a Q() that causes SQL JOINs, the choice lists built for forms and the admin can contain duplicate options for the same related instance.
bug_report.RootCause:
The code that builds choice lists or assigns filtered querysets makes an incorrect assumption that the QuerySet returned by rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to) (or equivalent calls) yields each related model instance exactly once. When limit_choices_to is a Q() that references related tables, the SQL produced can include JOINs that cause the underlying query to return multiple rows representing the same related model instance. The following locations exhibit this incorrect assumption (each finding given equal weight):

1) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py::Field.get_choices
- Behavior: calls rel_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to), optionally applies order_by, then iterates the queryset to produce choices: [(choice_func(x), str(x)) for x in qs].
- Incorrect assumption: the queryset yields unique model instances; no deduplication is performed before iteration.

2) django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py::ForeignObjectRel.get_choices
- Behavior: calls self.related_model._default_manager.complex_filter(limit_choices_to), optionally applies order_by, then iterates the queryset to produce choices: [(x.pk, str(x)) for x in qs].
- Incorrect assumption: the queryset yields unique model instances; no deduplication is performed before iteration.

3) django/forms/models.py::apply_limit_choices_to_to_formfield
- Behavior: when a form field has a queryset and a limit_choices_to, the function assigns formfield.queryset = formfield.queryset.complex_filter(limit_choices_to).
- Incorrect assumption: the resulting queryset will not contain duplicate model instances; no deduplication is applied at assignment time.

4) django/forms/models.py::ModelChoiceIterator.__iter__
- Behavior: iterates over self.queryset (or queryset.iterator()) and yields each object's choice without performing any deduplication.
- Incorrect assumption: the iterator assumes the queryset it receives has been prepared to contain unique model instances.

5) Admin callers that rely on Field.get_choices / remote_field.get_choices
- Behavior: admin components (e.g., RelatedFieldListFilter and formfield_for_choice_field) call field.get_choices and use its returned choices in the UI.
- Incorrect assumption: these callers rely on get_choices to supply unique choice tuples; when get_choices iterates a non-deduplicated queryset, duplicate options are surfaced in the admin UI. Note: other admin code (e.g., AllValuesFieldListFilter) uses distinct() in its lookup path, which illustrates an inconsistency.

Additional context: complex_filter accepts Q objects and adds them to the query, which can introduce JOINs that cause duplicate rows for the same instance. Other uses of complex_filter exist (e.g., validation paths), but the primary user-visible duplication arises where querysets are converted into choice lists or iterated to produce choices.
StepsToReproduce: Define two or more models such that filtering the related model with a Q() causes SQL JOINs (for example, ModelA has a ForeignKey to ModelB, and ModelB has another relation that is referenced by the Q object so the filter touches an additional table).

Create database rows so that the complex_filter(limit_choices_to) condition matches the same related instance via multiple joined rows (i.e., the underlying SQL would return multiple rows with the same related PK).
Set limit_choices_to on the ForeignKey (or use a reverse relation) using a Q() that references the related table (the Q() used in step 1).
Render a ModelChoiceField for that ForeignKey (or open the admin form/filter that uses Field.get_choices / remote_field.get_choices) so that choices are built from the filtered queryset.
Observe that the rendered choices list contains duplicate entries for the same related instance.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Form fields and admin choice lists for the ForeignKey/reverse relation show each related instance exactly once (no duplicate options), regardless of whether limit_choices_to is supplied as a plain dict or as a Q() that requires JOINs.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When limit_choices_to is supplied as a Q() that causes SQL JOINs, the code iterates or presents the raw queryset returned by complex_filter(limit_choices_to) without deduplication, producing duplicate options for the same related instance in forms and admin choice lists.

"""
Functions for creating and restoring url-safe signed JSON objects.

The format used looks like this:

>>> signing.dumps("hello")
'ImhlbGxvIg:1QaUZC:YIye-ze3TTx7gtSv422nZA4sgmk'

There are two components here, separated by a ':'. The first component is a
URLsafe base64 encoded JSON of the object passed to dumps(). The second
component is a base64 encoded hmac/SHA1 hash of "$first_component:$secret"

signing.loads(s) checks the signature and returns the deserialized object.
If the signature fails, a BadSignature exception is raised.

>>> signing.loads("ImhlbGxvIg:1QaUZC:YIye-ze3TTx7gtSv422nZA4sgmk")
'hello'
>>> signing.loads("ImhlbGxvIg:1QaUZC:YIye-ze3TTx7gtSv422nZA4sgmk-modified")
...
BadSignature: Signature failed: ImhlbGxvIg:1QaUZC:YIye-ze3TTx7gtSv422nZA4sgmk-modified

You can optionally compress the JSON prior to base64 encoding it to save
space, using the compress=True argument. This checks if compression actually
helps and only applies compression if the result is a shorter string:

>>> signing.dumps(list(range(1, 20)), compress=True)
'.eJwFwcERACAIwLCF-rCiILN47r-GyZVJsNgkxaFxoDgxcOHGxMKD_T7vhAml:1QaUaL:BA0thEZrp4FQVXIXuOvYJtLJSrQ'

The fact that the string is compressed is signalled by the prefixed '.' at the
start of the base64 JSON.

There are 65 url-safe characters: the 64 used by url-safe base64 and the ':'.
These functions make use of all of them.
"""

import base64
import datetime
import json
import time
import zlib

from django.conf import settings
from django.utils import baseconv
from django.utils.crypto import constant_time_compare, salted_hmac
from django.utils.encoding import force_bytes
from django.utils.module_loading import import_string
from django.utils.regex_helper import _lazy_re_compile

_SEP_UNSAFE = _lazy_re_compile(r'^[A-z0-9-_=]*$')


class BadSignature(Exception):
    """Signature does not match."""
    pass


class SignatureExpired(BadSignature):
    """Signature timestamp is older than required max_age."""
    pass


def b64_encode(s):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(s).strip(b'=')


def b64_decode(s):
    pad = b'=' * (-len(s) % 4)
    return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + pad)


def base64_hmac(salt, value, key, algorithm='sha1'):
    return b64_encode(salted_hmac(salt, value, key, algorithm=algorithm).digest()).decode()


def get_cookie_signer(salt='django.core.signing.get_cookie_signer'):
    Signer = import_string(settings.SIGNING_BACKEND)
    key = force_bytes(settings.SECRET_KEY)  # SECRET_KEY may be str or bytes.
    return Signer(b'django.http.cookies' + key, salt=salt)


class JSONSerializer:
    """
    Simple wrapper around json to be used in signing.dumps and
    signing.loads.
    """
    def dumps(self, obj):
        return json.dumps(obj, separators=(',', ':')).encode('latin-1')

    def loads(self, data):
        return json.loads(data.decode('latin-1'))


def dumps(obj, key=None, salt='django.core.signing', serializer=JSONSerializer, compress=False):
    """
    Return URL-safe, hmac signed base64 compressed JSON string. If key is
    None, use settings.SECRET_KEY instead. The hmac algorithm is the default
    Signer algorithm.

    If compress is True (not the default), check if compressing using zlib can
    save some space. Prepend a '.' to signify compression. This is included
    in the signature, to protect against zip bombs.

    Salt can be used to namespace the hash, so that a signed string is
    only valid for a given namespace. Leaving this at the default
    value or re-using a salt value across different parts of your
    application without good cause is a security risk.

    The serializer is expected to return a bytestring.
    """
    data = serializer().dumps(obj)

    # Flag for if it's been compressed or not
    is_compressed = False

    if compress:
        # Avoid zlib dependency unless compress is being used
        compressed = zlib.compress(data)
        if len(compressed) < (len(data) - 1):
            data = compressed
            is_compressed = True
    base64d = b64_encode(data).decode()
    if is_compressed:
        base64d = '.' + base64d
    return TimestampSigner(key, salt=salt).sign(base64d)


def loads(s, key=None, salt='django.core.signing', serializer=JSONSerializer, max_age=None):
    """
    Reverse of dumps(), raise BadSignature if signature fails.

    The serializer is expected to accept a bytestring.
    """
    # TimestampSigner.unsign() returns str but base64 and zlib compression
    # operate on bytes.
    base64d = TimestampSigner(key, salt=salt).unsign(s, max_age=max_age).encode()
    decompress = base64d[:1] == b'.'
    if decompress:
        # It's compressed; uncompress it first
        base64d = base64d[1:]
    data = b64_decode(base64d)
    if decompress:
        data = zlib.decompress(data)
    return serializer().loads(data)


class Signer:
    # RemovedInDjango40Warning.
    legacy_algorithm = 'sha1'

    def __init__(self, key=None, sep=':', salt=None, algorithm=None):
        self.key = key or settings.SECRET_KEY
        self.sep = sep
        if _SEP_UNSAFE.match(self.sep):
            raise ValueError(
                'Unsafe Signer separator: %r (cannot be empty or consist of '
                'only A-z0-9-_=)' % sep,
            )
        self.salt = salt or '%s.%s' % (self.__class__.__module__, self.__class__.__name__)
        # RemovedInDjango40Warning: when the deprecation ends, replace with:
        # self.algorithm = algorithm or 'sha256'
        self.algorithm = algorithm or settings.DEFAULT_HASHING_ALGORITHM

    def signature(self, value):
        return base64_hmac(self.salt + 'signer', value, self.key, algorithm=self.algorithm)

    def _legacy_signature(self, value):
        # RemovedInDjango40Warning.
        return base64_hmac(self.salt + 'signer', value, self.key, algorithm=self.legacy_algorithm)

    def sign(self, value):
        return '%s%s%s' % (value, self.sep, self.signature(value))

    def unsign(self, signed_value):
        if self.sep not in signed_value:
            raise BadSignature('No "%s" found in value' % self.sep)
        value, sig = signed_value.rsplit(self.sep, 1)
        if (
            constant_time_compare(sig, self.signature(value)) or (
                self.legacy_algorithm and
                constant_time_compare(sig, self._legacy_signature(value))
            )
        ):
            return value
        raise BadSignature('Signature "%s" does not match' % sig)


class TimestampSigner(Signer):

    def timestamp(self):
        return baseconv.base62.encode(int(time.time()))

    def sign(self, value):
        value = '%s%s%s' % (value, self.sep, self.timestamp())
        return super().sign(value)

    def unsign(self, value, max_age=None):
        """
        Retrieve original value and check it wasn't signed more
        than max_age seconds ago.
        """
        result = super().unsign(value)
        value, timestamp = result.rsplit(self.sep, 1)
        timestamp = baseconv.base62.decode(timestamp)
        if max_age is not None:
            if isinstance(max_age, datetime.timedelta):
                max_age = max_age.total_seconds()
            # Check timestamp is not older than max_age
            age = time.time() - timestamp
            if age > max_age:
                raise SignatureExpired(
                    'Signature age %s > %s seconds' % (age, max_age))
        return value

import json

from django.contrib.messages.storage.base import BaseStorage, Message
from django.core import signing
from django.http import SimpleCookie
from django.utils.crypto import constant_time_compare, salted_hmac
from django.utils.safestring import SafeData, mark_safe


class MessageEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
    """
    Compactly serialize instances of the ``Message`` class as JSON.
    """
    message_key = '__json_message'

    def default(self, obj):
        if isinstance(obj, Message):
            # Using 0/1 here instead of False/True to produce more compact json
            is_safedata = 1 if isinstance(obj.message, SafeData) else 0
            message = [self.message_key, is_safedata, obj.level, obj.message]
            if obj.extra_tags:
                message.append(obj.extra_tags)
            return message
        return super().default(obj)


class MessageDecoder(json.JSONDecoder):
    """
    Decode JSON that includes serialized ``Message`` instances.
    """

    def process_messages(self, obj):
        if isinstance(obj, list) and obj:
            if obj[0] == MessageEncoder.message_key:
                if obj[1]:
                    obj[3] = mark_safe(obj[3])
                return Message(*obj[2:])
            return [self.process_messages(item) for item in obj]
        if isinstance(obj, dict):
            return {key: self.process_messages(value)
                    for key, value in obj.items()}
        return obj

    def decode(self, s, **kwargs):
        decoded = super().decode(s, **kwargs)
        return self.process_messages(decoded)

    # HTTP headers. In order to leave some room for other cookies and headers,
    # restrict the session cookie to 1/2 of 4kb. See #18781.

from django.core import signing


class SessionStore(SessionBase):

    def load(self):
        """
        Load the data from the key itself instead of fetching from some
        external data store. Opposite of _get_session_key(), raise BadSignature
        if signature fails.
        """
        try:
            return signing.loads(
                self.session_key,
                serializer=self.serializer,
                # This doesn't handle non-default expiry dates, see #19201
                max_age=self.get_session_cookie_age(),
                salt='django.contrib.sessions.backends.signed_cookies',
            )
        except Exception:
            # BadSignature, ValueError, or unpickling exceptions. If any of
            # these happen, reset the session.
            self.create()
        return {}

    def create(self):
        """
        To create a new key, set the modified flag so that the cookie is set
        on the client for the current request.
        """
        self.modified = True

    def save(self, must_create=False):
        """
        To save, get the session key as a securely signed string and then set
        the modified flag so that the cookie is set on the client for the
        current request.
        """
        self._session_key = self._get_session_key()
        self.modified = True

    def exists(self, session_key=None):
        """
        This method makes sense when you're talking to a shared resource, but
        it doesn't matter when you're storing the information in the client's
        cookie.
        """
        return False

    def delete(self, session_key=None):
        """
        To delete, clear the session key and the underlying data structure
        and set the modified flag so that the cookie is set on the client for
        the current request.
        """
        self._session_key = ''
        self._session_cache = {}
        self.modified = True

    def cycle_key(self):
        """
        Keep the same data but with a new key. Call save() and it will
        automatically save a cookie with a new key at the end of the request.
        """
        self.save()

    def _get_session_key(self):
        """
        Instead of generating a random string, generate a secure url-safe
        base64-encoded string of data as our session key.
        """
        return signing.dumps(
            self._session, compress=True,
            salt='django.contrib.sessions.backends.signed_cookies',
            serializer=self.serializer,
        )

    def clear_expired(cls):

- No new method is required. The appropriate change is to broaden the exception coverage of _legacy_decode (by moving base64 decode into the try/except already present) so that any base64-related exceptions are handled in the same way as other legacy-decode errors.
- I checked other code paths that decode session-like strings:

Checkpoint 5: Final report — root cause, every location to change, and patch details

Root cause
- SessionBase._legacy_decode called base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) outside of its try/except block. When session_data is not a valid base64 ASCII string (for example, a modern signed cookie string or a malformed/tampered cookie), base64.b64decode raises binascii.Error ("Incorrect padding"), which was not handled and thus crashed request processing (500). This is exactly what the report's stacktrace shows (binascii.Error: Incorrect padding). The intended behavior for malformed legacy session data is to treat it as an empty session ({}), which other exception paths in _legacy_decode implement; the base64 call should therefore be inside that exception-handling logic.

Every location that needs to change
- Primary change (only location found in codebase):
  - File: django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py
  - Method: SessionBase._legacy_decode
  - Current behavior: base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) is called outside try/catch; binascii.Error escapes and crashes.
  - Fix: Move the base64.b64decode(...) call inside the try/except block that already wraps the subsequent processing; treat any exception from base64 decoding (binascii.Error, UnicodeEncodeError, etc.) as an invalid session and return {} (also keep existing SuspiciousOperation logging).
  - Rationale: All other exceptional conditions in _legacy_decode are already caught and handled by returning {}. base64 decoding should be treated the same because invalid session strings (including old/tampered/malformed) must not crash the app.

Patch (full replacement for the method)
- Replace existing _legacy_decode with:

def _legacy_decode(self, session_data):
    # RemovedInDjango40Warning: pre-Django 3.1 format will be invalid.
    try:
        encoded_data = base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii'))
        # could produce ValueError if there is no ':'
        hash, serialized = encoded_data.split(b':', 1)
        expected_hash = self._hash(serialized)
        if not constant_time_compare(hash.decode(), expected_hash):
            raise SuspiciousSession("Session data corrupted")
        return self.serializer().loads(serialized)
    except Exception as e:
        # ValueError, SuspiciousOperation, binascii.Error, UnicodeError,
        # unpickling exceptions. If any of these happen, just return an empty
        # dictionary (an empty session).
        if isinstance(e, SuspiciousOperation):
            logger = logging.getLogger('django.security.%s' % e.__class__.__name__)
            logger.warning(str(e))
        return {}

Notes / rationale
- Keeping a broad except Exception preserves the original behavior and ensures that any unexpected error during legacy decode (including unpickling errors for PickleSerializer) will produce an empty session rather than raising; this matches the code's documented intent (see comments in _legacy_decode).
- Alternatively, the except clause could be made explicit (except (binascii.Error, UnicodeEncodeError, ValueError, SuspiciousOperation, ...) as e:) to avoid hiding ProgrammingError, but that mirrors current code style which intentionally swallows these exceptions and returns {}. Given the code's existing pattern, minimal, targeted change is preferred.

Other places I checked (and reasons why they do not need changes)
- django/contrib/sessions/backends/db.py -> load() calls decode(s.session_data). This backend will now be safe because decode() -> _legacy_decode() will return {} instead of raising.
- django/contrib/sessions/backends/signed_cookies.py -> uses signing.loads directly in try/except and will not call _legacy_decode at all in the normal path; already robust.
- django/core/signing.py implements its own base64 decode with padding logic (b64_decode adds missing '=' padding) and does not need changes.
- No other occurrences of base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) were found in the repo.

Testing / verification steps
- Unit tests:
  - Add or update tests in tests/sessions_tests to assert that decode() returns {} for malformed session_data (non-base64 strings, incorrectly padded strings) rather than raising binascii.Error.
  - Existing tests around legacy decode behavior should continue to pass.
- Manual test (reproduce original report):
  - Insert an invalid (tampered or malformed) session_data into sessions table for a session key and perform a request that triggers db.SessionStore.load(). Before the fix, a 500 would occur with Incorrect padding; after the fix, the request should continue with an empty session (no crash).
- Regression check:
  - Ensure legitimate legacy session data still decodes correctly (remain compatible with _legacy_encode by using base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) inside the try).

Summary / final recommendation
- Apply the simple, low-risk change of moving the base64.b64decode call inside the try/except in SessionBase._legacy_decode so that malformed session_data does not crash the process and instead is treated as a cleared session.
- This is a single-line relocation of an existing call into the already-present exception handling and keeps the behavior of encoding/decoding for valid data unchanged while making the system resilient to malformed or legacy inputs (exactly what was intended by the original fallback design).

bug_report.Title: Malformed/legacy session_data can raise binascii.Error and cause 500 from db session backend
bug_report.Description: Requests can crash with an Internal Server Error (500) when the session store encounters malformed or legacy session_data that is not valid ASCII base64. The crash is observed when a browser sends an old/invalid session cookie and the database-backed session loader attempts to decode it.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py :: SessionBase._legacy_decode — The method performs base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) before entering its existing try/except block (see base.py line where encoded_data = base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii'))). This assumes session_data is an ASCII-compatible, correctly-padded base64 string. If session_data is not ASCII or is not valid base64 (for example, incorrectly padded), base64.b64decode or .encode('ascii') will raise binascii.Error or UnicodeEncodeError which are not caught by _legacy_decode and therefore propagate out of decode().

2) django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py :: SessionBase._legacy_encode/_legacy_decode — The legacy format encodes data as base64.b64encode(hash.encode() + b':' + serialized).decode('ascii'), so the decoder expects decoded bytes to have the form b'<hash>:<serialized>' and verifies expected_hash = self._hash(serialized) (then compares hash.decode() vs expected_hash). The split and subsequent verification are inside _legacy_decode's try/except (so ValueError from a missing ':' or serializer errors are handled and result in an empty session). The uncovered problem is that base64 decoding (and ASCII encoding of the input) is performed before that try/except, so base64-related or encoding errors escape handling.

3) django/contrib/sessions/backends/db.py :: SessionStore.load — The DB session loader calls self.decode(s.session_data) if a non-expired session row is found (return self.decode(s.session_data) if s else {}). There is no try/except around decode() here, so any exception propagated from SessionBase.decode/_legacy_decode (including binascii.Error from base64 decoding) will bubble up into request handling and can trigger a 500.

4) django/contrib/sessions/backends/signed_cookies.py :: SessionStore.load (contrast) — The signed_cookies backend wraps signing.loads(...) in a try/except and resets the session on error (calls create() and returns {}), so malformed input there does not produce an uncaught binascii.Error. Additionally, django/core/signing.py uses urlsafe base64 decoding with explicit padding handling, so signing.loads raises BadSignature rather than raw binascii.Error for signature failures. This contrast shows the exposure is specific to backends that rely on the legacy decode path (i.e., persist raw legacy base64 strings and call SessionBase.decode on them).

5) Scope: Any backend that loads persisted session_data and calls SessionBase.decode (and therefore may fall back to _legacy_decode) is potentially affected; the db backend is a confirmed example because it directly returns decode(s.session_data) without guarding decode() exceptions.
StepsToReproduce: Run a Django site configured to use the database session backend.

Insert or modify a session row in the django_session table so that session_data is an invalid or malformed base64 string (for example, a truncated or incorrectly-padded string that will cause base64.b64decode(...).a2b_base64 to raise binascii.Error).
Send a request to the site with the cookie corresponding to that session (visit any page that triggers session access, e.g. a protected page).

Observe an Internal Server Error (500) and a traceback showing binascii.Error: Incorrect padding originating from base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) during SessionBase._legacy_decode, bubbling through SessionStore.load.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a request includes malformed or legacy session data, the server should not crash. The session should be treated as empty or invalid (the user appears anonymous or is asked to re-authenticate) and the page should render normally without a 500 caused by session decoding.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Requests that include certain malformed or legacy session cookies cause a 500 Internal Server Error. The server traceback shows binascii.Error: Incorrect padding raised by base64.b64decode(session_data.encode('ascii')) inside SessionBase._legacy_decode; this exception propagates through db.SessionStore.load into request handling and aborts the request (e.g. login attempts from the affected browser fail).

Checkpoint 5: Final report — root cause and complete fix

Root cause (concise):
- When copying fields from an abstract base model to concrete subclasses, ModelBase uses copy.deepcopy(field). deepcopy preserves Field.creation_counter. Field.__eq__ / __hash__ / __lt__ were implemented using only creation_counter. As a result, deepcopied fields attached to different models but originating from the same abstract base ended up with identical creation_counter and therefore compared equal and hashed the same. That caused surprising deduplication when fields from different models were placed into shared sets or otherwise compared.

Every location that needs to change:
- Primary change: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py — modify Field.__eq__, Field.__lt__, Field.__hash__ to include model identity (if any) as part of equality/hash and use model as a tie-breaker in ordering.

What the current code does, what assumption it encodes, and what the fix should be:

- Current code (Field.__eq__):
  - Does: return self.creation_counter == other.creation_counter.
  - Assumption: creation_counter alone uniquely identifies a field instance.
  - Fix: Require both creation_counter equality and identical model to report equality. If model absent on either field, fall back to comparing creation_counter == creation_counter only when both models are None (this preserves legacy behavior for unattached fields).

- Current code (Field.__lt__):
  - Does: compare self.creation_counter < other.creation_counter.
  - Assumption: creation_counter order is sufficient for deterministic ordering.
  - Problems: deep-copied fields from abstract base can have identical creation_counter, causing ordering to be arbitrary or equality collisions.
  - Fix: Preserve creation_counter as primary ordering key. If creation_counters are equal, tie-break by model (None sorts earlier than actual models; otherwise compare model label_lower; fallback to id()) to produce a deterministic order that distinguishes fields attached to different models.

- Current code (Field.__hash__):
  - Does: return hash(self.creation_counter).
  - Assumption: creation_counter uniquely identifies field for hashing.
  - Fix: return hash((self.creation_counter, getattr(self, 'model', None))) so that fields attached to different models hash differently.

Any hardcoded values that need to become dynamic:
- The only hardcoded "constant" relevant to this bug is the use of creation_counter as sole identity. We do not remove creation_counter; rather we treat it as the primary key and make equality/hash/ordering use model identity as additional key where necessary. No other numeric constants in component classes need to change.

Any methods that need to be added or overridden:

bug_report.Title: Abstract model fields compare equal across different concrete models (creation_counter-only comparison)
bug_report.Description: When a Field is declared on an abstract model and copied into multiple concrete subclasses, the resulting Field instances can compare equal and hash-equal, causing deduplication/collisions (for example, putting the two fields into a set yields length 1). This is visible when using sets, dicts, or other consumers that rely on equality, hashing, or deterministic ordering of Field instances.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Field equality uses creation_counter only (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__eq__). The implementation returns self.creation_counter == other.creation_counter when comparing two Field instances (see lines where __eq__ returns creation_counter equality). This encodes the incorrect assumption that creation_counter alone is a unique identity for a Field instance.

2) Field ordering uses creation_counter only (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__lt__). The implementation compares self.creation_counter < other.creation_counter. This encodes the incorrect assumption that creation_counter defines a total order with no ties; ties can occur when a field is deep-copied into multiple concrete models.

3) Field hashing uses creation_counter only (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.__hash__). The implementation returns hash(self.creation_counter), so two distinct Field instances with the same creation_counter will hash-equal and collide in sets/dicts.

4) Abstract-base fields are deep-copied into concrete subclasses (django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase.__new__). During class creation, fields from abstract bases are copied via copy.deepcopy(field) and added to the concrete class (new_field = copy.deepcopy(field); new_class.add_to_class(field.name, new_field)). Because Field.__copy__/__deepcopy__ copies the instance __dict__, the creation_counter value is preserved on the copy. As a result, separate Field instances attached to different models can carry identical creation_counter values.

In relational terms (as found during investigation): equality should require creation_counter equality AND identical attached-model identity (i.e., the model referenced by the field instance). Hashing should incorporate both creation_counter and the attached-model identity to avoid collisions for deep-copied fields. Ordering semantics should preserve creation_counter as the primary key for order but provide a deterministic tie-breaker based on model identity when creation_counters are equal (for example comparing model labels or a stable model identity). The draft's statement that the model class is omitted is supported by the code.

- Why I checked this: the draft claims there is no public build_app_dict method.

- Analysis: The codebase does not define a public AdminSite.build_app_dict method. The draft's claim is correct.

3) Verify internal callers and template consumers
- Why I checked this: the draft claims get_app_list and app_index call the private builder, and templates only reference a limited set of model dict keys.
- What I fetched:
  - get_app_list calls self._build_app_dict(request) (django/contrib/admin/sites.py, line 506).
  - app_index calls self._build_app_dict(request, app_label) (django/contrib/admin/sites.py, line 537).
  - each_context uses get_app_list to populate 'available_apps' (django/contrib/admin/sites.py, lines 312–318).
  - index and app_index add the produced app_list/app_dict into the TemplateResponse context (index: lines 522–534; app_index: lines 536–556).
  - Template: django/contrib/admin/templates/admin/app_list.html references only these per-model keys: model.object_name, model.name, model.admin_url, model.add_url, model.view_only (template lines 10–32).
- Analysis: Internal callers in admin site code rely on the structure returned by _build_app_dict. The template and these callers only use the human-readable/URL/perms fields — so adding a new 'model' key would be additive (not required by existing core templates).

4) Verify permission-related logic referenced by _build_app_dict
- Why I checked this: _build_app_dict uses model_admin.has_module_permission and model_admin.get_model_perms, which affects which models are included.
- What I fetched:
  - _build_app_dict invokes model_admin.has_module_permission(request) and model_admin.get_model_perms(request) (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 451 and 455).
  - ModelAdmin.get_model_perms implementation returns the dict keys {'add','change','delete','view'} from has_* methods (django/contrib/admin/options.py lines 653–664).

- Analysis: The permission logic is separate from the structure of model_dict. Adding a 'model' key would not change how permissions are computed; the draft's references to the permission methods are accurate.

5) Verify claims about serialization checks / risk of adding non-serializable objects
- Why I checked this: the draft asserts there are no checks preventing non-JSON-serializable values in app_list and adding a class object may break external consumers that serialize the app_list.
- What I inspected:
  - _build_app_dict returns Python dicts containing strings, booleans, None, and perms dicts (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 433–499).
  - each_context places get_app_list(request) into template context as 'available_apps' and index/app_index place 'app_list' into TemplateResponse contexts (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 312–318, 524–531, 542–549). There is no serialization step in these methods.
- Analysis: The core admin producers (the methods above) do not perform any JSON serialization of app_list; they construct dicts and pass them to template rendering. Therefore, the statement that no explicit checks exist in the admin site producers is supported. However, whether adding a non-serializable value would break external consumers depends on external code (e.g., third-party code or user code that calls admin.site.get_app_list(request) and JSON-dumps it). The draft's risk statement is plausible but not something provable from core code alone; there is no evidence in Django core that app_list is serialized internally, so any serialization breakage would be a risk to external consumers, not an observed core failure.

bug_report.Title: AdminSite app_list per-model dicts omit Model class (no public build_app_dict API)
bug_report.Description: In the Django admin, the app_list context (produced by AdminSite._build_app_dict and returned by get_app_list / used by app_index) constructs per-model dictionaries that do not include the actual Model class object. The method that builds this structure is private (_build_app_dict) and there is no public build_app_dict API.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) AdminSite._build_app_dict (django/contrib/admin/sites.py::AdminSite._build_app_dict) constructs per-model dictionaries containing only serialized fields: 'name', 'object_name', 'perms', 'admin_url', and 'add_url' (and optionally 'view_only'). The code creating each model_dict does not include or expose the Model class object (the 'model' key is absent). Evidence: model_dict is constructed as a dict with those keys and no 'model' key (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 462–469, 472–480).

2) There is no public AdminSite.build_app_dict API in the codebase; the only builder present is the private _build_app_dict. Call sites within the admin use this private method (get_app_list and app_index call _build_app_dict). Location: django/contrib/admin/sites.py (definition at line 433; calls at lines 506 and 537). Search shows no public build_app_dict function defined in the repository.

3) Internal callers and templates encode the assumption that model dicts only need human-readable/URL/permission keys. The admin templates and AdminSite consumers reference only fields such as model.name, model.object_name, model.admin_url, model.add_url, and model.view_only (django/contrib/admin/templates/admin/app_list.html lines 10–32), and admin methods sort and return the produced dicts without expecting a 'model' key (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 506–515, 537–546).

4) Permission-related methods are used to determine which models appear in the app list; these methods operate on ModelAdmin internals and do not require a 'model' key in the produced dict. _build_app_dict calls model_admin.has_module_permission(request) and model_admin.get_model_perms(request) to decide inclusion and to populate the 'perms' dict (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 451 and 455; ModelAdmin.get_model_perms implementation in django/contrib/admin/options.py lines 653–664).

5) The admin producers do not perform or enforce serialization of the app_list or its model entries. _build_app_dict returns Python dicts which are placed into template contexts (each_context, index, and app_index pass the result into TemplateResponse), and there are no checks in these methods preventing non-JSON-serializable values from being present in the context (django/contrib/admin/sites.py lines 312–318, 524–531, 542–549). Consequently, if a Model class object were added directly into each model dict, external consumers that attempt to JSON-serialize or otherwise export the app_list could encounter failures — this is a compatibility risk for external code rather than an observed core error.
StepsToReproduce: Run a Django project with the admin enabled and log in as a staff/superuser.
Open the admin index (site root at /admin/) or the app-specific index.
Inspect the app list data produced by the admin (for example, call admin.site.get_app_list(request) from a view or shell with a RequestFactory request) and examine each app['models'] entry.
Observe that each model dictionary contains keys like 'name', 'object_name', 'perms', 'admin_url', 'add_url' but does not include a 'model' key referencing the Model class.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For each model entry in the admin app list (the app_list used by index and app_index), the context returned to views/templates should provide a way for consumers to access the actual Model class when desired (i.e., each model entry should expose the model object or otherwise make the class available through a supported API), so custom admin views and template-level consumers can use the class directly.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Per-model dictionaries produced for the admin app list omit the Model class (no 'model' key). The builder method that creates these dicts is private (_build_app_dict) and there is no public AdminSite.build_app_dict API.

import os
import sys
from io import StringIO

from django.apps import apps
from django.conf import settings
from django.core import serializers
from django.db import router
from django.db.transaction import atomic

# The prefix to put on the default database name when creating
# the test database.
TEST_DATABASE_PREFIX = 'test_'


class BaseDatabaseCreation:
    """
    Encapsulate backend-specific differences pertaining to creation and
    destruction of the test database.
    """
    def __init__(self, connection):
        self.connection = connection

    def _nodb_cursor(self):
        return self.connection._nodb_cursor()

    def log(self, msg):
        sys.stderr.write(msg + os.linesep)

    def create_test_db(self, verbosity=1, autoclobber=False, serialize=True, keepdb=False):
        """
        Create a test database, prompting the user for confirmation if the
        database already exists. Return the name of the test database created.
        """
        # Don't import django.core.management if it isn't needed.
        from django.core.management import call_command

        test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name()

        if verbosity >= 1:
            action = 'Creating'
            if keepdb:
                action = "Using existing"

            self.log('%s test database for alias %s...' % (
                action,
                self._get_database_display_str(verbosity, test_database_name),
            ))

        # We could skip this call if keepdb is True, but we instead
        # give it the keepdb param. This is to handle the case
        # where the test DB doesn't exist, in which case we need to
        # create it, then just not destroy it. If we instead skip
        # this, we will get an exception.
        self._create_test_db(verbosity, autoclobber, keepdb)

        self.connection.close()
        settings.DATABASES[self.connection.alias]["NAME"] = test_database_name
        self.connection.settings_dict["NAME"] = test_database_name

        if self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['MIGRATE']:
            # We report migrate messages at one level lower than that
            # requested. This ensures we don't get flooded with messages during
            # testing (unless you really ask to be flooded).
            call_command(
                'migrate',
                verbosity=max(verbosity - 1, 0),
                interactive=False,
                database=self.connection.alias,
                run_syncdb=True,
            )

        # We then serialize the current state of the database into a string
        # and store it on the connection. This slightly horrific process is so people
        # who are testing on databases without transactions or who are using
        # a TransactionTestCase still get a clean database on every test run.
        if serialize:
            self.connection._test_serialized_contents = self.serialize_db_to_string()

        call_command('createcachetable', database=self.connection.alias)

        # Ensure a connection for the side effect of initializing the test database.
        self.connection.ensure_connection()

        return test_database_name

    def set_as_test_mirror(self, primary_settings_dict):
        """
        Set this database up to be used in testing as a mirror of a primary
        database whose settings are given.
        """
        self.connection.settings_dict['NAME'] = primary_settings_dict['NAME']

    def serialize_db_to_string(self):

        Serialize all data in the database into a JSON string.
        Designed only for test runner usage; will not handle large
        amounts of data.
        """
        # Iteratively return every object for all models to serialize.
        def get_objects():
            from django.db.migrations.loader import MigrationLoader
            loader = MigrationLoader(self.connection)
            for app_config in apps.get_app_configs():
                if (
                    app_config.models_module is not None and
                    app_config.label in loader.migrated_apps and
                    app_config.name not in settings.TEST_NON_SERIALIZED_APPS
                ):
                    for model in app_config.get_models():
                        if (
                            model._meta.can_migrate(self.connection) and
                            router.allow_migrate_model(self.connection.alias, model)
                        ):
                            queryset = model._default_manager.using(
                                self.connection.alias,
                            ).order_by(model._meta.pk.name)

        out = StringIO()
        serializers.serialize("json", get_objects(), indent=None, stream=out)
        return out.getvalue()

    def deserialize_db_from_string(self, data):
        """

        the serialize_db_to_string() method.
        """
        data = StringIO(data)
        table_names = set()

        with atomic(using=self.connection.alias):

            # support deferred checks.
            with self.connection.constraint_checks_disabled():

            # because constraint checks were disabled.
            self.connection.check_constraints(table_names=table_names)

    def _get_database_display_str(self, verbosity, database_name):

        Return display string for a database for use in various actions.
        """
        return "'%s'%s" % (
            self.connection.alias,
            (" ('%s')" % database_name) if verbosity >= 2 else '',
        )

    def _get_test_db_name(self):

        created. Only useful when called from create_test_db() and
        _create_test_db() and when no external munging is done with the 'NAME'
        settings.
        """
        if self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['NAME']:
            return self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['NAME']
        return TEST_DATABASE_PREFIX + self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']

        cursor.execute('CREATE DATABASE %(dbname)s %(suffix)s' % parameters)

        """
        test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name()
