bug_report.Title: Label for ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget points to non-labelable element
bug_report.Description: In the admin / user-change form, the <label> for the ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget includes a for="id_..." attribute that points at a non-labelable element. The widget renders static summary markup (a <div> in tests) rather than a labelable form control, so the label's for attribute references an element that cannot be labelled.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget (django/contrib/auth/forms.py::ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget) renders static summary markup (tests show a <div id="id_password">) and sets read_only = True, but the class does not define an id_for_label method. Incorrect assumption encoded: the widget is treated as if it maps to a single labelable control (location: django/contrib/auth/forms.py: class ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget).

2) Base Widget.id_for_label (django/forms/widgets.py::Widget.id_for_label) returns the supplied id_ by default (implementation: def id_for_label(self, id_): return id_). Incorrect assumption encoded: returning id_ signals that associating a <label for="..."> is appropriate for every widget (location: django/forms/widgets.py: Widget.id_for_label).

3) BoundField.label_tag (django/forms/boundfield.py::BoundField.label_tag) computes an id for the field and calls widget.id_for_label(id_); if that call returns a truthy value, label_tag emits a for="..." attribute. Relationship used: id_ = widget.attrs.get('id') or self.auto_id; id_for_label = widget.id_for_label(id_); if id_for_label: include for=id_for_label. Because the base id_for_label returns id_ by default, label_tag will produce a for attribute even when the widget's rendered markup is non-labelable (location: django/forms/boundfield.py: BoundField.label_tag).

4) AdminReadonlyField (django/contrib/admin/helpers.py::AdminReadonlyField) contains a path that treats read-only widgets specially (it renders widget.render(...) directly and emits a label without a for attribute). However, UserChangeForm places the password field in ordinary form fieldsets (UserAdmin uses UserChangeForm as its form), so the BoundField.label_tag path can be used for the password field in the admin UI. Incorrect assumption exposed: having an admin-specific readonly rendering path does not guarantee that read_only widgets will always be rendered via that path (location: django/contrib/admin/helpers.py: AdminReadonlyField and django/contrib/auth/admin.py: UserAdmin setup).

5) Investigation gap: the widget template auth/widgets/read_only_password_hash.html was not present in the checked-out repository tree used for this investigation; tests assert the widget renders a <div id="id_password">, but the template source was not located here to independently confirm its literal markup (template reference: django/contrib/auth/forms.py: template_name = 'auth/widgets/read_only_password_hash.html').
StepsToReproduce: In a Django project with contrib.auth enabled, open the admin User change page for a user and inspect the HTML for the password field label (or instantiate a Form using ReadOnlyPasswordHashField and call f['password'].label_tag()).
Observe the generated <label> element for the password field and note whether it includes a for="id_password" attribute.
Inspect the element with that id and confirm it is a non-labelable element (for example, <div id="id_password">...).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a field's widget does not render a labelable control, the rendered <label> for that field should not include a for="..." attribute that references a non-labelable element; the label should be rendered without an associated for attribute.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The label includes for="id_password" (or similar), referencing the element produced by ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget (tests show a <div id="id_password">), resulting in a label for attribute that points at a non-labelable element.

bug_report.Title: BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores per-option id from ChoiceWidget.create_option, causing label 'for' mismatch for choice subwidgets
bug_report.Description: When rendering choice-based subwidgets (ChoiceWidget subclasses such as CheckboxSelectMultiple and RadioSelect), labels' for attributes can point to a different id than the input elements. The option dicts produced for subwidgets include per-option ids (derived from a base id when provided), but BoundWidget.id_for_label reconstructs an id from the widget name and index instead of using the per-option id stored in the option dict's attrs.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BoundWidget.id_for_label unconditionally reconstructs an id using the literal pattern 'id_%s_%s' % (self.data['name'], self.data['index']) and does not consult the option dict's attrs (where ChoiceWidget.create_option stores per-option ids). File/class/method: django/forms/boundfield.py: BoundWidget.id_for_label (lines 279-281: return 'id_%s_%s' % (self.data['name'], self.data['index'])).

2) BoundField.subwidgets computes a base id and passes it into choice subwidgets via attrs so per-option ids will be produced downstream when a base id exists. File/class/method: django/forms/boundfield.py: BoundField.subwidgets (lines 45-51: id_ = self.field.widget.attrs.get('id') or self.auto_id; attrs = {'id': id_} if id_ else {}; ... for widget in self.field.widget.subwidgets(..., attrs=attrs)).

3) ChoiceWidget.create_option is the authoritative producer of per-option ids: it builds option_attrs = self.build_attrs(self.attrs, attrs) and, if 'id' is present in option_attrs, sets option_attrs['id'] = self.id_for_label(option_attrs['id'], index) (i.e. base-id + '_' + index when add_id_index is True) and stores that id in the returned option dict's 'attrs'. File/class/method: django/forms/widgets.py: ChoiceWidget.create_option and ChoiceWidget.id_for_label (lines 621-628 and 645-652).

4) Templates expect the per-option id to be available at widget.attrs.id when rendering labels (input_option.html uses {% if widget.attrs.id %} for="{{ widget.attrs.id }}" {% endif %}). File: django/forms/templates/django/forms/widgets/input_option.html.

5) The consumer (BoundWidget.id_for_label) therefore violates the producer/consumer expectation: the authoritative id for an option lives in the option dict's attrs['id'] (created by ChoiceWidget.create_option), but BoundWidget.id_for_label ignores that value and reconstructs a legacy id string. The current hardcoded reconstruction ('id_%s_%s') is only correct under the particular assumption that the auto-generated base id uses the exact 'id_%s' pattern; when the base id differs (for example when widget.attrs['id'] or form.auto_id are set to a different format), label for attributes will not match input ids. File/class/method: django/forms/boundfield.py: BoundWidget.id_for_label (lines 279-281) and django/forms/widgets.py: ChoiceWidget.create_option (lines 621-628).
StepsToReproduce: Create a Form with a ChoiceField or MultipleChoiceField rendered with a choice widget that produces subwidgets (e.g. CheckboxSelectMultiple or RadioSelect).

Provide a base id so ChoiceWidget.create_option will produce per-option ids: either set form.auto_id to a non-default value that includes the field name or pass attrs={'id': '<base-id>'} to the widget.
Render the form or the specific field and inspect the generated HTML for the input elements and their labels.

Compare each input element's id attribute (from the rendered input element or widget.attrs.id in the template context) with the corresponding label's for attribute. Labels will use a reconstructed id ('id_<name>_<index>') while inputs use the per-option id produced by ChoiceWidget.create_option (base-id + '_' + index) when a base id was provided.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: For choice-based subwidgets, each label's for attribute matches the input element's id. When a base id is provided (via form.auto_id or widget.attrs['id']), per-option ids should be derived from that base id (e.g. base-id + '_' + index) and labels should reference those per-option ids.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Labels for choice subwidgets use an id reconstructed as 'id_<name>_<index>' (from BoundWidget.id_for_label) instead of the per-option id stored in widget.attrs.id by ChoiceWidget.create_option, causing the label for attribute to point to a different id than the corresponding input element when a non-default base id is present.

def _get_app_label_and_model_name(model, app_label=''):
    if isinstance(model, str):
        split = model.split('.', 1)
        return tuple(split) if len(split) == 2 else (app_label, split[0])
    else:
        return model._meta.app_label, model._meta.model_name


def _get_related_models(m):
    """Return all models that have a direct relationship to the given model."""
    related_models = [
        subclass for subclass in m.__subclasses__()
        if issubclass(subclass, models.Model)
    ]
    related_fields_models = set()
    for f in m._meta.get_fields(include_parents=True, include_hidden=True):
        if f.is_relation and f.related_model is not None and not isinstance(f.related_model, str):
            related_fields_models.add(f.model)
            related_models.append(f.related_model)
    # Reverse accessors of foreign keys to proxy models are attached to their
    # concrete proxied model.
    opts = m._meta
    if opts.proxy and m in related_fields_models:
        related_models.append(opts.concrete_model)
    return related_models


def get_related_models_tuples(model):
    """
    Return a list of typical (app_label, model_name) tuples for all related
    models for the given model.
    """
    return {
        (rel_mod._meta.app_label, rel_mod._meta.model_name)
        for rel_mod in _get_related_models(model)
    }


def get_related_models_recursive(model):
    """
    Return all models that have a direct or indirect relationship
    to the given model.

    Relationships are either defined by explicit relational fields, like
    ForeignKey, ManyToManyField or OneToOneField, or by inheriting from another
    model (a superclass is related to its subclasses, but not vice versa). Note,
    however, that a model inheriting from a concrete model is also related to
    its superclass through the implicit *_ptr OneToOneField on the subclass.
    """
    seen = set()
    queue = _get_related_models(model)
    for rel_mod in queue:
        rel_app_label, rel_model_name = rel_mod._meta.app_label, rel_mod._meta.model_name
        if (rel_app_label, rel_model_name) in seen:
            continue
        seen.add((rel_app_label, rel_model_name))
        queue.extend(_get_related_models(rel_mod))
    return seen - {(model._meta.app_label, model._meta.model_name)}

bug_report.Title: makemigrations generates migration that references models.Model but omits 'from django.db import models' causing NameError
bug_report.Description: makemigrations can produce a migration file whose bases tuple contains models.Model (for example: bases=(app.models.MyMixin, models.Model)) but the generated file does not include the import 'from django.db import models', causing a NameError when the migration module is imported.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) TypeSerializer special-case omits required import for the type object models.Model: In django/db/migrations/serializer.py, TypeSerializer.serialize special_cases contains the tuple (models.Model, "models.Model", []) so serializing the type object models.Model returns ("models.Model", set()) — i.e. the textual name is emitted but no "from django.db import models" import is reported. (See django/db/migrations/serializer.py:275-281.)

2) MigrationWriter relies on serializer-reported imports and will not synthesize the models import: In django/db/migrations/writer.py, MigrationWriter.as_string only merges a models import into the migrations import when the literal "from django.db import models" is present in the collected imports; otherwise it emits only "from django.db import migrations". Because the serializer did not report the models import, the writer omits it. (See django/db/migrations/writer.py:165-171.)

3) The bug is exposed when CreateModel serializes non-default bases: CreateModel sets self.bases = bases or (models.Model,) and only includes bases in its deconstructed kwargs when bases != (models.Model,), so a model inheriting a mixin plus models.Model will trigger serialization of the type object models.Model and therefore invoke TypeSerializer. That serialization path is where the missing import surfaces. (See django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:46-50 and 62-71.)

4) Inconsistent serialization patterns: DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path does include the import for django.db.models (it returns name "models.<ClassName>" together with imports {"from django.db import models"} when path.module == "django.db.models"), demonstrating that some serializers add the models import while TypeSerializer's special-case does not. This inconsistency explains why some serialized values produce the models import while others (the type object models.Model via TypeSerializer) do not. Checkpoint 4: Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (concrete code changes):
- In django/forms/formsets.py, update BaseFormSet.full_clean so that the formset-level non-form ErrorList instances include the CSS class marker 'nonform' (analogous to forms' use of 'nonfield').

Concretely, change:

1) At start of full_clean():
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class()
   -> to:
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(error_class='nonform')

2) In the except ValidationError handling where a ValidationError from self.clean() is converted to an ErrorList:
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(e.error_list)
   -> to:
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(e.error_list, error_class='nonform')

Rationale:
- ErrorList.__init__(..., error_class=None) accepts error_class keyword and composes the CSS class string. For forms, non-field errors are created using error_class='nonfield', so we mirror that pattern for formsets using 'nonform'. This allows custom ErrorList implementations to detect 'nonform' and render differently from 'nonfield'. The change is small, localized, and consistent with how forms add the 'nonfield' class.

Now I will challenge this fix across the checklist:

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- Current assumption: BaseFormSet non-form errors do not need to be distinct, i.e., they can remain plain ErrorList instances with the default 'errorlist' class; or there is no separate CSS marker for formset-level errors. My fix changes that by assuming formset-level errors should be distinguishable and by encoding that distinction in the CSS class 'nonform'.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- From the component classes I inspected:
  - ErrorList uses 'errorlist' as the base CSS class (hardcoded in ErrorList.__init__). That remains correct.
  - The string 'nonfield' is used by BaseForm (hardcoded in forms.py) to mark non-field errors at form level. That remains correct and unmodified.
  - There are no numeric hardcoded constants in ErrorList or NumberInput affecting this feature.
- If the assumption (we should mark formset non-form errors) is now true, the string 'nonform' must be added (and is not present anywhere else). There's no other hardcoded value that depends on 'nonform'. So the only new hardcoded value is the string 'nonform' passed to ErrorList; it is correct and necessary to implement the requested behavior.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- I checked complementary operations that might depend on how non-form errors are created or read:
  - BaseForm.non_field_errors() constructs ErrorList(error_class='nonfield') for form-level non-field errors. No change needed.
  - Any code that reads formset.non_form_errors() treats it as a list of error messages (ErrorList is a list subclass). Our change does not change the contents of the list, its type, or membership behavior. It only changes the CSS class used when the ErrorList is rendered as HTML.
  - The test helpers in django/test/testcases.py (assertFormsetError) work by calling non_form_errors() and checking membership or emptiness — they do not inspect HTML classes. So they continue to work.
  - Admin code: in django/contrib/admin/helpers.py, AdminErrorList extends forms.utils.ErrorList and in __init__ it extends inline_formset.non_form_errors() into the admin ErrorList (lines 421–431). That is the same behavior as before for 'nonfield' vs 'nonform' and is unchanged by this fix.
  - Anywhere code expects the ErrorList for non-form errors to be instantiated without keyword arguments will still work: the default error_class being ErrorList is still called sometimes without kwargs, but BaseForm and BaseFormSet already call error_class(...) with keyword argument 'nonfield' or will now call it with 'nonform' when initializing non-field/non-form errors. Custom error_class implementations should (already) accept an optional error_class argument because BaseForm uses it too. This fix does not introduce any new parameter type to ErrorList beyond what BaseForm already uses.

Concrete substitution trace for any parent complementary method:
- There is no parent class to BaseFormSet to re-evaluate, but we checked BaseForm methods that do the reverse (forms create non-field errors with error_class='nonfield'). BaseFormSet will now create non-form errors with error_class='nonform'. All code that uses these ErrorList instances (rendering, membership checks) will behave the same except rendering will include the extra CSS class.

4d) "Does every existing method still work?"
- Methods in BaseFormSet affected or related:
  - __init__: unaffected. It still stores self.error_class argument (default ErrorList).
  - _construct_form: unaffected (passes 'error_class': self.error_class to individual forms).
  - full_clean: we only change how _non_form_errors is constructed (add error_class='nonform'); functional behavior of validation unchanged. Both empty initialization and the exception handling path are adjusted.
  - non_form_errors: unaffected (still calls full_clean if needed and returns _non_form_errors).
  - is_valid, total_error_count: unaffected (they use len(non_form_errors()) etc).
  - add_fields, rendering methods: unaffected.

4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?"
- No new methods are necessary.
- I reviewed BaseForm methods that perform complementary operations (add_error sets error_class='nonfield'); BaseFormSet does not have any method equivalent to add_error for formset-level errors where callers would add messages into a keyed structure — BaseFormSet.full_clean handles that directly. No override required.

Checkpoint 5: Final report (complete analysis and exact changes)

Root cause:
- BaseForm (forms) adds a 'nonfield' CSS class to ErrorList instances for form-level non-field errors by invoking self.error_class(error_class='nonfield'). BaseFormSet (formsets), however, constructs its _non_form_errors using self.error_class() (no CSS marker) and later self.error_class(e.error_list) in the exception path. Therefore formset non-form errors are rendered as <ul class="errorlist"> (no distinguishing class), making it impossible for a custom ErrorList renderer to distinguish form-level non-field errors ('nonfield') from formset-level non-form errors.

Complete fix — every location that needs to change:
1) django/forms/formsets.py — modify BaseFormSet.full_clean in two spots.

Current code (relevant excerpt):
- Line ~335:
    self._errors = []
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class()

- Line ~383:
    except ValidationError as e:
        self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(e.error_list)

Proposed code:
- Change the initialization to include error_class='nonform':
    self._errors = []
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(error_class='nonform')

- Change the exception handling to pass error_class='nonform' also:
    except ValidationError as e:
        self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(e.error_list, error_class='nonform')

Why these changes:
- Mirror BaseForm's use of error_class='nonfield'. Ensures ErrorList.as_ul() renders <ul class="errorlist nonform"> for formset non-form errors so custom ErrorList renderers can distinguish them.

Other locations considered and why they don't need changes:
- AdminErrorList (django/contrib/admin/helpers.py): It extends inline_formset.non_form_errors() into a single ErrorList so the 'nonform' class on the original ErrorList won't be preserved in AdminErrorList's own error_class (which is the outer list), but that is consistent with current behavior for nested non-field errors. No change needed.
- Tests:
  - Tests that check the content (list membership) of formset.non_form_errors will continue to pass, because ErrorList remains a list and the content is unchanged.
  - Tests that explicitly assert rendered HTML strings for management form non-field errors (e.g. expecting '<ul class="errorlist nonfield">') refer to the ManagementForm (a Form), not BaseFormSet._non_form_errors; those expectations remain unchanged.
  - No tests in this repo currently expect 'nonform' (feature request). Adding 'nonform' may require adding tests to assert the class is present. (If upstream project wants, create tests that verify formset.non_form_errors().as_ul() includes class 'nonform'.)

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic:
- None of the existing hardcoded values need to be made dynamic. We are introducing a new hardcoded string 'nonform' (as BaseForm uses 'nonfield'), which encodes the new assumption that formset-level errors should be marked 'nonform'. That is the intended behavior.

Any methods that need to be added/overridden:
- No new methods are required. BaseFormSet.non_form_errors already returns an ErrorList; full_clean is the right place to ensure the ErrorList for non-form errors has the correct CSS class. Complementary form-side methods (add_error/non_field_errors) already exist and remain unchanged.

Patch (conceptual diff):

- File: django/forms/formsets.py
  - Change in BaseFormSet.full_clean:

    # before
    self._errors = []
    self._non_form_errors = self.error_class()
    ...
    except ValidationError as e:

Notes and rationale:
- This mirrors the pattern already used in forms: BaseForm.add_error and BaseForm.non_field_errors pass error_class='nonfield' to ErrorList so error lists for non-field errors get CSS class 'nonfield'. We implement the analogous behavior for formsets by adding 'nonform'.
- The change is minimal, local, backward-compatible (list behavior unchanged), and allows custom ErrorList subclasses to detect the 'nonform' CSS class when rendering, permitting the differentiation requested by the bug report.

Possible follow-up (optional, recommended):

bug_report.Title: FormSet non-form errors are not tagged with 'nonform' CSS class
bug_report.Description: FormSet-level (non-form) errors are rendered without a distinguishing CSS class. Forms add 'nonfield' to non-field ErrorList instances, but FormSets construct their non-form ErrorList without an equivalent 'nonform' marker, preventing renderers from distinguishing form field errors, form non-field errors, and formset non-form errors.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) django/forms/formsets.py: BaseFormSet.full_clean constructs the formset-level non-form errors using self.error_class() (initialization) and self.error_class(e.error_list) (ValidationError except path) with no error_class keyword. These two sites create the ErrorList instance(s) used for formset.non_form_errors() and therefore determine the CSS class used when rendering those errors (locations: BaseFormSet.full_clean at the initial assignment and in the except ValidationError handler). 2) django/forms/utils.py: ErrorList.__init__ and ErrorList.as_ul define the exact composition used for the rendered <ul> class attribute. ErrorList stores either 'errorlist' or 'errorlist <error_class>' (code: if error_class is None: self.error_class = 'errorlist' else: self.error_class = 'errorlist {}'.format(error_class)) and uses self.error_class as the class attribute in as_ul(), so passing error_class='nonform' would produce '<ul class="errorlist nonform">'. 3) django/forms/forms.py: BaseForm.non_field_errors and BaseForm.add_error show the established pattern that non-field/form-level error lists are constructed with an error_class kw (forms call self.error_class(error_class='nonfield')), i.e., the convention for forms is to tag non-field errors as 'nonfield'. FormSets do not currently follow that convention for formset-level non-form errors. 4) django/contrib/admin/helpers.py: AdminErrorList collects/merges errors from a form and its inline formsets by creating an ErrorList via super().__init__() (no extra marker) and then extending itself with the values of form.errors and inline formset errors (self.extend(form.errors.values()); self.extend(inline_formset.non_form_errors()); self.extend(errors_in_inline_form.values())). Because extend() iterates the supplied containers, this flattens inner ErrorList contents into the AdminErrorList. The merged AdminErrorList therefore renders as a single <ul> using the AdminErrorList instance's own error_class (default 'errorlist' here), and per-source UL wrappers (and their classes) are not preserved in that merged output. 5) Compatibility note (existing pattern): BaseForm already calls self.error_class(error_class='nonfield') when constructing non-field errors, so callers that set custom error_class types are already required to accept being constructed with an error_class kw. Nevertheless, third-party/custom ErrorList subclasses that override __init__ with incompatible signatures remain a general compatibility risk if used as an error_class. (This is a pre-existing constraint established by BaseForm usage.)
StepsToReproduce: Create a FormSet instance that produces a formset-level (non-form) error (for example, raise ValidationError in BaseFormSet.clean() or otherwise cause non_form_errors to be populated).
Render the formset non-form errors (e.g., call formset.non_form_errors().as_ul() or include {{ formset.non_form_errors }} in a template).
Inspect the resulting HTML for the <ul> element that contains the non-form errors.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: FormSet-level non-form errors are rendered with a distinguishing CSS class in addition to 'errorlist' (user-visible example: <ul class="errorlist nonform">...), so renderers can differentiate form field errors, form non-field errors, and formset non-form errors.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: FormSet non-form errors render as <ul class="errorlist"> (no 'nonform' class). Forms already render non-field errors as <ul class="errorlist nonfield">, so FormSets lack the symmetric 'nonform' marker.

class BaseIterable:
    def __init__(self, queryset, chunked_fetch=False, chunk_size=GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
        self.queryset = queryset
        self.chunked_fetch = chunked_fetch
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size


class ModelIterable(BaseIterable):
    """Iterable that yields a model instance for each row."""

    def __iter__(self):
        queryset = self.queryset
        db = queryset.db
        compiler = queryset.query.get_compiler(using=db)
        # Execute the query. This will also fill compiler.select, klass_info,
        # and annotations.
        results = compiler.execute_sql(chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size)
        select, klass_info, annotation_col_map = (compiler.select, compiler.klass_info,
                                                  compiler.annotation_col_map)
        model_cls = klass_info['model']
        select_fields = klass_info['select_fields']
        model_fields_start, model_fields_end = select_fields[0], select_fields[-1] + 1
        init_list = [f[0].target.attname
                     for f in select[model_fields_start:model_fields_end]]
        related_populators = get_related_populators(klass_info, select, db)
        known_related_objects = [
            (field, related_objs, operator.attrgetter(*[
                field.attname
                if from_field == 'self' else
                queryset.model._meta.get_field(from_field).attname
                for from_field in field.from_fields
            ])) for field, related_objs in queryset._known_related_objects.items()
        ]
        for row in compiler.results_iter(results):
            obj = model_cls.from_db(db, init_list, row[model_fields_start:model_fields_end])
            for rel_populator in related_populators:
                rel_populator.populate(row, obj)
            if annotation_col_map:
                for attr_name, col_pos in annotation_col_map.items():
                    setattr(obj, attr_name, row[col_pos])

            # Add the known related objects to the model.
            for field, rel_objs, rel_getter in known_related_objects:
                # Avoid overwriting objects loaded by, e.g., select_related().
                if field.is_cached(obj):
                    continue
                rel_obj_id = rel_getter(obj)
                try:
                    rel_obj = rel_objs[rel_obj_id]
                except KeyError:
                    pass  # May happen in qs1 | qs2 scenarios.
                else:
                    setattr(obj, field.name, rel_obj)

    """
    Iterable returned by QuerySet.values() that yields a dict for each row.
    """

    def __iter__(self):
        queryset = self.queryset
        query = queryset.query
        compiler = query.get_compiler(queryset.db)

        # extra(select=...) cols are always at the start of the row.
        names = [
            *query.extra_select,
            *query.values_select,
            *query.annotation_select,
        ]
        indexes = range(len(names))
        for row in compiler.results_iter(chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size):
            yield {names[i]: row[i] for i in indexes}


class ValuesListIterable(BaseIterable):
    """
    Iterable returned by QuerySet.values_list(flat=False) that yields a tuple
    for each row.
    """

    def __iter__(self):
        queryset = self.queryset
        query = queryset.query
        compiler = query.get_compiler(queryset.db)

        if queryset._fields:
            # extra(select=...) cols are always at the start of the row.
            names = [
                *query.extra_select,
                *query.values_select,
                *query.annotation_select,
            ]
            fields = [*queryset._fields, *(f for f in query.annotation_select if f not in queryset._fields)]
            if fields != names:
                # Reorder according to fields.
                index_map = {name: idx for idx, name in enumerate(names)}
                rowfactory = operator.itemgetter(*[index_map[f] for f in fields])
                return map(
                    rowfactory,
                    compiler.results_iter(chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size)
                )
        return compiler.results_iter(tuple_expected=True, chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size)


class NamedValuesListIterable(ValuesListIterable):
    """
    Iterable returned by QuerySet.values_list(named=True) that yields a
    namedtuple for each row.
    """

    def __iter__(self):
        queryset = self.queryset
        if queryset._fields:
            names = queryset._fields
        else:
            query = queryset.query
            names = [*query.extra_select, *query.values_select, *query.annotation_select]
        tuple_class = create_namedtuple_class(*names)
        new = tuple.__new__
        for row in super().__iter__():
            yield new(tuple_class, row)

    def __iter__(self):

        compiler = queryset.query.get_compiler(queryset.db)
        for row in compiler.results_iter(chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size):
